questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D) 48. This is an Algebra question testing Linear functions, rated easy. You are given a linear equation that models a car's speed over time and asked to evaluate it at a specific time.

Core Concepts

  • A linear equation in the form \(s = b + mt\) relates an output (here speed \(s\)) to an input (here time \(t\)). The number \(b\) is the starting value when \(t = 0\), and \(m\) is the rate of change per unit of \(t\).
  • To find the output at a specific input value, you substitute that value in place of the variable and simplify using order of operations (multiply before you add).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Start with the given equation: \(s = 40 + 2t\).
  • The question asks for the speed \(4\) seconds after the car began to accelerate, so let \(t = 4\).
  • Substitute \(t = 4\): \(s = 40 + 2(4)\).
  • Multiply first: \(2 \times 4 = 8\), giving \(s = 40 + 8\).
  • Add: \(s = 48\).

So the speed after \(4\) seconds is \(48\) miles per hour.

Why Each Answer

  • A) 40 — Trap: ignores the time term. This is the starting speed at \(t = 0\) (the constant \(40\)), not the speed after \(4\) seconds.
  • B) 42 — Trap: adds \(t\) once instead of \(2t\). This treats the rate as \(1\) per second (\(40 + 2 = 42\) or \(40 + t\)), misreading the coefficient.
  • C) 44 — Trap: forgets to multiply by the coefficient \(2\), computing \(40 + 4 = 44\) instead of \(40 + 2(4)\).
  • D) 48 — Correct: \(40 + 2(4) = 40 + 8 = 48\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a question gives you an equation and a specific value, just plug in and simplify carefully, doing all multiplication before addition. A quick check: type \(40 + 2 \cdot 4\) into Desmos or any calculator to confirm \(48\) instantly.
questions.question_text: The equation gives the speed \(s\), in miles per hour, of a certain car \(t\) seconds after it began to accelerate. What is the speed, in miles per hour, of the car \(4\) seconds after it began to accelerate?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is C: \(8^2 + b^2 = 20^2\). This is a Geometry and Trigonometry item (skill: Right triangles and trigonometry), difficulty easy.

Core Concepts A right triangle is a triangle containing one 90-degree angle. The two sides that form the right angle are the legs; the side opposite the right angle (the longest side) is the hypotenuse. The Pythagorean theorem states that for a right triangle with legs \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\), the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs: \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown Read the figure: the small square at the bottom-right vertex marks the right angle, so the two sides meeting there are the legs. One leg is the vertical side labeled \(8\); the other leg is the horizontal side labeled \(b\). The side opposite the right angle is the slanted side labeled \(20\), so \(20\) is the hypotenuse. Substitute the legs \(8\) and \(b\) and the hypotenuse \(20\) into \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\): \(8^2 + b^2 = 20^2\). That equation is choice C.

Why Each Answer Choice C is correct because it places the two legs' squares on one side and the hypotenuse's square on the other, exactly as the Pythagorean theorem requires. Choice A (\(8b = 20\)) multiplies the legs and sets the product equal to the hypotenuse; this has no geometric basis (Factual error). Choice B (\(8 + b = 20\)) adds the legs linearly, but side lengths of a right triangle relate through squares, not a plain sum (slope/operation confusion). Choice D (\(8^2 - b^2 = 20^2\)) subtracts a leg's square instead of adding it; the Pythagorean theorem adds the two legs' squares, never subtracts (sign/operation error).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway Find the right-angle mark first. The side opposite it is always the hypotenuse and goes alone on the \(c^2\) side; the two sides touching the mark are the legs and their squares add. Spotting the hypotenuse instantly rules out any equation that doesn't isolate \(20^2\) as the sum of the other two squares.

questions.skill: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is D) 219. This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis item testing one-variable data distributions, specifically reading a histogram to reason about the maximum value. Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts A histogram groups numerical data into equal-width intervals called bins. The height (frequency) of each bar tells how many data values fall in that bin, where a value is counted in a bin if it is at least the left edge and less than the right edge. The maximum of a data set is its single largest value, so it must lie inside the rightmost bin that has a bar (a nonzero frequency).

Step-by-Step Breakdown Read the bins from the figure: \([0,50)\) has 5 values, \([50,100)\) has 3, \([100,150)\) has 4, \([150,200)\) has 3, and \([200,250)\) has 5. The frequencies total \(5+3+4+3+5=20\), matching the 20 lengths. The rightmost bar with data is \([200,250)\), so the largest length is at least \(200\) feet but less than \(250\) feet. The maximum must satisfy \(200 \le \text{max} \lt 250\).

Why Each Answer D) 219 is correct because \(200 \le 219 \lt 250\), placing it in the rightmost bin. A) 69 lies in \([50,100)\) and would not be the overall maximum (trap: reading a left-side bar). B) 119 lies in \([100,150)\), an interior bin, not the largest (out-of-range value). C) 169 lies in \([150,200)\), still short of the final bin (close-but-too-small trap). Only a value in the highest occupied interval can be the maximum.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway For "maximum" questions on a histogram, ignore the bar heights and look only at the far-right bar that still has data: the answer must fall between that bar's left and right edges. Match each choice to its interval and pick the one inside the last bin.
questions.question_text: The histogram shows the distribution of 20 lengths, in feet, in a data set. The first bar represents the lengths that are at least 0 feet but less than 50 feet, and so on. Which of the following could be the maximum length, in feet, in this data set?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is \(k = 28\). This is an Algebra question testing Linear equations in one variable, at an easy difficulty level. We are told \(k\) is a constant and the equation \(7x + 28 = 7x + k\) has infinitely many solutions; we must find \(k\).

Core Concepts

  • A linear equation in one variable can have three possible outcomes: exactly one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.
  • Infinitely many solutions means that the equation is true for every possible value of \(x\). This happens only when the two sides of the equation are identical expressions, i.e. an identity.
  • For two linear expressions of the form \(ax + b\) to be identical, both the coefficient of \(x\) (the \(a\) value) AND the constant term (the \(b\) value) must match on each side.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Write the equation: \(7x + 28 = 7x + k\).
  • Compare the coefficients of \(x\): the left side has \(7x\) and the right side has \(7x\). These already match, so the \(x\)-terms are identical.
  • For the equation to be true for all \(x\), the constant terms must also be equal. The left constant is \(28\) and the right constant is \(k\).
  • Set the constants equal: \(k = 28\).
  • Check: substituting \(k = 28\) gives \(7x + 28 = 7x + 28\), which is true for every value of \(x\) (you can also subtract \(7x\) from both sides to get \(28 = 28\), a true statement independent of \(x\)). This confirms infinitely many solutions.

Why Each Answer
This is a student-produced response, so there are no multiple-choice traps. The single correct value is \(k = 28\). A common mistake is to think the equation needs to be "solved for \(x\)" or to set \(k = 0\); but the condition of infinitely many solutions forces the constant on the right to match the constant on the left, giving \(k = 28\). Any other value of \(k\) (for example, \(k = 0\) or \(k = 7\)) would make the equation \(28 = k\) after subtracting \(7x\), which is false for that mismatched constant and yields NO solution rather than infinitely many.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Mental trigger: when the \(x\)-coefficients on both sides are already the same, "infinitely many solutions" simply means "make the constants equal too." If the \(x\)-coefficients matched but the constants did NOT, you'd have NO solution instead. Spotting that the \(7x\) terms are identical lets you read off \(k = 28\) in one step.
questions.question_text: In the given equation, \(k\) is a constant. The equation has infinitely many solutions. What is the value of \(k\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is \(33\) centimeters. This is an Algebra question testing Linear equations in one variable, at an easy difficulty level. We need the length of one of the two equal parts of a line segment.

Core Concepts

  • Total equals the sum of its parts: When a whole is split into pieces, the lengths of all the pieces add up to the total length.
  • Equal parts: If two pieces have the same length, you can find one of them by taking their combined length and dividing by \(2\).
  • Setting up an equation: Let \(x\) be the length of one of the two equal parts. Since there are two of them, together they measure \(2x\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The whole segment is \(113\) cm and is split into three parts: one known part of \(47\) cm and two equal parts each of length \(x\).
  • Write the total as the sum of the parts: \(47 + x + x = 113\), which simplifies to \(47 + 2x = 113\).
  • Subtract \(47\) from both sides to isolate the equal parts: \(2x = 113 - 47\), so \(2x = 66\).
  • Divide both sides by \(2\) to find one part: \(x = \dfrac{66}{2} = 33\).
  • Check: \(47 + 33 + 33 = 113\), which matches the total length. The answer is confirmed.

Why Each Answer
This is a student-produced response, so there are no answer choices. The single correct value is \(33\). A common mistake is to forget that there are two equal parts and divide \(66\) by something other than \(2\), or to subtract \(47\) and stop at \(66\) without halving it. Always re-read whether the question asks for the combined length or just one part.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "whole split into parts" problems, write a single addition equation: (known part) + (unknown parts) = (total). Subtract the known amount first, then divide by how many equal pieces remain. Here that is \((113 - 47) \div 2 = 33\).
questions.question_text: A line segment that has a length of \(113\) centimeters (cm) is divided into three parts. One part is \(47\) cm long. The other two parts have lengths that are equal to each other. What is the length, in cm, of one of the other two parts of equal length?

questions.passage: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, \(x\) and \(y\). A line of best fit is also shown.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is \(y = -x + 2.3\). This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis item on the skill Two-variable data: models and scatterplots, at medium difficulty. The task is to match the drawn line of best fit to its equation.

Core Concepts A line in slope-intercept form is written \(y = mx + b\), where \(m\) is the slope (the steepness and direction of the line) and \(b\) is the \(y\)-intercept (the \(y\)-value where the line crosses the vertical axis at \(x = 0\)). A line that falls from left to right has a negative slope (\(m \lt 0\)); a line that rises has a positive slope (\(m \gt 0\)). You can read both values directly off a graphed line.

Step-by-Step Breakdown Step 1: Read the direction. The line drops as it moves left to right, so the slope is negative, meaning \(m = -1\) for the listed choices (not \(+1\)). Step 2: Estimate the steepness. Going from near \((-14, 16)\) down to about \((0, 2.3)\) is a fall of roughly \(14\) over a run of \(14\), so the slope is about \(-1\). Step 3: Read the \(y\)-intercept. Extending the line to \(x = 0\), it crosses the \(y\)-axis just above \(2\), so \(b \approx 2.3\). Step 4: Combine: \(y = -x + 2.3\).

Why Each Answer \(y = -x + 2.3\) is correct: negative slope and a \(y\)-intercept just above \(2\) match the drawn line. \(y = x - 16.3\) is wrong (slope/intercept confusion): it has a positive slope, but the line clearly falls. \(y = -x + 16.3\) is wrong (intercept error): the slope sign is right, but an intercept of \(16.3\) would cross the \(y\)-axis near the top of the grid, not just above \(2\). \(y = x - 2.3\) is wrong (slope sign error): the intercept magnitude is close, but a positive slope rises, contradicting the falling line.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway First lock in the slope's sign from the line's direction; that alone usually cuts the choices in half. Then read where the line meets the \(y\)-axis to pin the intercept. Sign first, intercept second.

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is \(b = 8\). This is an Advanced Math question testing the skill of writing Equivalent expressions, and its difficulty is rated easy.

Core Concepts

  • Like terms are terms that contain the exact same variable raised to the exact same power. For example, \(7x^6\), \(9x^6\), and \(8x^6\) are all like terms because each one has the variable part \(x^6\).
  • Combining like terms means adding or subtracting their numerical coefficients (the numbers in front) while keeping the shared variable part unchanged. In symbols, \(ax^6 + bx^6 = (a+b)x^6\).
  • A coefficient is the number multiplying the variable part. In \(7x^6\), the coefficient is \(7\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Start with the given expression: \(7x^6 + 9x^6 - 8x^6\).
  • All three terms share the same variable part \(x^6\), so they are like terms and can be combined.
  • Combine the coefficients, keeping \(x^6\) factored out: \((7 + 9 - 8)x^6\).
  • Work left to right: \(7 + 9 = 16\), then \(16 - 8 = 8\). This gives \(8x^6\).
  • The problem states the expression equals \(bx^6\). Matching \(8x^6 = bx^6\) shows that \(b = 8\).

Why Each Answer
This is a student-produced response, so there are no answer choices to eliminate. The single correct value is \(b = 8\), found by adding and subtracting the coefficients \(7\), \(9\), and \(-8\). A common mistake would be to also change the exponent (for example, adding the exponents to get \(x^{18}\)); the exponent stays \(x^6\) because combining like terms never alters the variable part. Another trap is mis-handling the subtraction sign and getting \(7 + 9 + 8 = 24\); be careful that the third term is subtracted.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When every term has the identical variable part, you can ignore the variable entirely and just do the arithmetic on the coefficients: \(7 + 9 - 8 = 8\). The variable part rides along unchanged. This turns many "equivalent expression" questions into quick mental math.
questions.question_text: The expression \(7x^6 + 9x^6 - 8x^6\) is equivalent to \(bx^6\), where \(b\) is a constant. What is the value of \(b\)?

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C, \((10, 58)\). This is an Algebra question testing your skill with systems of two linear equations in two variables. Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • The graph of a linear equation like \(y = mx + b\) is a straight line. Every point \((x, y)\) on that line makes the equation true.
  • The point of intersection of two lines is the single point that lies on BOTH lines at once. That means its \((x, y)\) coordinates satisfy BOTH equations simultaneously.
  • When both equations are already solved for \(y\) (each written as "\(y = \) something"), the fastest way to find the intersection is setting the two right-hand sides equal. Since both expressions equal the same \(y\), they must equal each other at the shared point.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The two equations are \(y = 5x + 8\) and \(y = 6x - 2\).
  • Because both equal \(y\), set the right-hand sides equal to each other:
    \[5x + 8 = 6x - 2\]
  • Subtract \(5x\) from both sides to collect the \(x\) terms on one side:
    \[8 = x - 2\]
  • Add \(2\) to both sides to isolate \(x\):
    \[10 = x\]
  • Now substitute \(x = 10\) into either original equation. Using the first:
    \[y = 5(10) + 8 = 50 + 8 = 58\]
  • Check with the second equation to be safe: \(y = 6(10) - 2 = 60 - 2 = 58\). Both give \(y = 58\), so the point is confirmed.
  • The intersection point is \((x, y) = (10, 58)\).

Why Each Answer

  • A) \((5, 6)\) — Incorrect. This just lists the two slopes (\(5\) and \(6\)) as a point. Trap type: Misread Coefficients. The slopes are not the coordinates of the intersection.
  • B) \((6, 5)\) — Incorrect. Same slope numbers as A but swapped. Trap type: Misread Coefficients / Reversed Order. Still has nothing to do with solving the system.
  • C) \((10, 58)\) — Correct. Plugging \(x = 10\) into both equations yields \(y = 58\), so this point lies on both lines.
  • D) \((58, 10)\) — Incorrect. These are the right two numbers but with \(x\) and \(y\) swapped. Trap type: Reversed Coordinates. A point is written \((x, y)\), and here \(x = 10\), \(y = 58\), not the reverse.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When both equations are already in "\(y =\)" form, immediately set them equal to each other instead of substituting or graphing by hand. You can also confirm fast in Desmos: type both equations and read the intersection dot. Always double-check coordinate ORDER, the answer choices love to swap \(x\) and \(y\) (like option D) to catch a rushed solver.
questions.question_text: At what point \((x, y)\) do the graphs of the equations \(y = 5x + 8\) and \(y = 6x - 2\) intersect in the \(xy\)-plane?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A: The length of the rectangle, in feet.
Domain: Advanced Math. Skill: Nonlinear functions. Difficulty: Medium.
We must interpret what the piece \(72w\) means inside the area model \(y = (72w)(w)\).

Core Concepts

  • Variable: A letter like \(w\) stands for an unknown quantity. Here \(w\) is the width of the rectangle, measured in feet.
  • "Times" means multiply: The phrase "a length that is \(72\) times its width" tells us to multiply the width by \(72\). So length \(= 72 \times w = 72w\).
  • Area of a rectangle: Area \(=\) length \(\times\) width. The units of area are square feet because feet \(\times\) feet \(=\) square feet.
  • Interpreting parts of a formula: Each factor in a product can carry its own real-world meaning. We match each factor to the words in the problem.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Name the width. Let \(w\) be the width of the rectangle, in feet.
  • Step 2 — Build the length. The length is \(72\) times the width, so length \(= 72w\), in feet.
  • Step 3 — Build the area. Area \(=\) length \(\times\) width \(= (72w)(w)\). This equals \(72w^2\) and matches the given function \(y = (72w)(w)\).
  • Step 4 — Match the requested piece. The function is written as (length)(width) \(= (72w)(w)\). The first factor, \(72w\), is the length. So \(72w\) represents the length of the rectangle, in feet.

Why Each Answer

  • A (correct): Length \(= 72 \times\) width \(= 72w\), measured in feet. This is exactly the first factor of the area product.
  • B (incorrect) — Confuses a factor with the whole output: The area is the entire output \(y = (72w)(w)\), not the single factor \(72w\). Area is in square feet, while \(72w\) is in feet.
  • C (incorrect) — Wrong operation: The difference between length and width would be \(72w - w = 71w\), not \(72w\). Subtraction was never indicated.
  • D (incorrect) — Mislabels the factor: The width is \(w\) by itself. The expression \(72w\) is \(72\) times that width, which is the length, not the width.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a modeling function is a product, read it factor by factor and match each factor to the sentence. A quick units check seals it: \(72w\) carries units of feet (a length), while the full product \((72w)(w)\) carries square feet (an area). If the units do not match the word, the interpretation is wrong.
questions.question_text: A rectangle has a length that is \(72\) times its width. The function \(y = (72w)(w)\) represents this situation, where \(y\) is the area, in square feet, of the rectangle and \(y > 0\). Which of the following is the best interpretation of \(72w\) in this context?

question_options.option_text: The area of the rectangle, in square feet
The length of the rectangle, in feet
The difference between the length and the width of the rectangle, in feet
The width of the rectangle, in feet

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is B. This is an Algebra item on Linear functions (difficulty: easy). You are given the linear function \(f(x) = 29\) and must pick the table of \(x\) and \(f(x)\) values that the function actually produces.

Core Concepts A linear function can be written \(f(x) = mx + b\), where \(m\) is the slope (rate of change) and \(b\) is the \(y\)-intercept. When the slope \(m = 0\), the function is a constant function: \(f(x) = b\) for every input. Its output never changes no matter what \(x\) is, so its graph is a horizontal line. Here \(f(x) = 29\) means \(m = 0\) and \(b = 29\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown Because the output is the constant 29 for every input, evaluate at each listed \(x\): \(f(0) = 29\), \(f(1) = 29\), and \(f(2) = 29\). A correct table must therefore pair \(x = 0, 1, 2\) with \(f(x) = 29, 29, 29\). Scanning the choices, only the table whose \(f(x)\) column is \(29, 29, 29\) fits.

Why Each Answer B is correct: it lists \(f(x) = 29\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2\), exactly matching the constant function. A is wrong (Factual error): it shows \(f(x) = 0\) for all \(x\), which would be \(f(x) = 0\), not \(f(x) = 29\). C is wrong (slope confusion): values \(0, 29, 58\) increase by 29 each step, describing \(f(x) = 29x\), a non-constant line. D is wrong (slope confusion): values \(29, 0, -29\) decrease by 29 each step, describing \(f(x) = -29x + 29\), again not constant.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway When a function is written with no \(x\) on the right side, like \(f(x) = 29\), the output is locked: every row of the table must show the same number. Spotting that "all outputs equal" instantly rules out any table whose \(f(x)\) values change.
questions.question_text: For the given linear function \(f\), which table gives three values of \(x\) and their corresponding values of \(f(x)\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is B, \(y = 160\). This is a medium Geometry and Trigonometry item testing Lines, angles, and triangles, specifically the converse of the corresponding-angles relationship for a transversal crossing two lines.

Core Concepts When a transversal cuts two lines, pairs of angles in the same relative position at each intersection are called corresponding angles. Converse of the Corresponding Angles Postulate: if a transversal makes a pair of corresponding angles equal, the two lines are parallel. Two angles that form a straight line are a linear pair and sum to \(180^\circ\). To prove \(r\) and \(s\) are parallel you need information that forces a valid pair of equal corresponding (or equal alternate, or supplementary co-interior) angles between the two intersections.

Step-by-Step Breakdown At the top intersection (line \(r\)), \(w\) and \(x\) are a linear pair, so \(x = 180 - w = 180 - 160 = 20\). At the bottom intersection (line \(s\)), \(y\) and \(z\) are a linear pair, so \(y + z = 180\). Angle \(w\) (top) and angle \(y\) (bottom) sit in the same relative position, making them corresponding angles. By the converse postulate, \(r \parallel s\) exactly when \(w = y\). Since \(w = 160\), the lines are parallel precisely when \(y = 160\).

Why Each Answer B (\(y = 160\)) is correct: it sets \(y = w = 160\), equal corresponding angles, which forces \(r \parallel s\). A (\(x = 20\)) is a trap because \(x = 20\) is already guaranteed by \(w = 160\) (linear pair); it describes only line \(r\) and says nothing connecting the two lines. C (\(w + y = 180\)) gives \(y = 20\), so the corresponding angles \(160^\circ\) and \(20^\circ\) are unequal, which would prove the lines are NOT parallel, not that they are. D (\(y + z = 180\)) is always true as a linear pair at the bottom intersection regardless of the lines' direction, so it carries no new information.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway To prove two cut lines parallel, look for the angle pair that links the two intersections (corresponding, alternate, or co-interior). Any statement that only involves a single intersection, or that is automatically true (a linear pair summing to \(180^\circ\)), can never be the sufficient condition.
questions.question_text: In the figure shown, line \(k\) intersects lines \(r\) and \(s\). If \(w = 160\), which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines \(r\) and \(s\) are parallel?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C (80). This is a Geometry and Trigonometry question testing the Circles skill at a medium difficulty level. You are given a circle's equation in general form and must find the perimeter of a square in which the circle is inscribed.

Core Concepts

  • Standard form of a circle: \((x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2\), where \((h,k)\) is the center and \(r\) is the radius.
  • Completing the square: To turn \(x^2 + bx\) into a perfect square, add \(\left(\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2\). Whatever you add to one side of an equation you must add to the other side.
  • Diameter: \(d = 2r\) (twice the radius).
  • Inscribed circle: A circle inscribed in a square touches all four sides. Its diameter equals the side length of the square.
  • Perimeter of a square: \(P = 4s\), where \(s\) is the side length.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

Start with the given equation:

\[x^2 - 4x + y^2 - 8y - 80 = 0\]

Group the \(x\) terms and \(y\) terms, and move the constant to the right side:

\[(x^2 - 4x) + (y^2 - 8y) = 80\]

Complete the square for \(x\): half of \(-4\) is \(-2\), and \((-2)^2 = 4\). Complete the square for \(y\): half of \(-8\) is \(-4\), and \((-4)^2 = 16\). Add both amounts to each side:

\[(x^2 - 4x + 4) + (y^2 - 8y + 16) = 80 + 4 + 16\]

\[(x - 2)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 100\]

Compare to standard form: \(r^2 = 100\), so \(r = 10\).

The diameter is \(d = 2r = 2(10) = 20\). Because the circle is inscribed in the square, the side length equals the diameter: \(s = 20\).

The perimeter is \(P = 4s = 4(20) = 80\).

Why Each Answer

  • A (20): Incorrect. This is the diameter (one side length), not the perimeter. Trap: stopping at the side length instead of multiplying by 4.
  • B (40): Incorrect. This uses the radius \(10\) as the side and computes \(4 \times 10\), or treats the diameter as a semiperimeter. Trap: confusing radius with side length.
  • C (80): Correct. Side \(= 20\) and \(P = 4 \times 20 = 80\).
  • D (320): Incorrect. This comes from using \(r^2 = 100\) wrongly (e.g., \(80 + 4 + 16\) misread) or multiplying the diameter by an extra factor. Trap: skipping the square root and overusing the value \(100\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For a circle inscribed in a square, the chain is always: radius \(\rightarrow\) diameter \((2r)\) \(\rightarrow\) side \(=\) diameter \(\rightarrow\) perimeter \((4s)\). A quick mental check: the perimeter equals \(8r\) directly, since \(4 \times 2r = 8r = 8(10) = 80\). You can also paste the equation into Desmos to read the radius straight off the graph.
questions.question_text: In the \(xy\)-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is \(184\). This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis question testing Percentages, at a medium difficulty level. We need the number of people who attended all three webinars in a chain of percentage reductions.

Core Concepts

  • A percent is a fraction out of \(100\). To convert a percent to a decimal, divide by \(100\) (move the decimal point two places left): \(46\% = 0.46\) and \(32\% = 0.32\).
  • "Percent of" means multiply: to find \(p\%\) of a number, multiply the number by the decimal form of \(p\%\). For example, \(46\%\) of \(200\) is \(200 \times 0.46\).
  • When percentages are applied in sequence (a percent of a result that was itself a percent), you apply each step one at a time to the most recent count.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Start: \(1{,}250\) people attended the first webinar.
  • Step 1 — second webinar: \(46\%\) of those \(1{,}250\) people attended the second webinar. Compute \(46\%\) of \(1{,}250\): \[1{,}250 \times 0.46 = 575.\] So \(575\) people attended both the first and second webinars.
  • Step 2 — third webinar: \(32\%\) of the people who attended the first and second webinars (that is, \(32\%\) of \(575\)) attended the third webinar. Compute \(32\%\) of \(575\): \[575 \times 0.32 = 184.\]
  • Therefore \(184\) people attended all three webinars.

Why Each Answer
The correct value is \(184\), obtained by applying each percentage in turn to the running count. Common wrong values come from misreading the chain:

  • \(575\) is the count after only the second webinar — stopping one step too early (Incomplete Step).
  • \(400\) comes from taking \(32\%\) of \(1{,}250\) instead of \(32\%\) of \(575\) (Wrong Base — applying the second percent to the original total).
  • Adding or combining the percents (e.g. \(78\%\) of \(1{,}250\)) is invalid because the percentages act sequentially, not together (Combining Rates Error).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For chained percentages, multiply straight through: \(1{,}250 \times 0.46 \times 0.32 = 184\). Always apply each new percent to the most recent subgroup, not the original total. You can verify instantly in a calculator or Desmos by typing \(1250 \times 0.46 \times 0.32\).
questions.question_text: A real estate company offers a series of three webinars. \(1,250\) people attended the first webinar. \(46\%\) of the people who attended the first webinar attended the second webinar, and \(32\%\) of the people who attended the first and second webinars attended the third webinar. How many people attended all three webinars?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is an Advanced Math question on Nonlinear functions (exponential functions), at a medium difficulty level. The task is to pick the table of \((x, f(x))\) pairs that matches the exponential function \(f(x) = 24(2)^{\frac{x}{6}}\).

Core Concepts

  • An exponential function has the form \(f(x) = a\,b^{kx}\), where \(a\) is the starting value, \(b\) is the base, and the exponent controls how fast it grows.
  • Zero exponent rule: any nonzero number raised to the power \(0\) equals \(1\), so \(b^0 = 1\).
  • Negative exponent rule: \(b^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{b}\). More generally \(b^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{b^n}\).
  • To evaluate the function at a value, substitute that value for \(x\) and simplify the exponent first, then the power, then the multiplication.

Step-by-Step Breakdown
Evaluate \(f(x) = 24(2)^{\frac{x}{6}}\) at each \(x\)-value listed in the tables: \(-6, 0, 6, 12\).

At \(x = -6\):

\[f(-6) = 24(2)^{\frac{-6}{6}} = 24(2)^{-1} = 24\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 12\]

At \(x = 0\):

\[f(0) = 24(2)^{\frac{0}{6}} = 24(2)^{0} = 24(1) = 24\]

At \(x = 6\):

\[f(6) = 24(2)^{\frac{6}{6}} = 24(2)^{1} = 48\]

At \(x = 12\):

\[f(12) = 24(2)^{\frac{12}{6}} = 24(2)^{2} = 24(4) = 96\]

So the correct pairs are \(f(-6)=12\), \(f(0)=24\), \(f(6)=48\), \(f(12)=96\).

Why Each Answer

  • A (\(12, 0, 48, 96\)): Incorrect. It lists \(f(0)=0\), but a zero exponent gives \(2^0=1\), so \(f(0)=24\), not \(0\). Trap: misapplying the zero-exponent rule.
  • B (\(12, 24, 48, 96\)): Correct. Every value matches the computed outputs above.
  • C (\(-12, 24, 48, 96\)): Incorrect. It lists \(f(-6)=-12\), but a negative exponent produces a positive fraction, giving \(24(1/2)=12\), not \(-12\). Trap: confusing a negative exponent with a negative output.
  • D (\(12, 24, 48, 72\)): Incorrect. It lists \(f(12)=72\), but \(2^{2}=4\) so \(f(12)=24(4)=96\). Trap: treating the growth as linear (adding \(24\) each step) instead of doubling.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Because the exponent is \(\frac{x}{6}\), every increase of \(6\) in \(x\) raises the exponent by \(1\), which multiplies the output by the base \(2\): \(12 \to 24 \to 48 \to 96\). Spotting that constant doubling pattern lets you confirm the right table almost instantly, or check it quickly in Desmos by typing the function and reading off the table.
questions.question_text: Which table gives four values of \(x\) and their corresponding values of \(f(x)\) for the given exponential function?

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is \(6.75\) grams. This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis question testing ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units (density), at a medium difficulty level.

Core Concepts

  • Volume of a cube: A cube has all edges equal in length. If the edge length is \(s\), the volume is \(V = s^3\) (length times width times height, all equal to \(s\)).
  • Density: Density is mass per unit of volume. The defining relationship is \(\text{density} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). Rearranging to solve for mass gives \(\text{mass} = \text{density} \times \text{volume}\).
  • Units: Here volume is in cubic centimeters (\(\text{cm}^3\)) and density is in grams per cubic centimeter (\(\text{g/cm}^3\)), so multiplying them cancels the cubic-centimeter units and leaves grams.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Find the volume. The edge length is \(s = 3.000\) cm, so \[V = s^3 = (3.000)^3 = 27\ \text{cm}^3.\]
  • Step 2 — Apply the density relationship to find mass. With density \(0.250\) g/cm\(^3\): \[\text{mass} = \text{density} \times \text{volume} = 0.250 \times 27.\]
  • Step 3 — Multiply: \[0.250 \times 27 = 6.75\ \text{grams}.\]

Why Each Answer
This is a student-produced response, so there are no multiple-choice traps. The single correct value is \(6.75\). Watch for these common mistakes: forgetting to cube the edge and instead using \(3.000\) directly (giving \(0.75\)); squaring instead of cubing the edge, \(3^2 = 9\) (giving \(2.25\)); or dividing by the density instead of multiplying. Each of these misapplies either the volume formula or the density relationship.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Whenever a problem gives density and a shape's dimensions, the play is almost always \(\text{mass} = \text{density} \times \text{volume}\). Compute the volume first from the geometry, then multiply. Keeping units attached (\(\text{g/cm}^3 \times \text{cm}^3 = \text{g}\)) is a quick check that you set the product up correctly.
questions.question_text: To study fluctuations in leaf water potential, samples of wood were taken from \(22\) trees. Each sample was cut in the shape of a cube. The length of the edge of one of these cubes is \(3.000\) centimeters. This cube has a density of \(0.250\) grams per cubic centimeter. What is the mass of this cube, in grams?

questions.skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C: \(0\) and \(-\frac{18}{5}\). This is an Advanced Math question on the skill of solving nonlinear equations in one variable (here, an absolute value equation). Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • Absolute value \(|A|\) is the distance of \(A\) from \(0\), so it is never negative.
  • To solve, first isolate the \(|\cdot|\) term (get it alone on one side).
  • The rule: if \(|A| = B\) with \(B \ge 0\), then there are two cases, \(A = B\) or \(A = -B\). If \(B < 0\), there is no solution because absolute value cannot be negative.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

Start with the equation:

\[-2|5x + 9| + 7 = -11\]

Subtract \(7\) from both sides to begin isolating the absolute value:

\[-2|5x + 9| = -18\]

Divide both sides by \(-2\):

\[|5x + 9| = 9\]

Since \(9 \ge 0\), split into two cases.

Case 1: \(5x + 9 = 9\). Subtract \(9\): \(5x = 0\), so \(x = 0\).

Case 2: \(5x + 9 = -9\). Subtract \(9\): \(5x = -18\), so \(x = -\frac{18}{5}\).

The two solutions are \(0\) and \(-\frac{18}{5}\).

Why Each Answer

  • A. \(0\) — Incomplete (Partial Solution trap): \(0\) is one valid solution but it ignores Case 2, so it misses \(-\frac{18}{5}\).
  • B. \(0\) and \(-\frac{7}{5}\) — Arithmetic trap: this comes from mistakenly using \(5x + 9 = 7\) (carrying the \(7\) instead of \(-9\)), giving \(5x = -2\)... an incorrect setup. The second value does not satisfy the original equation.
  • C. \(0\) and \(-\frac{18}{5}\) — Correct: both values satisfy \(|5x+9| = 9\), as shown above.
  • D. There is no solution. — Sign trap: a student might see the negative coefficient \(-2\) and the negative right side and wrongly conclude the absolute value equals a negative number. After correctly isolating, \(|5x+9| = 9 \ge 0\), so solutions do exist.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Always isolate the absolute value completely before splitting into cases. A fast check: plug each candidate back in. For \(x = -\frac{18}{5}\), \(5x = -18\), so \(5x + 9 = -9\) and \(|-9| = 9\). You can also graph \(y = -2|5x+9| + 7\) and \(y = -11\) in Desmos and read off the two intersection x-values.
questions.question_text: What are all solutions to the given equation?

questions.skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D) \(84\). This is an Advanced Math question (skill: Nonlinear equations in one variable and systems of equations in two variables), difficulty: easy. You are asked for the sum of the two solutions of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - 84x - 14 = 0\).

Core Concepts

  • A quadratic equation is any equation that can be written in the standard form \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are numbers and \(a \neq 0\). Here \(a\) is the number in front of \(x^2\), \(b\) is the number in front of \(x\), and \(c\) is the constant term.
  • A quadratic equation usually has two solutions (the values of \(x\) that make the equation true).
  • Vieta's formula for the sum of roots: for \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), the sum of the two solutions equals \(-\dfrac{b}{a}\). This lets you find the sum without actually solving for each root.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Write the equation in standard form and identify the coefficients: \(x^2 - 84x - 14 = 0\). Since the \(x^2\) term has no visible number, \(a = 1\). The \(x\) term is \(-84x\), so \(b = -84\). The constant is \(c = -14\).
  • Apply the sum-of-roots formula: \[\text{sum} = -\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{-84}{1}.\]
  • A negative divided into a negative gives a positive: \[-\frac{-84}{1} = 84.\]
  • So the two solutions add up to \(84\), which matches choice D.

Why Each Answer

  • A) \(0\) — Incorrect. This would be the sum only if \(b = 0\) (an equation like \(x^2 - 14 = 0\), whose roots cancel). Trap: ignoring the \(-84x\) term.
  • B) \(7\) — Incorrect. This comes from misusing the constant term, e.g. relating it to \(-14\). Trap: confusing the sum of roots with a manipulation of \(c\).
  • C) \(14\) — Incorrect. This is just the constant \(c = -14\) read as a positive value. Trap: grabbing the constant instead of using \(-\frac{b}{a}\).
  • D) \(84\) — Correct. \(-\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{-84}{1} = 84\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For any quadratic \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\): the sum of the roots is \(-\frac{b}{a}\) and the product of the roots is \(\frac{c}{a}\). Memorizing these saves you from running the full quadratic formula whenever a question only asks for the sum or product. Mental trigger: "sum = negative b over a."
questions.question_text: What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is \(k = 4096\). This is a hard Geometry and Trigonometry item testing Area and volume — specifically the volume of a right circular cone combined with the Pythagorean theorem.

Core Concepts A right circular cone has an apex, a circular base of radius \(r\), a height \(h\) (the perpendicular distance from the apex to the center of the base), and a slant height \(l\) (the straight-line distance from the apex to any point on the base circumference). These three lengths satisfy the Pythagorean relationship \(r^2 + h^2 = l^2\), because the radius, the height, and the slant height form a right triangle with the right angle at the center of the base. The volume of a cone is \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown In the figure, \(A\) is the apex and \(B\) lies on the base circumference, so segment \(AB\) is the slant height: \(l = 32\). The height is \(h = 16\). First find \(r^2\) from the Pythagorean theorem: \[r^2 = l^2 - h^2 = 32^2 - 16^2 = 1024 - 256 = 768.\] Then substitute into the volume formula: \[V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi (768)(16).\] Since \(\frac{1}{3}(768) = 256\), this gives \[V = 256\pi (16) = 4096\pi.\] The volume is stated as \(k\pi\), so \(k = 4096\).

Why Each Answer The correct value is \(k = 4096\), obtained by correctly treating \(AB\) as the slant height and applying both the Pythagorean theorem and the cone volume formula. A common trap is to treat \(AB = 32\) as the radius, giving \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi (32)^2(16) = \frac{16384}{3}\pi\) (not an integer \(k\)). Another trap is to forget the factor \(\frac{1}{3}\), yielding \(768 \cdot 16 = 12288\). A third error is to use \(l\) itself as \(r^2\) or to mix up which leg is the height, both of which break the right-triangle relationship.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway Whenever a cone problem gives a slant height and a height (or radius), draw the right triangle formed by \(r\), \(h\), and \(l\) first. The slant height is always the hypotenuse, so \(r^2 = l^2 - h^2\). Solve for \(r^2\) directly — you never need \(r\) itself for the volume.
questions.question_text: For the right circular cone shown, \(B\) is a point on the circumference of the base, and the length of segment \(AB\) (not shown) is \(32\) centimeters. If the height of the cone is \(16\) centimeters and the volume of the cone is \(k\pi\) cubic centimeters, what is the value of \(k\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A, \((3,\ 8 - \frac{1}{m})\). This is an Algebra question on the skill "Linear equations in two variables," rated hard. We are given two perpendicular lines and asked which point lies on the second line.

Core Concepts

  • Slope of a line. In the form \(y = mx + b\), the number \(m\) is the slope (how steep the line is) and \(b\) is the y-intercept.
  • Perpendicular slopes. When two lines meet at a right angle, their slopes are negative reciprocals of each other. If one line has slope \(m\), the perpendicular line has slope \(-\frac{1}{m}\). The product of the two slopes is \(-1\).
  • Point-slope form. A line with slope \(s\) passing through point \((x_1, y_1)\) can be written as \(y - y_1 = s(x - x_1)\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Find the slope of line \(\ell\). Line \(k\) is \(y = mx + b\), so its slope is \(m\). Line \(\ell\) is perpendicular to line \(k\), so its slope is the negative reciprocal: \(-\frac{1}{m}\).
  • Step 2 — Use the shared point. The two lines intersect at \((2, 8)\), so this point is on line \(\ell\). Using point-slope form: \[y - 8 = -\frac{1}{m}(x - 2)\]
  • Step 3 — Test \(x = 3\). Every answer choice has an x-coordinate of \(3\), so substitute \(x = 3\): \[y - 8 = -\frac{1}{m}(3 - 2) = -\frac{1}{m} \\ y = 8 - \frac{1}{m}\]
  • Step 4 — Identify the point. The point on line \(\ell\) with \(x = 3\) is \((3,\ 8 - \frac{1}{m})\), which is Choice A.

Why Each Answer

  • A — Correct. \((3,\ 8 - \frac{1}{m})\) matches our result: moving \(1\) unit right from \(x=2\) to \(x=3\) drops \(y\) by \(\frac{1}{m}\), since the perpendicular slope \(-\frac{1}{m}\) is negative.
  • B — \((3,\ 8 + \frac{1}{m})\). Wrong Sign trap. It uses the correct magnitude \(\frac{1}{m}\) but adds instead of subtracts. Because \(m > 1\), the perpendicular slope is negative, so \(y\) must decrease as \(x\) increases.
  • C — \((3,\ 8 - m)\). Wrong Slope trap. It uses the slope of line \(k\) (which is \(m\)) instead of the perpendicular slope \(-\frac{1}{m}\). It forgets to take the negative reciprocal.
  • D — \((3,\ 8 + m)\). Wrong Slope and Wrong Sign trap. It uses line \(k\)'s slope \(m\) and the wrong direction, compounding both mistakes.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Whenever you see "perpendicular," immediately flip and negate the slope: \(m \to -\frac{1}{m}\). Then, since all choices share the same x-value, you only need to track the change in \(y\) over a one-unit step in \(x\) — that change equals the slope itself. A negative slope means \(y\) goes down, which instantly rules out the "\(+\)" options.
questions.question_text: In the \(xy\)-plane, line \(k\) and line \(\ell\) are perpendicular and intersect at the point \((2, 8)\). If line \(k\) is defined by the equation \(y = mx + b\), where \(m\) and \(b\) are constants and \(m > 1\), which of the following points lies on line \(\ell\)?

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D) 47. This is an Algebra question testing your skill with systems of two linear equations in two variables, rated hard. You are given a system and asked for the value of the combined expression \(\frac{11}{4}x+6y\).

Core Concepts

  • System of linear equations: two equations that share the same unknowns \(x\) and \(y\). The solution \((x,y)\) is the single pair of values that makes BOTH equations true at the same time.
  • Elimination method: when both equations contain an identical term (here \(2y\) appears in each), you can add or subtract the equations to cancel that term and solve for the other variable.
  • Substitution: once you know one variable, plug it back into either original equation to find the other.
  • Linear combination shortcut: the target expression \(\frac{11}{4}x+6y\) can often be built directly by scaling and adding the given equations, so you may not even need \(x\) and \(y\) separately.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

The system is:

\[\frac{5}{4}x+2y=17\]

\[\frac{3}{4}x+2y=15\]

Both equations have a \(2y\) term, so subtract the second from the first to eliminate \(y\):

\[\left(\frac{5}{4}x+2y\right)-\left(\frac{3}{4}x+2y\right)=17-15\]

\[\frac{5}{4}x-\frac{3}{4}x=2\]

\[\frac{2}{4}x=2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}x=2\]

Multiply both sides by \(2\): \(x=4\).

Substitute \(x=4\) into the second equation:

\[\frac{3}{4}(4)+2y=15\]

\[3+2y=15 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2y=12 \quad\Rightarrow\quad y=6\]

Now evaluate the target expression with \(x=4\) and \(y=6\):

\[\frac{11}{4}(4)+6(6)=11+36=47\]

Why Each Answer

  • A) 4 — Incorrect. This is just the value of \(x\), not the requested expression. Trap: stopping after solving for one variable.
  • B) 6 — Incorrect. This is the value of \(y\) alone. Trap: reporting an intermediate quantity instead of computing \(\frac{11}{4}x+6y\).
  • C) 32 — Incorrect. This is a partial or mis-combined total (for example, mistakenly using \(6y=36\) but dropping the \(11\), or other arithmetic slip). Trap: incomplete addition.
  • D) 47 — Correct. \(\frac{11}{4}(4)+6(6)=11+36=47\), matching the value of the requested expression.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Watch for the linear-combination shortcut: notice that \(\frac{11}{4}=\frac{5}{4}+2\cdot\frac{3}{4}\) and \(6=2+2\cdot 2\). So adding the first equation to \(2\) times the second gives \(\frac{11}{4}x+6y=17+2(15)=47\) directly — no need to find \(x\) and \(y\) at all. When a problem asks for a strange combined expression rather than a single variable, test whether it is a quick sum or multiple of the given equations first.
questions.question_text: The solution to the given system of equations is \((x,y)\). What is the value of \(\frac{11}{4}x+6y\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is \(-6\). This is an Algebra item on linear equations in two variables, rated hard. We are given three points of a line in a table and must find \(\frac{A}{B}\) when the line is written as \(Ax+By=C\).

Core Concepts A linear relationship has a constant slope \(m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\). In slope-intercept form a line is \(y=mx+b\). The standard form \(Ax+By=C\) is obtained by moving the \(x\)-term to the left. A key fact: the ratio \(\frac{A}{B}\) is unique even though \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) themselves are not, because multiplying the whole equation by a constant cancels in the ratio.

Step-by-Step Breakdown Read two points from the table, \((-2,19)\) and \((0,31)\). The slope is \(m=\frac{31-19}{0-(-2)}=\frac{12}{2}=6\). Check with \((2,43)\): \(\frac{43-31}{2-0}=\frac{12}{2}=6\), so the data is consistent. Since \((0,31)\) is the \(y\)-intercept, the line is \(y=6x+31\). Subtract \(6x\) from both sides to reach standard form: \(-6x+y=31\), so \(A=-6\) and \(B=1\).

Why Each Answer The value \(\frac{A}{B}=\frac{-6}{1}=-6\) is correct. Note that \(\frac{A}{B}=-m\) always, so any valid scaling of the equation (for example \(6x-y=-31\), giving \(A=6\), \(B=-1\)) still yields \(\frac{A}{B}=-6\). A common trap is answering \(6\) (the slope itself, forgetting the sign flip when moving \(6x\) across), or \(31\) (the intercept, which is \(C\), not part of the ratio).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway For \(y=mx+b\) written as \(Ax+By=C\), the shortcut is \(\frac{A}{B}=-m\). Find the slope and negate it; you never need the intercept for this ratio.
questions.question_text: The table shows three values of \(x\) and their corresponding values of \(y\). The linear relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) can be represented by an equation written in the form \(Ax+By=C\), where \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are constants. What is the value of \(\frac{A}{B}\)?

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A, the point \((r,-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8})\). This is an Algebra question testing systems of two linear equations in two variables (difficulty: hard). The key insight is recognizing that the two equations describe the same line, so every solution can be written in terms of a free parameter \(r\).

Core Concepts

  • A system of linear equations is two or more equations considered together. A point \((x,y)\) is a solution only if it satisfies every equation in the system.
  • If one equation is a constant multiple of the other, the two equations represent the same line. Such a system has infinitely many solutions \(-\) every point on that single line works.
  • To list points on a line, solve for \(y\) in terms of \(x\). Then any \(x\)-value you choose (call it \(r\)) produces a matching \(y\)-value, giving an ordered pair \((x,y)=(r,\ y\text{-expression})\).
  • Remember the ordered-pair convention: the first coordinate is \(x\) and the second is \(y\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Compare the equations \(5x+8y=9\) and \(15x+24y=27\). Multiplying the first by \(3\) gives \(15x+24y=27\), which is exactly the second equation. So both equations are the same line and the system has infinitely many solutions.
  • Work with the simpler equation \(5x+8y=9\). Subtract \(5x\) from both sides: \(8y=-5x+9\).
  • Divide every term by \(8\): \(y=-\frac{5}{8}x+\frac{9}{8}\).
  • Let the \(x\)-coordinate be any real number \(r\). Substitute \(x=r\): \(y=-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8}\).
  • The matching point is \((x,y)=\left(r,\ -\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8}\right)\), which is choice A.

Why Each Answer

  • A \(-\) Correct: \((r,-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8})\). Plug in: \(5r+8\left(-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8}\right)=5r-5r+9=9\). It satisfies the equation for every \(r\).
  • B \(-\) Incorrect (Swapped coordinates): \((-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8},r)\) puts the expression in the \(x\)-slot and \(r\) in the \(y\)-slot. Testing gives \(5(-\frac{5r}{8}+\frac{9}{8})+8r=\frac{39r}{8}+\frac{45}{8}\), which is not \(9\) for all \(r\).
  • C \(-\) Incorrect (Botched algebra): \((-\frac{5r}{8}+9,\frac{5r}{8}+27)\) comes from misusing the constant \(9\) and the sign on the slope. Substituting yields \(\frac{15r}{8}+261\), far from \(9\).
  • D \(-\) Incorrect (Wrong coefficients): \((\frac{r}{3}+9,-\frac{r}{3}+27)\) uses fabricated fractions unrelated to the \(-\frac{5}{8}\) slope. Substituting gives \(-r+261\), which is not \(9\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a system's second equation is a clean multiple of the first, stop \(-\) it is one line with infinitely many solutions, and the answer must be a parametric point. Quick check: substitute the candidate point into \(5x+8y\) and see if it collapses to \(9\). Only the choice whose first coordinate is the free variable \(r\) and whose second coordinate equals \(-\frac{5}{8}r+\frac{9}{8}\) survives.
questions.question_text: For each real number \(r\), which of the following points lies on the graph of each equation in the \(xy\)-plane for the given system?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is A. This is an Advanced Math item on Nonlinear functions (easy): it tests whether you can read an ordered pair off a parabola and interpret each coordinate in the context of a launched ball's height over time.

Core Concepts On a coordinate graph, every point is written as \((x, y)\). Here the horizontal axis is labeled Time (seconds), so \(x\) is the number of seconds after launch. The vertical axis is labeled Height above ground (meters), so \(y\) is the ball's height. A point \((x, y)\) therefore reads as: at time \(x\) seconds, the height is \(y\) meters. The y-intercept (where \(x = 0\)) is the launch/initial height, and the vertex (the highest point of a downward-opening parabola) is the maximum height.

Step-by-Step Breakdown The marked point is \((1.0, 3.9)\). Match each coordinate to its axis: the first coordinate \(1.0\) lies on the Time axis, so \(1.0\) second has elapsed since launch. The second coordinate \(3.9\) lies on the Height axis, so the ball is \(3.9\) meters above the ground. Putting it together: \(1.0\) second after launch, the ball's height is \(3.9\) meters.

Why Each Answer A is correct: it assigns \(1.0\) to time and \(3.9\) to height, exactly matching the axes. B swaps the coordinates (treats \(3.9\) as time and \(1.0\) as height) — a coordinate-reversal trap. C misreads the point as launch conditions; the initial height is the \(y\)-intercept at \(x = 0\), which the graph shows is \(3\) meters, and \(3.9\) is not a velocity — Factual error. D claims \((1.0, 3.9)\) is the maximum, but the vertex (peak) of the parabola sits to the left near \(x \approx 0.6\) at about \(4.7\) meters, higher than \(3.9\); the marked point is on the way down, not the peak.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway Always read coordinates in axis order: first number to the horizontal axis, second to the vertical. Whatever each axis is labeled becomes the meaning of that coordinate — here "\(x\) seconds, \(y\) meters." That single habit kills both the swap trap (B) and the max-height trap (D).
questions.question_text: The graph shows the height above ground, in meters, of a ball \(x\) seconds after the ball was launched upward from a platform. Which statement is the best interpretation of the marked point \((1.0, 3.9)\) in this context?

question_options.option_text: \(3.9\) seconds after being launched, the ball's height above ground is \(1.0\) meter.
The ball was launched from an initial height of \(1.0\) meter with an initial velocity of \(3.9\) meters per second.
\(1.0\) second after being launched, the ball reached its maximum height of \(3.9\) meters.
\(1.0\) second after being launched, the ball's height above ground is \(3.9\) meters.

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A: \(16\) is the amount, in dollars, the technician earned for each hour she worked at her regular job. This is an Algebra question testing Linear equations in two variables (interpreting a coefficient in context). Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts

  • A linear equation in two variables can model a real-world total. Here the total earnings are \(\$700\).
  • In a term like \(16h\), the variable \(h\) is a quantity (a count of something) and the number multiplying it, \(16\), is the coefficient. The coefficient is a rate: how many dollars are produced per one unit of \(h\).
  • Unit reasoning is the key tool: if \(h\) is measured in hours and the product \(16h\) is measured in dollars, then \(16\) must carry the units "dollars per hour."

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The equation is \(16h + 13c = 700\), where \(h\) = hours at the regular job and \(c\) = hours at the second job.
  • Look at the term \(16h\). Multiplying \(16\) by the number of regular-job hours gives the money earned at the regular job.
  • Check the units: \((\text{dollars per hour}) \times (\text{hours}) = \text{dollars}\). So \(16\) must be a pay rate in dollars per hour.
  • Therefore \(16\) is the amount in dollars earned for each hour at the regular job.

Why Each Answer

  • A (correct): \(16\) multiplies \(h\), the regular-job hours, so it is the dollars earned per regular-job hour.
  • B (incorrect) — Swapped reference: The pay rate for the second job is \(13\), the coefficient of \(c\), not \(16\).
  • C (incorrect) — Confuses coefficient with variable: The number of regular-job hours is \(h\) itself, not the rate \(16\) attached to it.
  • D (incorrect) — Confuses coefficient with the other variable: The number of second-job hours is \(c\), not \(16\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When asked to interpret a number in a word-problem equation, check its units. A coefficient sitting in front of a variable is always a rate (output units per one unit of that variable); the variable itself is the count. Match \(16\) to the variable it touches (\(h\), regular-job hours) to read off "dollars per regular-job hour."
questions.question_text: In one week in 2017, a technician earned a total of \(\$700\) by working at her regular job and at a second job doing part-time work. The equation \(16h + 13c = 700\) represents this situation, where \(h\) is the number of hours worked at her regular job and \(c\) is the number of hours worked at her second job. Which of the following is the best interpretation of \(16\) in this context?

question_options.option_text: The number of hours the technician worked in one week at her second job
The amount, in dollars, the technician earned for each hour she worked at her regular job
The amount, in dollars, the technician earned for each hour she worked at her second job
The number of hours the technician worked in one week at her regular job

questions.skill: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D: \(46, 47, 47, 47, 48\). This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis question on the skill "One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread." Difficulty: medium. You are asked which list has the smallest standard deviation.

Core Concepts

  • Mean: add all values and divide by how many there are. \(\text{mean} = \dfrac{\text{sum}}{\text{count}}\).
  • Deviation: how far each value sits from the mean, found by subtracting the mean from the value.
  • Variance: the average of the squared deviations, \(\dfrac{\sum(x-\text{mean})^2}{n}\).
  • Standard deviation (SD): the square root of the variance. It measures spread. Values packed tightly around the mean give a small SD; values spread far from the mean give a large SD.
  • Key shortcut: all four lists here are symmetric with the same mean of \(47\), so you do not need to finish the square-root step. Whichever list keeps its values closest to \(47\) wins.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Option A \(44, 45, 47, 49, 50\): mean \(=\dfrac{235}{5}=47\). Deviations \(-3, -2, 0, 2, 3\). Variance \(=\dfrac{9+4+0+4+9}{5}=\dfrac{26}{5}=5.2\), so \(\text{SD}\approx 2.28\).
  • Option B \(45, 45, 47, 49, 49\): mean \(=47\). Deviations \(-2, -2, 0, 2, 2\). Variance \(=\dfrac{4+4+0+4+4}{5}=\dfrac{16}{5}=3.2\), so \(\text{SD}\approx 1.79\).
  • Option C \(45, 46, 47, 48, 49\): mean \(=47\). Deviations \(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\). Variance \(=\dfrac{4+1+0+1+4}{5}=\dfrac{10}{5}=2.0\), so \(\text{SD}\approx 1.41\).
  • Option D \(46, 47, 47, 47, 48\): mean \(=47\). Deviations \(-1, 0, 0, 0, 1\). Variance \(=\dfrac{1+0+0+0+1}{5}=\dfrac{2}{5}=0.4\), so \(\text{SD}\approx 0.63\).

Comparing the variances: \(0.4 < 2.0 < 3.2 < 5.2\). Option D has the smallest spread.

Why Each Answer

  • D (correct): three of its five values equal the mean and the other two are only \(1\) unit away, giving the smallest variance \((0.4)\) and therefore the smallest standard deviation.
  • A (incorrect) — Largest Spread trap: its values reach \(3\) units from the mean, producing the biggest variance \((5.2)\), the opposite of what is asked.
  • B (incorrect) — Misjudged Clustering trap: it looks tight because of repeated values, but those repeats sit \(2\) units from the mean, giving variance \(3.2\).
  • C (incorrect) — Evenly-Spread trap: a neat sequence of consecutive integers still spreads symmetrically out to \(2\) units, giving variance \(2.0\), larger than D.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When every list shares the same mean, skip the square root entirely and just compare how close the values huddle to the center. The list with the most repeats of (or values nearest) the mean wins. A quick scan shows D is the only list with three values sitting exactly on the mean, so it is the tightest without any arithmetic.
questions.question_text: Which of the following lists represents a data set with the smallest standard deviation?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is \(56^\circ\) (choice B). This is an easy Geometry and Trigonometry item testing Lines, angles, and triangles, specifically the corresponding-angle property of similar triangles.

Core Concepts Two triangles are similar when they have the same shape: their corresponding angles are congruent (equal in measure) and their corresponding sides are in proportion. The order of the letters in a similarity statement is what tells you which parts correspond. When we write triangle \(CAE \sim\) triangle \(CBD\), the first letters correspond (\(C \leftrightarrow C\)), the second letters correspond (\(A \leftrightarrow B\)), and the third letters correspond (\(E \leftrightarrow D\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown Step 1: Read the similarity statement, triangle \(CAE \sim\) triangle \(CBD\), and match vertices by position: \(C \leftrightarrow C\), \(A \leftrightarrow B\), \(E \leftrightarrow D\). Step 2: The angle \(CAE\) is the angle at vertex \(A\); its corresponding angle is the angle at vertex \(B\), which is angle \(CBD\). Step 3: Corresponding angles of similar triangles are congruent, so the measure of angle \(CAE\) equals the measure of angle \(CBD\). Step 4: We are told the measure of angle \(CBD\) is \(56^\circ\), so the measure of angle \(CAE\) is \(56^\circ\). Step 5: The fact that \(AE = 24(BD)\) describes a side ratio and is not needed to find the angle; congruent angles do not depend on the scale factor.

Why Each Answer Choice B (\(56^\circ\)) is correct because angle \(CAE\) corresponds to angle \(CBD\), and corresponding angles in similar triangles are equal. Choice A (\(24^\circ\)) is a trap that misuses the side multiplier \(24\) as if it were an angle measure (factual error). Choice C (\((24 + 56)^\circ = 80^\circ\)) wrongly adds the side multiplier to the given angle, which has no geometric justification. Choice D (\((24 \cdot 56)^\circ = 1344^\circ\)) wrongly multiplies the side ratio by the angle, producing an impossible angle measure for a triangle. All three distractors come from combining the extraneous side information with the angle instead of using the corresponding-angles rule.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway In a similarity statement, line the two triangles up letter by letter: matching positions are corresponding angles, and corresponding angles are always equal. If a problem gives a side ratio along with an angle, the side ratio is usually a distractor for an angle question, congruent angles never depend on the scale factor.
questions.question_text: In the figure shown, triangle \(CAE\) is similar to triangle \(CBD\). The measure of angle \(CBD\) is \(56^\circ\), and \(AE = 24(BD)\). What is the measure of angle \(CAE\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B (15). This is a Problem-Solving and Data Analysis question testing Probability and conditional probability, at a medium difficulty level. We are asked how many of the \(375\) visitors are in room C.

Core Concepts

  • Probability: the probability of an event is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. Here, the probability of picking a visitor from a room equals (visitors in that room) \(\div\) (total visitors).
  • Probabilities sum to 1: every visitor is in exactly one of rooms A, B, or C, so these three rooms cover every possibility. The probabilities of all the possible (mutually exclusive) outcomes must add up to \(1\).
  • Converting a probability to a count: if you know a probability \(p\) and the total \(N\), the number of items in that category is \(p \times N\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Find the probability for room C. Since the three rooms account for all visitors, \(P(A) + P(B) + P(C) = 1\). Substitute the known values: \(0.64 + 0.32 + P(C) = 1\).
  • Step 2 — Solve for \(P(C)\): \(P(C) = 1 - 0.64 - 0.32 = 0.04\).
  • Step 3 — Convert that probability into a count of visitors by multiplying by the total of \(375\): \[0.04 \times 375 = 15.\]
  • So \(15\) visitors are located in room C.

Why Each Answer

  • A (4): Incorrect. This uses only the leftover probability \(0.04\) but multiplies or reads it incorrectly (e.g., treating \(0.04\) as roughly the count itself or mis-scaling). The actual count is \(0.04 \times 375 = 15\), not \(4\).
  • B (15): Correct. \(P(C) = 0.04\) and \(0.04 \times 375 = 15\).
  • C (77): Incorrect — Distractor from a math slip. There is no operation on the given numbers that yields \(77\); it does not match \(0.04 \times 375\).
  • D (120): Incorrect — Confuses a different probability with room C. \(0.32 \times 375 = 120\), which is the count for room B, not room C.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a problem lists categories that together cover everything, the missing probability is just \(1\) minus the others. Then multiply that probability by the total to get a count. Mental trigger: "the parts of a whole always add to 1."
questions.question_text: At a convention center, there are a total of \(375\) visitors. Each visitor is located in either room A, room B, or room C. If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room A is \(0.64\), and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room B is \(0.32\). How many visitors are located in room C?

questions.skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A) 26. This is an Algebra question testing the skill of solving a system of two linear equations in two variables. Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts

  • A system of equations is two (or more) equations that must be true at the same time. The solution \((x, y)\) is the single pair of values that satisfies both equations.
  • Elimination is a method where you add or subtract the equations to cancel one variable. When one equation has a term like \(\frac{x}{4}\) and the other has its opposite \(-\frac{x}{4}\), adding the equations makes the \(x\)-terms cancel because \(\frac{x}{4} + \left(-\frac{x}{4}\right) = 0\).
  • Read the question carefully: it asks for \(2y\), not \(y\). Sometimes the quantity you are asked for is produced directly by the algebra, saving a step.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

The two equations are:

\[y = \frac{x}{4} + 6 \\ y = -\frac{x}{4} + 20\]

Add the left sides together and the right sides together:

\[y + y = \left(\frac{x}{4} + 6\right) + \left(-\frac{x}{4} + 20\right)\]

On the left, \(y + y = 2y\). On the right, \(\frac{x}{4}\) and \(-\frac{x}{4}\) cancel, leaving only the constants:

\[2y = 6 + 20 \\ 2y = 26\]

The question asks for \(2y\), and the elimination step gives it directly: \(2y = 26\).

Why Each Answer

  • A) 26 — Correct. Adding the equations cancels \(x\) and yields \(2y = 26\).
  • B) 20 — Incorrect (Trap: Grabbing a number from the equation). 20 is the constant in the second equation, not the value of \(2y\).
  • C) 14 — Incorrect (Trap: Wrong operation). This is \(20 - 6\); it comes from subtracting the constants instead of adding them, which would only be valid if you were eliminating a matching \(y\)-term, not \(x\).
  • D) 6 — Incorrect (Trap: Grabbing a number / solving for the wrong quantity). 6 is the constant in the first equation. Even \(y\) itself is \(13\) (since \(2y = 26\)), so 6 is neither \(y\) nor \(2y\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When the two equations are each already solved for the same variable and contain opposite \(x\)-terms, just add them: the variable cancels instantly. Also, always check exactly what is requested — here \(2y\) falls out of the addition, so there is no need to find \(x\) or even \(y\) separately.
questions.question_text: The solution to the given system of equations is \((x, y)\). What is the value of \(2y\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B, \(y = 22\). This is an Algebra question testing Linear equations in two variables, rated easy difficulty.

Core Concepts

  • A variable is a letter that stands for a number we want to describe. Here \(y\) is defined to mean one specific thing: the total amount of fat, in pounds, the polar bear ate in these \(5\) days.
  • When a quantity is given directly in the problem, the equation that "describes" it simply sets the variable equal to that given value.
  • Read carefully what \(y\) represents. It is the total over the whole \(5\)-day span, not a daily rate and not a sum of unrelated numbers.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1: List the given information. Over \(5\) days the polar bear ate \(22.0\) pounds of fat in total.
  • Step 2: Identify what \(y\) means. The problem states \(y\) is the amount of fat, in pounds, eaten in these \(5\) days, which is exactly that total.
  • Step 3: Set them equal. Since \(y\) is the total and the total is \(22.0\) pounds, we write \(y = 22\) (note \(22.0 = 22\)).

Why Each Answer

  • A. \(y = 22 + 5\): Incorrect. This adds the number of days to the pounds of fat. Trap type: Combining Unrelated Units. Days and pounds cannot be added together, and the total fat is already \(22\).
  • B. \(y = 22\): Correct. The total fat eaten in the \(5\) days is \(22.0\) pounds, so the variable equal to that total is \(y = 22\).
  • C. \(y = \frac{22}{5}\): Incorrect. Dividing \(22\) by \(5\) gives the average pounds eaten per day, not the total over \(5\) days. Trap type: Answers a Different Question (rate instead of total).
  • D. \(y = 5\): Incorrect. This uses the number of days instead of the pounds of fat. Trap type: Wrong Quantity. \(5\) is the time span, not the amount eaten.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a question asks for an equation that "describes" a total that is stated outright, the answer is usually just variable = that number. Watch for distractors that divide (giving a rate) or add a second, unrelated number. Match the units to what the variable is defined to mean.
questions.question_text: In \(5\) days, a polar bear ate \(22.0\) pounds of fat. Which equation describes the amount of fat \(y\), in pounds, the polar bear ate in these \(5\) days?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D: \(M = 100(0.78)^{\frac{t}{11.11}}\). This is an Advanced Math question on Nonlinear functions (exponential models), difficulty: medium. The task is to translate a percent-decrease-per-interval description into an exponential decay equation.

Core Concepts

  • An exponential model has the form \(M = a\cdot b^{\,n}\), where \(a\) is the starting amount, \(b\) is the growth/decay factor applied each cycle, and \(n\) is the number of cycles that have passed.
  • A percent decrease of \(r\%\) per cycle means the amount remaining each cycle is \((100 - r)\%\). The decay factor is \(b = 1 - \frac{r}{100}\), not \(\frac{r}{100}\).
  • When one cycle of decay takes a fixed length of time, the number of cycles after \(t\) minutes is \(\dfrac{t}{\text{minutes per cycle}}\). This exponent must be a quotient (division), never a sum.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Find the decay factor. The mass drops by \(22\%\) each interval, so \(100\% - 22\% = 78\%\) of the mass remains. As a decimal, the base is \(b = 1 - 0.22 = 0.78\).
  • Find the exponent. One \(22\%\) drop happens every \(11.11\) minutes. After \(t\) minutes, the number of completed \(11.11\)-minute intervals is \(\dfrac{t}{11.11}\), so the exponent is \(\dfrac{t}{11.11}\).
  • Assemble the model. Using the starting mass \(100\) grams shown in every choice: \[M = 100(0.78)^{\frac{t}{11.11}}.\] This matches choice D.
  • Sanity check. At \(t = 11.11\), the exponent equals \(1\), giving \(M = 100(0.78) = 78\) grams — exactly a \(22\%\) loss after one interval, as required.

Why Each Answer

  • A \(\big(M = 100(0.22)^{t+11.11}\big)\) — incorrect. Two errors: the base \(0.22\) is the fraction lost rather than the fraction remaining (Confuses decrease with remaining amount), and the exponent \(t + 11.11\) adds time instead of counting intervals (Should divide, not add).
  • B \(\big(M = 100(0.22)^{\frac{t}{11.11}}\big)\) — incorrect. The exponent \(\frac{t}{11.11}\) is right, but the base \(0.22\) again uses the percent lost instead of the \(0.78\) remaining (Confuses decrease with remaining amount).
  • C \(\big(M = 100(0.78)^{t+11.11}\big)\) — incorrect. The base \(0.78\) is correct, but the exponent \(t + 11.11\) adds time rather than counting how many \(11.11\)-minute intervals have elapsed (Should divide, not add).
  • D \(\big(M = 100(0.78)^{\frac{t}{11.11}}\big)\) — correct. The base \(0.78\) captures that \(78\%\) remains each interval, and the exponent \(\frac{t}{11.11}\) correctly counts the elapsed intervals.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "decreases by \(r\%\) every \(k\) units of time," instantly write \(b = 1 - \frac{r}{100}\) and exponent \(\frac{t}{k}\). Watch the two classic traps: using \(r\) instead of \(1-r\) for the base, and adding the interval length to \(t\) instead of dividing by it.
questions.question_text: A researcher observes a sample of a nuclide. An exponential model estimates that the mass, in grams, of the sample decreases by \(22\%\) every \(11.11\) minutes. Which of the following equations could represent this model, where \(M\) is the estimated mass, in grams, of the sample \(t\) minutes after the researcher began observing the sample?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C, \(y = 8x + 15\). This is an Algebra question testing Linear functions, and its difficulty is easy.

Core Concepts

  • Slope-intercept form: A line can be written as \(y = mx + b\), where \(m\) is the slope (how steep the line is) and \(b\) is the \(y\)-intercept (the \(y\)-value where the line crosses the vertical axis).
  • Parallel lines: Two lines are parallel when they never cross. In the \(xy\)-plane this happens exactly when they have the same slope \(m\) but different \(y\)-intercepts.
  • The \(y\)-intercept point: Any point of the form \((0, b)\) lies on the \(y\)-axis, so its \(y\)-value \(b\) is the \(y\)-intercept of a line passing through it.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Read the slope of line \(k\). It is given as \(y = 8x + 7\), which is already in \(y = mx + b\) form, so its slope is \(m = 8\).
  • Line \(j\) is parallel to line \(k\), so it shares the same slope: \(m = 8\).
  • Line \(j\) passes through \((0, 15)\). Since the \(x\)-coordinate is \(0\), this point is on the \(y\)-axis, so the \(y\)-intercept is \(b = 15\).
  • Substitute \(m = 8\) and \(b = 15\) into \(y = mx + b\) to get \(y = 8x + 15\).

Why Each Answer

  • A) \(y = 15x + 7\): Incorrect. This swaps the roles of the numbers, using \(15\) as the slope and \(7\) as the intercept. Trap: Confuses slope and intercept.
  • B) \(y = -15x + 7\): Incorrect. Same swap as A plus a sign flip on the slope; \(15\) is not the slope and the slope of a parallel line is not negated. Trap: Confuses slope/intercept and sign error.
  • C) \(y = 8x + 15\): Correct. Matches the required slope \(8\) (parallel to line \(k\)) and the intercept \(15\) (from the point \((0,15)\)).
  • D) \(y = -8x + 15\): Incorrect. The intercept is right, but the slope is \(-8\). A negated slope gives a perpendicular-looking line, not a parallel one. Trap: Sign error on the slope.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "parallel" problems, copy the slope straight from the given line and only change the intercept. When a point has \(x = 0\), its \(y\)-value is the intercept, so you can write the answer instantly without extra computation.
questions.question_text: Line \(k\) is defined by \(y = 8x + 7\). Line \(j\) is parallel to line \(k\) in the \(xy\)-plane and passes through the point \((0, 15)\). Which equation defines line \(j\)?

questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D) \(9\). This is an Algebra question testing Linear functions at a medium difficulty level. You must first find the unknown constant \(c\) using the first function, then use it to find the slope of the second function.

Core Concepts

  • A linear function graphs as a straight line, and any straight line has a single constant slope (steepness).
  • Function notation: \(p(c) = -6\) means "when the input is \(c\), the output is \(-6\)," which is the point \((c, -6)\) on the graph of \(y = p(x)\).
  • Slope formula between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\): \[m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\]

Step-by-Step Breakdown
Step 1 — Find \(c\) using function \(p\). We are given two points on \(y = p(x)\): \((c, -6)\) and \((5, 42)\), and the slope is \(8\). Plug into the slope formula:

\[8 = \frac{42 - (-6)}{5 - c} = \frac{48}{5 - c}\]

Multiply both sides by \((5 - c)\):

\[8(5 - c) = 48\]

Divide both sides by \(8\):

\[5 - c = 6 \quad\Rightarrow\quad c = -1\]

Step 2 — Find the slope of function \(t\). Since \(c = -1\), the statement \(t(c) = -7\) becomes \(t(-1) = -7\), giving the point \((-1, -7)\). We also have \(t(6) = 56\), the point \((6, 56)\). Apply the slope formula:

\[m = \frac{56 - (-7)}{6 - (-1)} = \frac{63}{7} = 9\]

The slope of \(y = t(x)\) is \(9\).

Why Each Answer

  • A) \(-1\) — Incorrect. This is the value of the constant \(c\), not a slope. Trap type: Right Number, Wrong Question (reports an intermediate result).
  • B) \(2\) — Incorrect. This results from a sign/arithmetic slip, such as computing \(\frac{56 - 7}{6 + 1}\) wrong or mishandling the negatives. Trap type: Computation Error.
  • C) \(8\) — Incorrect. This is the slope of function \(p\), not function \(t\). Trap type: Wrong Function (copies the given slope instead of solving for the new one).
  • D) \(9\) — Correct. \(\frac{63}{7} = 9\), the slope of \(y = t(x)\).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a shared constant links two functions, always solve for that constant first, then carry it into the second relationship. A fast check: rise \(= 56 - (-7) = 63\), run \(= 6 - (-1) = 7\), and \(63 \div 7 = 9\). You can confirm instantly in Desmos by entering both points and reading the slope.
