  • The completion must follow necessarily from the stated evidence, not merely sound reasonable.
  • A conclusion drawn about both species must rest on something the text says is true for both species.
  • Watch the logical direction: if both birds prefer a condition, then the logical flip is that they are not drawn to the opposite of that condition.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets the scene: both the small white heron and the small dark heron are long-legged wetland birds.
  • Sentence 2 states the researchers' goal: to learn how the birds choose where to live.
  • Sentence 3 lists the habitat features studied (geographic location, water depth during breeding season).
  • Sentence 4 gives the key finding: only small white herons prefer deep water during breeding season, but both species prefer areas with standing water for more than 60 days per year.
  • Sentence 5 is the conclusion to complete: "neither species is very drawn to areas where __________."
  • Because both species are drawn TO areas with standing water for more than 60 days, it follows logically that neither species is drawn to the opposite condition: areas with standing water for far fewer than 60 days.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): "there is standing water for far fewer than 60 days per year." Both species prefer standing water for more than 60 days, so the logical inverse, areas with standing water for far fewer than 60 days, is exactly what neither species would be drawn to. This is the only choice supported for both birds.
  • B (Out of Scope): "species with breeding seasons longer than 60 days are likely to be present." The text discusses how long standing water lasts, not the length of any species' breeding season, and says nothing about birds choosing habitats based on other species being present.
  • C (Vague / Unsupported): "there are any features that attract the other species." The text never claims the birds avoid features that attract a different species; the herons share the standing-water preference rather than avoiding each other.
  • D (Half-Right Trap): "there is relatively deep water during the breeding season." Deep water during breeding season is preferred by only the small white heron, so it cannot support a conclusion about "neither species." It also reverses the logic, since one species actually likes this feature.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a conclusion uses a negative word like "neither," find the condition the text says both subjects prefer, then flip it to its opposite. Discard any choice that is true for only one of the two subjects (like deep water here) because it can never justify a claim about both.
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: there is relatively deep water during the breeding season.
there are any features that attract the other species.
species with breeding seasons longer than 60 days are likely to be present.
there is standing water for far fewer than 60 days per year.

questions.passage: It is hard for publishers and printers to create very long books that balance the requirements of readability, durability, and cost. Among some exceptionally long novels published in English, Haruki Murakami's 1Q84 (translated from Japanese) was published in a 1,157-page edition and runs to an estimated 407,000 words, while John Sayles's A Moment in the Sun (written originally in English) was published in a 1,100-page edition and runs to an estimated 625,000 words. This indicates that __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is (A). This is an Information and Ideas question testing the Inferences skill at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to finish the text with the conclusion that the given facts most directly support.

Core Concepts

  • Logical inference: A valid inference must follow only from the information stated, with no outside assumptions added.
  • Words per page: This is simply the total word count divided by the total number of pages. If a book has more words but fewer pages, it must pack more words onto each page (a higher words-per-page average).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up the problem: making very long books that balance readability, durability, and cost is difficult.
  • Sentence 2 gives two data sets. 1Q84: 1,157 pages and about 407,000 words. A Moment in the Sun: 1,100 pages and about 625,000 words.
  • Compare them directly. A Moment in the Sun has MORE words (625,000 vs. 407,000) yet FEWER pages (1,100 vs. 1,157) than 1Q84.
  • More words spread across fewer pages can only mean one thing: each page of A Moment in the Sun holds, on average, more words than each page of 1Q84.
  • That conclusion is exactly what the blank needs.

Why Each Answer

  • (A) Correct. With more total words on fewer total pages, A Moment in the Sun must average more words per page than 1Q84. This is a direct arithmetic consequence of the stated numbers.
  • (B) Out of Scope. The text notes 1Q84 was translated from Japanese but gives no word count for the original Japanese text, so nothing here shows that translation increases word count.
  • (C) Out of Scope. The passage discusses pages and words only; it says nothing about reading speed or how long either book takes to read.
  • (D) Unsupported Assumption. Paper thickness is never mentioned. Fewer pages could come from many causes (font size, margins, words per page), so we cannot conclude anything about paper.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
On inference completion questions, stick to what the numbers force. Here, the only claim provable from "more words, fewer pages" is a higher words-per-page density. Any answer that introduces a new topic (translation, reading time, paper) is a trap, no matter how reasonable it sounds in real life.
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: the edition of 1Q84 is printed on thinner paper than the edition of A Moment in the Sun.
translating a text from Japanese to English is likely to increase the word count.
page count is likely to be a more reliable indicator of how long it takes to read a book than word count.
the edition of A Moment in the Sun has more words per page than the edition of 1Q84.

questions.passage: Portrait of Marquess Massimiliano Stampa is one of dozens of remaining works by the Italian Renaissance artist Sofonisba Anguissola. __________ in 1557, her painting can now be found at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B (Completed). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense, rated easy. Your job is to choose the verb form that correctly connects the opening phrase to the main sentence.

Core Concepts

  • Main clause: A group of words with a subject and a verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence. Here the main clause is “her painting can now be found at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore.” Its subject is her painting.
  • Introductory modifying phrase: A phrase placed at the start of a sentence, set off by a comma, that describes the subject that follows. It is NOT a complete sentence on its own.
  • Past participle: The verb form (usually ending in -ed, like completed) used to describe something that receives an action. “Completed in 1557” means the painting was finished in 1557 — the painting receives the action.
  • Comma splice: The error of joining two complete sentences with only a comma.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Look at what comes after the comma: “her painting can now be found…” That is already a complete sentence (it has the subject her painting and the verb can be found).
  • So the part before the comma must be a modifying phrase, not a second complete sentence — otherwise two sentences would be glued together with just a comma.
  • The phrase describes the painting and tells us it was finished in 1557. Because the painting receives the action of being finished, we need the past participle.
  • “Completed in 1557, her painting can now be found…” reads cleanly: the phrase modifies her painting, and the sentence stays grammatical.

Why Each Answer

  • A. Will complete — Wrong Verb Form. This is an active future-tense verb meaning the painting will perform the action of completing something, which makes no sense, and it cannot serve as an introductory modifier.
  • B. Completed — Correct. The past participle forms an introductory modifying phrase that correctly describes her painting as having been finished in 1557.
  • C. Completes — Wrong Verb Form. This is an active present-tense verb suggesting the painting completes something itself; it does not work as a modifier and creates an illogical, ungrammatical opening.
  • D. Was completed — Creates a Comma Splice. “Was completed in 1557” is a complete clause, so joining it to the second complete clause with only a comma produces two sentences spliced together.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a sentence opens with a phrase, a comma, and then a full sentence, the opener almost always needs to be a modifier, not a verb that can stand alone. Test the trigger: if the second half is already a complete sentence, choose the -ed participle (modifier) over a finite verb like was completed to avoid a comma splice.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: Synthesized calcium phosphate nanoparticles (CaPNPs) can be used to improve the healing and regeneration of broken bones; this function, well suited for multiple medical applications, __________ from the biocompatible properties of these particles.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C (stems). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense (verb forms), at a medium difficulty level. The task is to choose the verb form that correctly completes the sentence as a grammatically complete clause.

Core Concepts

  • Finite verb: A verb that is conjugated for a subject and tense (for example, stems, stem, stemmed). A complete clause MUST have a finite verb acting as its main predicate.
  • Non-finite forms: Verb forms that are NOT conjugated and cannot stand alone as a main verb. These include the present participle (stemming), the perfect participle (having stemmed), and the infinitive (to stem).
  • Subject-verb agreement: A singular subject takes a singular present-tense verb. In the present tense, the third-person singular verb adds -s (it stems).
  • Independent clause: A group of words with a subject and a finite verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The sentence is split by a semicolon. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, so what follows the semicolon must itself be a complete sentence with its own subject and finite main verb.
  • Identify the subject of the second clause: this function (singular).
  • The phrase set off by commas, well suited for multiple medical applications, is a non-essential modifier describing the subject. Mentally remove it to see the core: "this function __________ from the biocompatible properties of these particles."
  • The blank is the only spot for the main verb. It must be a finite verb that agrees with the singular subject this function.
  • The singular present-tense form is stems. Plugging it in gives a complete sentence: "this function stems from the biocompatible properties of these particles."

Why Each Answer

  • C (stems) — Correct: It is a finite, third-person singular present-tense verb that agrees with this function and supplies the main predicate, producing a complete independent clause.
  • A (stemming) — Wrong (Non-finite/Fragment): A present participle cannot serve as a main verb on its own. Without a helping verb (such as is), it leaves the clause with no finite verb, creating a sentence fragment.
  • B (having stemmed) — Wrong (Non-finite/Fragment): A perfect participle is non-finite and also misstates the timing, implying a completed prior action. It cannot anchor the independent clause as a standalone predicate.
  • D (to stem) — Wrong (Non-finite/Fragment): An infinitive names an action without conjugating it, so it cannot act as the main verb of the clause, leaving the sentence incomplete.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a clause needs its main verb, cross out any phrase between commas, then ask: "Does the remaining sentence have a verb that could stand alone?" Only a finite, conjugated form (here, stems) passes that test. Participles ending in -ing, perfect participles, and to + verb infinitives are classic traps because they look like verbs but cannot run a clause by themselves.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: The Austronesian language family comprises some 1,200 languages—including the __________ Madurese and Bikol, which are spoken by 14 million and 4.6 million speakers, respectively—and accounts for one-fifth of the world's languages, making it of keen interest to linguists like Diane Massam.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A ("languages" with no punctuation). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the skill of Boundaries (punctuation between sentence elements), at medium difficulty.

Core Concepts

  • An appositive is a noun (or noun phrase) placed next to another noun to rename or specify it. Example: in "the poet Maya Angelou," the name "Maya Angelou" is an appositive that identifies which poet.
  • A restrictive (essential) appositive narrows down exactly which thing is meant and is NOT set off by punctuation: "the languages Madurese and Bikol." A nonrestrictive (extra) appositive simply adds information and IS set off by commas, dashes, or a colon: "my oldest sibling, Jordan, lives nearby."
  • Key rule: do not place a comma, dash, or colon between a noun and a restrictive appositive that is needed to identify it. The noun and the names form one tight, uninterrupted unit.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Read the relevant phrase with the blank filled by each option: "including the __________ Madurese and Bikol."
  • Identify the structure: "the" + a noun + the specific names. The blank is the noun "languages," and "Madurese and Bikol" are the two languages being named.
  • Ask whether the names are essential. Without "Madurese and Bikol," the phrase "including the languages" tells us nothing specific, so the names are restrictive (essential) and must attach directly to "languages."
  • Because the appositive is restrictive, no punctuation belongs between "languages" and "Madurese and Bikol." The phrase should read smoothly: "the languages Madurese and Bikol."
  • Therefore the blank takes the bare word with no punctuation after it.

Why Each Answer

  • A. languages — Correct. It keeps "the languages Madurese and Bikol" as one uninterrupted restrictive phrase, exactly as the convention requires.
  • B. languages— — Incorrect (Unnecessary Punctuation). A dash signals a nonrestrictive break or interruption, but the names are essential and cannot be separated from the noun they identify.
  • C. languages: — Incorrect (Misused Colon). A colon must follow a complete idea to introduce a list or explanation; here it wrongly splits the noun from its essential appositive.
  • D. languages, — Incorrect (Unnecessary Comma). A comma would mark the names as extra, nonrestrictive information, but they are restrictive and must stay directly joined to "languages."

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When you see a noun immediately followed by a specific name (a person, place, title, or term), test whether the name is needed to identify the noun. If it is essential, attach it with NO punctuation. Mental trigger: "essential name, no comma." When three of four choices just add different punctuation marks and one adds nothing, the clean no-punctuation choice is very often correct.

questions.passage: For the past 20 million years, Earth's magnetic poles in the far north and far south have remained roughly where they are today. This has not always been the __________ throughout geologic history, Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places several times through a process called polar wandering.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C (case, though;). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill, and it is rated hard. The job is to choose the punctuation that correctly ends one sentence and joins it to the next.

Core Concepts

  • An independent clause is a group of words that has its own subject and verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence.
  • Two independent clauses CANNOT be joined by a comma alone (that error is a comma splice). They must be separated by one of: a period, a semicolon, a colon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
  • A semicolon ( ; ) acts like a soft period: it joins two complete, closely related independent clauses.
  • The word though here is an adverb meaning "however." When it sits at the end of a clause, it is set off with a comma ("..., though").
  • If a period is used to end a sentence, the next word must be capitalized because it begins a new sentence.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Clause 1: "This has not always been the case, though" — this has a subject ("This") and a verb ("has been"), so it is a complete independent clause. The adverb though is tacked on at the end and needs a comma before it.
  • Clause 2: "throughout geologic history, Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places several times..." — this has a subject ("poles") and a verb ("have swapped"), so it is also a complete independent clause.
  • Because we have two independent clauses, we need a strong boundary (period or semicolon) between them, not just a comma.
  • We also need a comma before though to set it off at the end of Clause 1.
  • That gives the pattern: case + comma + though + semicolon. The semicolon then correctly links the two clauses while keeping throughout lowercase.

Why Each Answer

  • A. case; though, — Incorrect (misplaced boundary). The semicolon lands before though, which wrongly chops the sentence so that though starts Clause 2 with a stray comma. It breaks up Clause 1 and leaves the boundary in the wrong spot.
  • B. case, though. — Incorrect (capitalization error). A period ends the sentence, so the next word would have to be capitalized. But the text continues with lowercase "throughout," so a period cannot be used here.
  • C. case, though; — Correct. The comma sets off the trailing adverb though, and the semicolon joins the two independent clauses without forcing a capital letter on "throughout."
  • D. case, though — Incorrect (comma splice). Only a comma separates the two independent clauses, which is not a strong enough boundary.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When you spot two complete sentences sitting next to each other, your boundary must be a period or a semicolon. Quick test: if the option uses a period, check whether the next word is capitalized. If it is lowercase (like "throughout" here), a period is automatically out, which often leaves the semicolon as the answer.

questions.passage: Russian-born visual artist Helga Stentzel turns household items into strange and surprising works of art. In her prints, tan sweatpants take on the form of a camel as they dangle from a __________ the red handles of a pair of pliers become the thongs of flip flops—flip flops made of nails. This "household surrealism," Stentzel says, "is about finding magic in the mundane."
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B (clothesline;). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill at a medium difficulty level. The job is to choose the punctuation that correctly separates the two halves of the sentence.

Core Concepts
A few definitions you need from scratch:

  • Independent clause: a group of words that has its own subject and verb and could stand alone as a complete sentence.
  • Comma splice: the error of joining two independent clauses with only a comma. This is grammatically incorrect.
  • Semicolon (;): a mark that links two closely related independent clauses without needing a joining word like and or but. It works like a soft period.
  • Colon (:): introduces an explanation, example, or list. What comes before a colon must be a complete sentence, and what follows should elaborate on it.
  • Dash (—): can also separate clauses, but it signals a sharp break or added emphasis rather than a neutral link.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Read the first part: tan sweatpants take on the form of a camel as they dangle from a clothesline. Subject = sweatpants, verb = take. This is a complete, independent clause.
  • Read the second part: the red handles of a pair of pliers become the thongs of flip flops. Subject = handles, verb = become. This is also a complete, independent clause.
  • Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone, so we need a punctuation mark strong enough to separate them.
  • The second clause is not an explanation or a list that defines the first, so a colon does not fit. The two ideas are parallel observations, so a neutral semicolon is the cleanest choice. A semicolon also keeps the punctuation clear, since a dash already appears later in the sentence.

Why Each Answer

  • A. clothesline, — Incorrect (Comma Splice). A single comma cannot hold two independent clauses together.
  • B. clothesline; — Correct. The semicolon properly joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
  • C. clothesline— — Incorrect (Wrong Punctuation Tone). A dash can technically separate clauses, but it signals an abrupt break and would clash with the dash already used later in the sentence, making the structure muddy.
  • D. clothesline: — Incorrect (Misused Colon). A colon must introduce an explanation, example, or list. The second clause is an independent, parallel statement, not an elaboration of the first.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a question gives you a comma, semicolon, dash, and colon as the four choices, first check whether both sides are complete sentences. If they are and neither side explains or lists the other, the semicolon is almost always the answer. Mental trigger: semicolon = soft period between two equal, complete ideas.

questions.passage: Nineteenth-century Modernista architects championed nature in their designs. Granted, the dramatic archways and botanical glasswork of Palau Mornau, a Modernista private home designed by Manuel Raspall, couldn't exactly grow in a forest. __________ one sees natural influences in Raspall's penchant for curves (rather than right angles) and plant- and animal-inspired flourishes.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B (Still,). This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Transitions skill at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to choose the transition word that best fits the logical relationship between the sentence before the blank and the sentence containing the blank.

Core Concepts
A transition word signals how two ideas relate. The main categories you need here are:

  • Contrast / concession (Still, However, Nevertheless, Yet): signals that the new idea pushes back against or limits the previous idea.
  • Addition (Furthermore, Moreover, In addition): signals that the new idea piles on more of the same kind of support.
  • Comparison (Similarly, Likewise): signals that two separate things share a likeness.
  • Restatement (In other words, That is): signals that the new sentence re-expresses the previous idea in different words.

A key clue word is Granted, which begins the sentence before the blank. Granted introduces a concession (an admission of a point that seems to weaken the writer's case). A concession almost always sets up a contrast: the writer admits something, then pivots back to the real point.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1: Modernista architects "championed nature in their designs." This sets up the theme: nature-inspired architecture.
  • Sentence 2: "Granted, the dramatic archways and botanical glasswork... couldn't exactly grow in a forest." The word Granted concedes a limitation: these are man-made features, not literally natural.
  • Sentence 3 (the blank): "__________ one sees natural influences in Raspall's penchant for curves... and plant- and animal-inspired flourishes." This sentence returns to the main point: nature's influence is still visible.
  • The relationship is therefore concession-then-pivot: "True, it's not literally nature, BUT you still see nature's influence." That calls for a contrast transition.

Why Each Answer

  • B (Still,) — Correct: "Still" signals contrast and works hand-in-hand with the concession word "Granted." It conveys "despite that admission, nature's influence is nonetheless visible," which exactly matches the logic.
  • A (Furthermore,) — Addition trap: "Furthermore" adds another supporting point in the same direction. But sentence 3 reverses direction from the concession, so addition is wrong.
  • C (Similarly,) — Comparison trap: "Similarly" claims two things are alike. The sentences are not drawing a likeness between two parallel items; they are contrasting an admission with the main claim.
  • D (In other words,) — Restatement trap: "In other words" would mean sentence 3 restates sentence 2. But sentence 3 says the opposite of sentence 2's concession, so it is not a restatement.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When you see a concession word like Granted, Admittedly, True, or Of course in the sentence before the blank, expect the blank to pivot back with a contrast transition (Still, However, Nevertheless, Yet). The concession-pivot pattern is one of the most common setups on Transitions questions.

questions.passage: In Panama, citizens must be at least 18 years old to vote in their country's elections. __________ citizens in the Isle of Man need only be 16 years old to cast their vote.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B) By comparison,. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Transitions skill, and it is rated easy. The task is to choose the transition that best captures the logical relationship between the two sentences.

Core Concepts
A transition is a word or phrase that signals how one idea relates to the idea before it. Each transition type expresses a specific relationship:

  • Comparison/contrast (by comparison, however, in contrast, similarly): points out how two things are alike or different.
  • Sequence (firstly, next, finally): orders items in a list or steps in a process.
  • Example (for example, for instance): introduces a specific case that illustrates a general claim.
  • Cause and effect (therefore, as a result, thus): shows that one idea produces or follows logically from another.

The strategy is to read both sentences, decide the relationship in plain words, and then match that relationship to the transition.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1: In Panama, the minimum voting age is 18.
  • Sentence 2: In the Isle of Man, the minimum voting age is only 16.
  • The two sentences present the same kind of fact (a minimum voting age) for two different places, and the numbers are different (18 vs. 16).
  • So the writer is setting one fact next to another to highlight a difference. That is a comparison/contrast relationship.
  • The transition that signals "here is how this case differs from the one I just gave" is By comparison,.

Why Each Answer

  • A) Firstly, — Trap: Wrong Relationship (sequence). "Firstly" begins a numbered list or sequence of steps, but the second sentence is not the first item in any list; it is a contrasting fact.
  • B) By comparison, — Correct. It directly signals that the two voting ages are being weighed against each other, fitting the 18-versus-16 difference.
  • C) For example, — Trap: Wrong Relationship (illustration). The Isle of Man's voting age is not an example of Panama's voting age; the second sentence is a separate, contrasting fact, not an instance of the first.
  • D) Therefore, — Trap: Wrong Relationship (cause and effect). "Therefore" claims the second fact results from the first, but Panama's rules do not cause the Isle of Man's rules.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When two sentences state the same type of fact about two different subjects with different values, the relationship is almost always comparison/contrast. Cover the choices, name the relationship in your own words first, then pick the transition that matches — this stops you from being lured by a grammatically smooth but logically wrong option.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

questions.passage: Generally, sleek vehicles are more aerodynamic than bulkier ones. For example, the streamlined nose of the Airbus A320 jet helps it glide through wind with relative ease. __________ a boxy semitruck encounters more wind resistance, making it less aerodynamic.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B, "On the other hand,". This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Transitions skill, and its difficulty is rated easy. Your job is to choose the transition word or phrase that best fits the logical relationship between the sentence before the blank and the sentence that contains the blank.

Core Concepts
A transition is a word or phrase that signals how two ideas relate to each other. Different transitions signal different relationships:

  • Contrast transitions (however, on the other hand, by contrast, conversely) signal that the second idea is opposite to or different from the first.
  • Illustration / detail transitions (specifically, for example, in particular) signal that the second idea gives a more detailed or narrower version of the first.
  • Cause and effect transitions (as a result, therefore, consequently) signal that the second idea is a result of the first.
  • Conclusion / summary transitions (in conclusion, in summary, to sum up) signal that the writer is wrapping up and restating the main point.

The strategy is to read both sides of the blank, decide what relationship connects them, and then pick the transition that names that relationship.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 (the general rule): "Generally, sleek vehicles are more aerodynamic than bulkier ones." This sets up the main idea: sleeker equals more aerodynamic.
  • Sentence 2 (the first example): "For example, the streamlined nose of the Airbus A320 jet helps it glide through wind with relative ease." This gives a sleek, highly aerodynamic example.
  • Sentence 3 (the blank): "__________ a boxy semitruck encounters more wind resistance, making it less aerodynamic." This gives the opposite case: a bulky, less aerodynamic example.
  • Relationship: Sentence 2 (sleek and aerodynamic) and Sentence 3 (boxy and less aerodynamic) describe opposite situations. That is a contrast.
  • Match the transition: A contrast transition is needed, and "On the other hand" is exactly that.

Why Each Answer

  • A. "Specifically," - Incorrect (Wrong Relationship: Illustration). "Specifically" introduces a narrower detail about the same idea. But the semitruck is not a detail about the jet; it is an opposing case, so this does not fit.
  • B. "On the other hand," - Correct. This is a contrast transition, and it perfectly signals the shift from the aerodynamic jet to the less aerodynamic semitruck.
  • C. "As a result," - Incorrect (Wrong Relationship: Cause/Effect). This claims the semitruck's wind resistance is caused by the jet's gliding. There is no cause-and-effect link between the two examples, so it does not fit.
  • D. "In conclusion," - Incorrect (Wrong Relationship: Summary). This signals a final summary of points already made, but Sentence 3 introduces a new, contrasting example rather than wrapping up, so it does not fit.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For transition questions, cover the answer choices and ask yourself one question: "Does the second idea agree with, add detail to, result from, or oppose the first?" Here the two vehicles are opposites, so a contrast word is the trigger. Spotting opposing pairs (sleek vs. boxy, easy vs. resistance) is a fast signal that the answer is a contrast transition like "On the other hand."

questions.passage: As a federalist, New York physician and writer Charles McKnight favored the US Constitution's provisions for a strong centralized government and supported the document's ratification: __________ essays he published in the New-York Journal in December 1787 under the pseudonym "Examiner" disparaged the arguments of the anti-federalists, who opposed the Constitution's adoption.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is (B) fittingly. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Transitions skill, rated hard. The task is to choose the word or phrase that best captures the logical relationship between the two halves of the sentence.

Core Concepts
A transition is a word or phrase that signals how one idea connects to the next. Different transitions signal different relationships:

  • Result/consistency (so, fittingly, accordingly, as expected): the second idea is the natural, expected outcome of the first.
  • Restatement (in other words, that is): the second idea repeats the first in different words, adding no new information.
  • Comparison (by comparison, similarly, likewise): two separate things are weighed against each other.
  • Contrast (nevertheless, however, but): the second idea is surprising or opposed to the first.

The strategy is to figure out the real-world relationship between the two clauses, then match it to the transition that names that exact relationship.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Clause 1: Charles McKnight was a federalist who favored a strong central government and supported ratifying the US Constitution. This tells us his beliefs.
  • Clause 2: The essays he published attacked ("disparaged") the anti-federalists, the people who opposed the Constitution. This tells us his actions.
  • Relationship: His actions (attacking the Constitution's opponents) are exactly what we would predict from his beliefs (supporting the Constitution). The second clause is the expected, consistent result of the first.
  • Match: A word signaling "this is the natural, appropriate outcome" fits the blank. "Fittingly" means in a way that is suitable and expected, so it fits perfectly.

Why Each Answer

  • (A) in other words — Trap: False Restatement. This signals that clause 2 simply re-says clause 1, but clause 2 adds new, specific information (the essays, the journal, the pseudonym), so it is not a restatement.
  • (B) fittingly — Correct. It shows that the essays attacking anti-federalists were the natural, appropriate extension of McKnight's pro-Constitution convictions.
  • (C) by comparison — Trap: No Second Item. Comparison requires two distinct things being measured against each other, but here we have one person's beliefs leading to his own consistent actions, not a comparison.
  • (D) nevertheless — Trap: Wrong Direction (Contrast). This signals a surprise or contradiction, but his actions agree with his beliefs, so there is no contrast to flag.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For transition questions, cover the answer choices and decide in plain words whether clause 2 agrees with, contrasts with, or restates clause 1. Here clause 2 agrees with and follows naturally from clause 1, so eliminate every contrast word (nevertheless) and restatement word (in other words) immediately, then pick the consistency word.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Epazoyucan is a municipality in the state of Hidalgo, Mexico.
  • Municipalities are governmental regions responsible for providing many public services to their residents.
  • One service they provide is traffic control.
  • Epazoyucan covers an area of roughly 140 km².
  • Hidalgo is divided into 84 municipalities.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing Rhetorical Synthesis, rated easy. The task is to pick the sentence that best uses the notes to emphasize the size of Epazoyucan.

Core Concepts
Rhetorical Synthesis questions give you a bulleted set of research notes and a specific writing goal. Your job is to match the goal to the note that contains the right kind of information.

  • Size means physical extent or area, usually expressed in units such as square kilometers (km2).
  • Information about services, government structure, or how many municipalities exist does not describe size.
  • The best choice is the one whose details directly serve the stated goal, ignoring true-but-irrelevant facts.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1: Pin down the goal — emphasize the size of Epazoyucan.
  • Step 2: Scan the notes for any measurement of size. Only one note qualifies: "Epazoyucan covers an area of roughly 140 km2."
  • Step 3: Find the answer choice built around that area figure. Choice A states the municipality "covers an area of roughly 140 km2," directly conveying size.
  • Step 4: Confirm the other choices rely on notes about services or governmental structure, which do not address size.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): It includes the area measurement (\(140\text{ km}^2\)), the only note that conveys physical size, so it fulfills the goal.
  • B (Out of Scope): It describes the public services Epazoyucan provides — true, but says nothing about size.
  • C (Out of Scope): It emphasizes that Hidalgo is divided into 84 municipalities, a fact about political division, not the size of Epazoyucan.
  • D (Out of Scope): It focuses on traffic control as an example of a public service, which is unrelated to size.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Underline the goal word first ("size") and then hunt the notes for the single matching detail — here, a number with a unit. The choice carrying that exact data point is almost always the answer; the others are real facts placed there to tempt you off-goal.
questions.question_text: The student wants to emphasize the size of Epazoyucan. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

question_options.option_text: Epazoyucan—a governmental region in the state of Hidalgo, Mexico—provides many public services to its residents.
Providing traffic control is just one example of the public services that municipalities provide.
Epazoyucan is one of 84 governmental regions, known as municipalities, across Hidalgo.
The municipality of Epazoyucan in Hidalgo, Mexico, covers an area of roughly 140 km².

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The United States has designated more than 500 areas National Wildlife Refuges (NWRs).
  • Some NWRs were established specifically to protect endangered species.
  • The Crocodile Lake NWR is a 6,686-acre area in Florida.
  • It was established to protect the endangered American crocodile.
  • The Pearl Harbor NWR is a 61-acre area in Hawaii.
  • It was established to protect the endangered Hawaiian stilt.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Rhetorical Synthesis skill at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to pick the sentence that best uses the notes to emphasize a similarity between the two National Wildlife Refuges (NWRs).

Core Concepts
Rhetorical Synthesis questions give you a set of research notes and a specific writing goal. To answer correctly you must:

  • Lock onto the stated goal. The goal here is to emphasize a similarity — a feature the two refuges share in common.
  • Match the goal exactly. The right choice must (1) mention both NWRs and (2) point to something they have in common. A choice that names only one refuge cannot show a similarity, and a choice that stresses how they differ shows a contrast, not a similarity.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Find the shared trait in the notes. The notes say the Crocodile Lake NWR "was established to protect the endangered American crocodile" and the Pearl Harbor NWR "was established to protect the endangered Hawaiian stilt." Both were established to protect an endangered species — that is the similarity.
  • Step 2 — Note the differences (to avoid traps). They differ in size (6,686 acres vs. 61 acres) and location (Florida vs. Hawaii). A correct "similarity" answer must avoid leading with these differences.
  • Step 3 — Require both refuges. To emphasize a similarity between the two, the sentence must name both NWRs together.
  • Step 4 — Test the choices. Only one choice names both refuges and states a shared purpose: protecting endangered species.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): "Both the Crocodile Lake NWR and the Pearl Harbor NWR were established to protect endangered species." This names both refuges and states the exact trait they share, directly accomplishing the goal of emphasizing a similarity.
  • B (Incorrect — Incomplete / One-Sided): It mentions only the Pearl Harbor NWR, so it cannot emphasize a similarity between the two refuges.
  • C (Incorrect — Wrong Goal / Contrast): It contrasts the sizes (6,686 acres vs. 61 acres), highlighting a difference rather than a similarity.
  • D (Incorrect — One-Sided / Out of Scope): It focuses on the Crocodile Lake NWR and the total number of refuges, ignoring the Pearl Harbor NWR, so no similarity between the two is shown.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "emphasize a similarity between two things" goals, use a quick two-part filter: (1) cross out any choice that names only one thing, and (2) cross out any choice built on a difference or contrast (watch for words like "while," "only," or "but"). The survivor that states a shared feature of both is your answer.
questions.question_text: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two NWRs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

question_options.option_text: While the Crocodile Lake NWR extends across a 6,686-acre area, the Pearl Harbor NWR encompasses only 61 acres.
Some NWRs, such as Hawaii's Pearl Harbor, were established specifically to protect endangered species.
Both the Crocodile Lake NWR and the Pearl Harbor NWR were established to protect endangered species.
The US has designated more than 500 areas NWRs, including the Crocodile Lake NWR in Florida.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Felipe Posada (pseudonym The Invisible Realm) is a New York City–based artist who specializes in the form of art known as surrealist collage.
  • Manifestation of the unconscious mind is a central aspect of surrealist collage.
  • Irrational juxtaposition of disparate elements is a central aspect of surrealist collage.
  • Posada's Synchronicity irrationally juxtaposes images of a well-dressed man, a clouded mountain range, and a doorway to the stars.
  • Posada: "My art is a journey through the invisible realm—a space where intuition, memories, visions, and dreams are free to take visual form."
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Rhetorical Synthesis skill, at a medium difficulty level. The task is to pick the sentence that best uses the notes to accomplish one specific rhetorical goal.

Core Concepts
Rhetorical Synthesis questions give you a bulleted list of research notes and a stated goal. Your job is to match the goal precisely. Key ideas to know from scratch:

  • The goal is a contract. Whatever the prompt asks for is the ONLY thing that matters. Here the goal is to "provide a specific example of irrational juxtaposition in surrealist collage."
  • "Irrational juxtaposition" means placing unrelated, disparate things side by side in a way that does not follow logic.
  • "Specific example" means concrete, named details, not a general definition or restatement. To show an example of juxtaposition, the sentence must actually name the unrelated things being placed together.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify the goal: give a specific example of irrational juxtaposition.
  • Find the note that contains the concrete example: Posada's Synchronicity juxtaposes "a well-dressed man, a clouded mountain range, and a doorway to the stars." These three unrelated images ARE the example.
  • The winning choice must name those disparate images, because only naming them demonstrates the juxtaposition rather than just describing or labeling it.
  • Choice A names all three images and states they are juxtaposed irrationally in Synchronicity. It delivers exactly the concrete example the goal demands.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): Lists the three disparate elements being combined (a well-dressed man, a clouded mountain range, a doorway to the stars) in the specific work Synchronicity. This is a true, concrete example of irrational juxtaposition.
  • B (Out of Scope / Wrong Focus): Quotes the artist's philosophy about "intuition, memories, visions, and dreams." That speaks to the unconscious-mind theme, not to a specific example of juxtaposition, so it misses the goal.
  • C (Too General): States that Synchronicity is surrealist collage in which irrational juxtaposition is a central aspect. It labels the concept but never names what is juxtaposed, so it gives no actual example.
  • D (Too General / Off-Goal): Defines surrealist collage as manifesting the unconscious mind and juxtaposing disparate elements. It restates definitions and adds the unconscious-mind idea, but again never lists the specific images, so it provides no example.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a goal asks for a "specific example," eliminate any choice that only defines, labels, or describes the concept in general terms. The right answer will contain concrete, named details, here the three actual images, that you could point to and say "that is the example."
questions.question_text: The student wants to provide a specific example of irrational juxtaposition in surrealist collage. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

question_options.option_text: Synchronicity by artist Felipe Posada is an example of surrealist collage, a form in which irrational juxtaposition is a central aspect.
The irrational juxtaposition of disparate elements in Felipe Posada's art invokes "a space where intuition, memories, visions, and dreams are free to take visual form."
Images of a well-dressed man, a clouded mountain range, and a doorway to the stars are juxtaposed irrationally in the surrealist collage piece Synchronicity by artist Felipe Posada.
Surrealist collage, such as Felipe Posada's Synchronicity, manifests the unconscious mind and irrationally juxtaposes disparate elements.

questions.passage: As with other river deltas, the Kolyma River delta is __________: it is a constantly evolving network of channels and strips of land that change in size and shape as the river deposits new sedimentary particles where the river meets the waters of the East Siberian Sea.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is (B) dynamic. This is a Craft and Structure question testing the Words in Context skill. Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts
A Words in Context question asks you to choose the single word that best fits a blank based on clues elsewhere in the sentence. Two tools matter here:

  • The colon (:) signals that what follows explains or restates what came before it. So whatever is after the colon is a direct definition of the blank.
  • Vocabulary: dynamic = characterized by constant change and activity; unrivaled = having no equal, the best; sustainable = able to be kept up at a steady level; immutable = never changing.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The sentence opens by comparing the Kolyma River delta to other deltas: "As with other river deltas, the Kolyma River delta is __________."
  • A colon follows the blank, so the rest of the sentence defines the blank.
  • The definition reads: "a constantly evolving network of channels and strips of land that change in size and shape as the river deposits new sedimentary particles."
  • The key clues are "constantly evolving" and "change in size and shape." The blank must therefore mean something like "constantly changing" or "active."
  • Match this meaning to the choices: "dynamic" directly means constantly changing and active. It fits.

Why Each Answer

  • (B) dynamic — Correct. It means marked by continuous change and activity, exactly matching "constantly evolving" and "change in size and shape."
  • (A) unrivaled — Out of Scope. The sentence says "As with other river deltas," which compares this delta to others rather than ranking it as unmatched. Nothing addresses superiority.
  • (C) sustainable — Wrong Meaning. Sustainable suggests being maintained at a steady level, but the text stresses change, not steadiness.
  • (D) immutable — Opposite. Immutable means unchanging, the direct contradiction of "constantly evolving."

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a colon follows the blank, the words after it are a built-in definition. Predict your own word from those clues first (here, "changing"), then pick the choice closest to your prediction. Watch for opposite traps like "immutable" that describe the reverse of the clue.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: Noting the correspondence of Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa to his self-portrait in red chalk, artist Lillian Schwartz argued that the former is a self-portrait, too—that by mapping his own features onto those of its ostensible subject, Lisa del Giocondo, Leonardo depicted himself as a woman. Indeed, by subjecting both works to digital analysis, Schwartz __________ the two faces' structural resemblance.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is (A) corroborated. This is a Craft and Structure question testing Words in Context, rated hard. The task is to choose the word that most logically and precisely fits the blank based on the surrounding meaning.

Core Concepts
A Words in Context question asks you to pick the single word whose meaning best fits the logic of the sentence. The key is to read the clues around the blank and predict the meaning before checking the choices. Definitions you need here:

  • corroborate — to confirm or support a claim with evidence.
  • amalgamate — to merge or blend separate things into one.
  • promulgate — to announce or make widely known (often a law, doctrine, or idea).
  • consolidate — to combine or strengthen things into a single, more solid whole.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up the claim: artist Lillian Schwartz argued that the Mona Lisa is actually a hidden self-portrait of Leonardo da Vinci, based on the visual correspondence between the painting and his red-chalk self-portrait.
  • Sentence 2 (the one with the blank) begins with "Indeed," signaling that it reinforces the previous claim, and tells us how: "by subjecting both works to digital analysis, Schwartz __________ the two faces' structural resemblance."
  • The action in the blank is what the digital analysis lets her do TO the "structural resemblance." Since she is using objective analysis to back up an existing argument, the blank must mean something like "confirmed" or "provided evidence for."
  • Predicted meaning: confirmed / supported with evidence. The word that matches this prediction is corroborated.

Why Each Answer

  • (A) corroborated — Correct. It means to confirm with evidence, which exactly describes how the digital analysis supported her claim about the faces' structural resemblance.
  • (B) amalgamated — Incorrect (Wrong Meaning). It means to merge things together. She is not blending the two faces into one; she is verifying that they resemble each other.
  • (C) promulgated — Incorrect (Out of Scope). It means to announce or publicize. The sentence is about using analysis to confirm the resemblance, not about broadcasting it to the public.
  • (D) consolidated — Incorrect (Wrong Meaning). It means to combine or strengthen into one solid whole. Like (B), it wrongly suggests merging rather than verifying an existing similarity.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
Cover the choices and predict your own word first. Here the transition "Indeed" plus "digital analysis" points to evidence supporting a claim, so predict "confirmed." Watch out for the trap of choosing combine-type words (amalgamated, consolidated) just because two images are involved—the sentence is about proving a resemblance, not fusing the pictures.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: While modern composers may often get inspiration from past greats like Ludwig van Beethoven, the extent of their influences is broad. The music of Ernesto Lecuona, for example, can be said to __________ elements of both the classical European tradition and the social, political, and cultural landscape of his native Cuba.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D (exhibit). This is a Craft and Structure, Words in Context question at medium difficulty. The task is to choose the single word that most logically and precisely fills the blank.

Core Concepts
In a Words in Context question, the blank must agree with the logic of the surrounding sentence. You do not pick the fanciest word; you pick the one whose meaning matches the relationship the sentence describes. Key vocabulary here:

  • exhibit — to show, display, or manifest a quality or feature.
  • defy — to openly resist or refuse to obey.
  • neglect — to ignore or fail to attend to.
  • foretell — to predict or announce something before it happens.

Step-by-Step Breakdown
Sentence 1 establishes the theme: modern composers draw from broad influences. Sentence 2 gives Ernesto Lecuona as an example, saying his music combines "elements of both the classical European tradition" and "the social, political, and cultural landscape of his native Cuba." The verb in the blank describes the relationship between Lecuona's music and those two sets of elements. Because his music contains and presents both kinds of elements, the blank needs a word meaning to show or display them.

Why Each Answer

  • A. defy — Trap: Opposite Meaning. To defy these elements would mean to resist them, but the passage says his music draws on them, not fights them.
  • B. neglect — Trap: Opposite Meaning. To neglect would mean to ignore the elements, contradicting the point that his music incorporates them.
  • C. foretell — Trap: Out of Scope / Wrong Sense. Foretell means to predict the future; music cannot predict an existing classical tradition or its own cultural landscape.
  • D. exhibit — Correct. Exhibit means to display or manifest, which precisely captures how Lecuona's music shows elements of both traditions.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For Words in Context, predict your own word for the blank before reading the choices. Here a natural prediction is "show" or "display." Then match that prediction to a choice: "exhibit" is the synonym, and the opposite-meaning traps (defy, neglect) fall away immediately.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

questions.passage: During the 2007–2010 financial crisis, the United States furnished billions of dollars to selected countries' central banks via mechanisms called swap lines. Aditi Sahasrabuddhe found that countries' policy environments seem to have been __________ swap-line decisions: the probability that banks would be granted swap lines was 0.20 in countries open to foreign-capital inflows and 0.03 in countries with policies restricting such inflows.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D, "material to." This is a Craft and Structure / Words in Context question rated hard. The task is to choose the word or phrase that, when placed in the blank, most logically and precisely describes the relationship the data demonstrates between a country's policy environment and swap-line decisions.

Core Concepts
For Words in Context items, the surrounding sentence supplies the meaning the blank must match. Here the structure is "X seem to have been __________ Y," where X = countries' policy environments and Y = swap-line decisions. The colon that follows introduces evidence that defines the relationship, so the blank must agree with what that evidence shows. Key vocabulary:

  • Material to — relevant to; having a significant bearing or effect on something.
  • Predicated on — completely based on or dependent upon.
  • Mediated by — brought about indirectly through an intervening agent or middleman.
  • Decoupled from — separated or disconnected from.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up the topic: during the 2007–2010 financial crisis the U.S. provided funds to selected central banks through swap lines.
  • Sentence 2 reports Sahasrabuddhe's finding and then gives the data after the colon: the probability of being granted swap lines was 0.20 for countries open to foreign-capital inflows but only 0.03 for countries restricting such inflows.
  • That contrast (0.20 vs. 0.03) shows the policy environment clearly mattered to whether swap lines were granted — it influenced the outcome but did not fully determine it (the restrictive group still had a nonzero 0.03 chance).
  • So the blank needs a phrase meaning "relevant to / a significant factor in," without overstating it as total dependence. "Material to" fits precisely.

Why Each Answer

  • A. predicated on — Trap: Extreme Language. "Predicated on" means wholly dependent on. If swap-line decisions were entirely predicated on openness, the restrictive countries would have a probability of 0, not 0.03. The data shows influence, not absolute dependence.
  • B. mediated by — Trap: Out of Scope. "Mediated by" implies an indirect process working through an intervening agent. The text describes a direct statistical association between policy openness and outcomes, with no middleman mechanism mentioned.
  • C. decoupled from — Trap: Opposite Meaning. "Decoupled from" means disconnected. The 0.20-versus-0.03 gap proves the two are strongly connected, the reverse of what this word claims.
  • D. material to — Correct. It captures exactly what the numbers show: the policy environment had a significant, relevant effect on swap-line decisions without implying it was the sole cause.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a colon is followed by numbers or data, let that evidence calibrate the strength of your word choice. A moderate, accurate phrase ("material to") usually beats an absolute one ("predicated on") when the data shows a strong but not perfect relationship — watch for nonzero values that rule out total dependence.
