questions.passage: Though John Crowley, author of Four Freedoms, is perhaps not as well known as the most widely read American writers of the past fifty years, influential figures have championed his work, including the poet James Merrill and the literary critic Harold Bloom. In his afterword to Crowley's book Little, Big, Bloom praises the novel's adroit blend of what playwright Friedrich Schiller termed the naive and sentimental modes—while Schiller thought works could be classified as either naive (seeking to describe reality) or sentimental (seeking to develop ideas), Little, Big demonstrates that a work can be both.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
Correct answer: A. Domain: Craft and Structure; Skill: Text Structure and Purpose. Difficulty: medium. The task is to identify the single overall purpose the author had in writing the passage.

Core Concepts

  • Main purpose = the author's primary reason for writing the text as a whole, not a minor detail. Ask: "What is the one thing this paragraph is trying to do?"
  • Distractor traps for purpose questions: choices that are too narrow (only cover one detail), out of scope (mention something the text never does), or opposite (state the reverse of what the text shows).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 introduces author John Crowley and notes that, although he is not famous, influential figures such as poet James Merrill and literary critic Harold Bloom have championed his work.
  • Sentence 2 zooms in on Bloom: in his afterword to Crowley's Little, Big, Bloom praises the novel's "adroit blend" of the naive and sentimental modes. The text then explains that, while Schiller treated those modes as mutually exclusive, Little, Big shows a work can be both.
  • Function of the whole: the passage builds toward explaining the specific reason a respected critic admires a particular novel. That is the author's main goal.

Why Each Answer

  • A (correct): "To present a reason why a literary critic is impressed by a certain novel." The literary critic is Bloom, the novel is Little, Big, and the reason is its skillful blend of the two modes. This captures the text's overall purpose.
  • B — Out of Scope: The text never discusses what inspired Crowley to write; it discusses why a critic admires the result.
  • C — Out of Scope / Misuse of Detail: James Merrill is named only as an admirer. The text never compares Merrill's poetry to Crowley's writing.
  • D — Opposite: The passage shows a work can be both naive and sentimental, which refutes (rather than argues for) the idea that all writing must fall into one of two categories.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "main purpose" questions, sum up the passage in your own words before reading the options, then eliminate any choice that is too narrow, brings in something never mentioned, or states the opposite of the text. The answer almost always restates the passage's central action verb here, "explaining why someone admires something."
questions.question_text: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

question_options.option_text: To argue that all writing must be classified as belonging to one of two categories
To explain what inspired an author to write a particular work
To compare the work of a writer with the work of a poet who admired him
To present a reason why a literary critic is impressed by a certain novel

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from George Eliot's 1857 short story "The Sad Fortunes of the Rev.

Amos Barton." Mr. Ely is a clergyman in the town of Milby.

By the laity of Milby and its neighbourhood [Mr. Ely] was regarded as a man of quite remarkable powers and learning, who must make a considerable sensation in London pulpits and drawing-rooms on his occasional visit to the metropolis; and by his brother clergy he was regarded as a discreet and agreeable fellow. Mr. Ely never got into a warm discussion; he suggested what might be thought, but rarely said what he thought himself; he never let either men or women see that he was laughing at them, and he never gave any one an opportunity of laughing at him.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is a Craft and Structure question testing Text Structure and Purpose, at medium difficulty. The task is to describe how the passage is organized as a whole.

Core Concepts
An "overall structure" question asks you to summarize what each part of the text does and how the parts relate. The key skills are:

  • Divide the text into its functional chunks (here, the first part vs. the second part).
  • State the job each chunk performs (e.g., presents an opinion, gives an explanation, draws a contrast).
  • Match those jobs to the answer choice that describes BOTH parts accurately.

Watch for choices that describe one half correctly but distort the other, or that add ideas (naivety, falling reputation, public-vs-private contrast) the text never states.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Part 1 (the opinions): The laity of Milby regard Mr. Ely as a man of "quite remarkable powers and learning," and his fellow clergy regard him as "a discreet and agreeable fellow." Both groups hold him in high, favorable esteem.
  • Part 2 (the behaviors): The text then lists how he acts. He "never got into a warm discussion," "suggested what might be thought, but rarely said what he thought himself," and "never gave any one an opportunity of laughing at him." These cautious habits keep him from ever exposing himself to criticism.
  • Linking the parts: The careful behaviors in Part 2 are precisely what lets him keep the favorable reputation described in Part 1. So the structure is: favorable opinion stated, then behaviors that sustain it.

Why Each Answer

  • B (correct): It "presents the favorable opinion of Mr. Ely that other people hold" (Part 1) "and then describes the behaviors... that enable him to maintain that favorable opinion" (Part 2). This matches both halves exactly.
  • A (incorrect) - Out of Scope / Unsupported: The text never claims his neighbors are more naive than Londoners, nor that anyone is being "misled." It reports genuine esteem, not deception of gullible people.
  • C (incorrect) - Factually Inaccurate: Nothing shows his reputation declining; there are no "events that caused their regard... to subside." His standing remains intact throughout.
  • D (incorrect) - Distorts the Text: The passage does not contrast a public self with a hidden private self. It explains how he avoids exposing any opinion at all, not a gap between two versions of him.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "overall structure" questions, write a two-word label for each half before reading the choices (here: "reputation, then behaviors"). Then eliminate any choice that mislabels either half or smuggles in a new idea the text never supports.
questions.question_text: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

question_options.option_text: It implies that Mr. Ely's neighbors are more naive in their estimation of him than people in London are and then explains why his neighbors have been so easily misled.
It highlights the disparity between Mr. Ely's public and private behavior and then conveys why he labors to obscure his true self from other people.
It shows that Mr. Ely had originally been held in high regard by his friends and then details the events that caused their regard for him to subside.
It presents the favorable opinion of Mr. Ely that other people hold and then describes the behaviors of Mr. Ely that enable him to maintain that favorable opinion.

questions.passage:
Text 1 is adapted from E.M. Forster's 1910 novel Howards End.

Text 2 discusses Howards End. King's Cross and St. Pancras are adjacent railway terminals in London from which trains travel to the countryside.

Text 1
To Margaret the station of King's Cross had always suggested Infinity. Its very situation—withdrawn a little behind the facile splendours of St. Pancras—implied a comment on the materialism of life. Those two great arches, colourless, indifferent, shouldering between them an unlovely clock, were fit portals for some eternal adventure, whose issue might be prosperous, but would certainly not be expressed in the ordinary language of prosperity.

Text 2
The interplay between opposing ideological positions in Howards End is broadly articulated in the novel's organization of geographic space. On the one hand, the modern metropolis of London represents capitalism's emphasis on pragmatism and the accumulation of material wealth; on the other, the English countryside, accessible via King's Cross, fosters an idealism that values tradition, authentic personal connection, and the aesthetic—what the novel calls "the infinite."
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C. This is a Craft and Structure question testing Cross-Text Connections at a hard difficulty level. The task is to determine how the author of Text 2 (a critic analyzing the novel) would interpret the depiction of King's Cross given in Text 1 (the novel itself).

Core Concepts

  • Cross-Text Connections: These questions give you two texts on a shared topic and ask how one author would respond to, agree with, or apply ideas to the other. The strategy is to (1) pin down each text's central claim, then (2) find the single answer choice that is fully supported by BOTH texts working together.
  • Reading for stance, not just topic: You must capture the attitude or value each author assigns to King's Cross, not merely that they both mention it.
  • Key vocabulary in these texts: "Infinity" / "the infinite" = something beyond ordinary material life; "idealism" = valuing intangible goods like tradition, beauty, and genuine human connection over money; "materialism/pragmatism" = valuing wealth and practical gain.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Text 1's claim: To Margaret, King's Cross "had always suggested Infinity." Its plain, "colourless, indifferent" arches are "fit portals for some eternal adventure" whose reward "would certainly not be expressed in the ordinary language of prosperity." So Margaret links the station to a non-material, spiritual or idealistic kind of richness.
  • Text 2's claim: The novel maps two opposing ideologies onto geography. London = capitalism, pragmatism, material wealth. The countryside, "accessible via King's Cross," = idealism that values "tradition, authentic personal connection, and the aesthetic—what the novel calls 'the infinite.'"
  • Connecting them: Text 2 explicitly ties King's Cross to the countryside and to "the infinite" and "authentic personal connection." Text 1 shows Margaret feeling exactly that — the station promises "Infinity" and a prosperity beyond ordinary material terms. So Text 2's author would read Margaret's impression as King's Cross being the doorway to the intangible, idealistic rewards of rural life.

Why Each Answer

  • C (Correct): It names King's Cross as "a point of connection between London and the countryside" that suggests "the intangible abundance" (matching Text 1's non-ordinary prosperity and "Infinity") found through "authentic engagements" (matching Text 2's "authentic personal connection"). Both texts directly support every part of this statement.
  • A (Incorrect — Opposite/Reversal): It casts King's Cross as the "intrusion of materialism and modernity" into the countryside. This reverses both texts: Text 1 sets King's Cross apart from "the materialism of life," and Text 2 ties it to idealism, not to materialism invading rural space.
  • B (Incorrect — Distorted Tone): It claims Margaret feels "disillusionment" about authentic connection. Text 1's tone is hopeful, not disillusioned — the station is a "portal for some eternal adventure." The choice twists her optimism into despair.
  • D (Incorrect — Opposite/Reversal): It says the contrast with St. Pancras shows "the ascendancy of the pragmatic capitalistic outlook." But Text 1 says the very situation of King's Cross "implied a comment on the materialism of life" and suggested "Infinity" — a critique of materialism, not its triumph.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
On Cross-Text questions, hunt for an explicit bridge word that appears in both texts. Here, both texts use "the infinite"/"Infinity" and both link King's Cross to the countryside. The right answer almost always echoes that shared bridge; trap answers usually flip the author's value (calling something materialistic when the text calls it idealistic, or vice versa).
questions.question_text: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement about King's Cross, as it is depicted in Text 1?

question_options.option_text: As a point of connection between London and the countryside, King's Cross suggests to Margaret the possibility of acquiring the intangible abundance promised by the kinds of authentic engagements that the novel's rural spaces seem to offer.

The austerity conveyed by King's Cross's appearance mirrors Margaret's disillusionment with the prospect of having authentic connections with other people in a world that chiefly values more conventional forms of prosperity.

Because it is situated at the beginning of Margaret's journey from the city to the country, King's Cross emblematizes the intrusion of the forces of materialism and modernity into the rural spaces that the novel associates with idealism and tradition.

King's Cross has a relatively unassuming appearance whose sharp contrast with the more aesthetically pleasing appearance of St. Pancras suggests to Margaret the ascendancy of the pragmatic capitalistic outlook among London's inhabitants.

questions.passage: Mexican architect Luis Barragán's prolific career, which spanned the 1920s to the 1980s, evolved through distinct phases. After traveling to the United States and Europe in the early 1930s and immersing himself in a broader architectural discourse, Barragán began incorporating principles derived from functionalism and modernism in his work, as seen in the apartment building at 14 Parque Melchor Ocampo, whose unadorned geometric forms contrast with his earlier projects in Guadalajara, such as the Carmen Orozco House, which evince the aesthetics of traditional Mediterranean and Mexican styles.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the skill of Central Ideas and Details. Difficulty: medium. The task is to find the statement about the Carmen Orozco House that the passage's information best supports.

Core Concepts
This is an inference/detail question. You are not asked what is stated word-for-word, but which conclusion the text most directly justifies. Key vocabulary to anchor on:

  • Functionalism / modernism — design movements that favor plain, simple, geometric shapes and reject decorative detail.
  • Unadorned — without ornamentation or decoration.
  • Evince — to clearly show or display.
  • Contrast — a key signal word: it tells you two things are being set against each other as opposites.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence function: The passage tracks how Barragán's style changed over time. He started with one approach, then shifted to another after traveling.
  • Early phase: His earlier Guadalajara projects, including the Carmen Orozco House, "evince the aesthetics of traditional Mediterranean and Mexican styles" — meaning they were decorative and rooted in tradition.
  • Later phase: After his early-1930s travels to the US and Europe, he adopted "principles derived from functionalism and modernism," producing work with "unadorned geometric forms."
  • The pivot: The text explicitly says the later "unadorned geometric forms contrast with his earlier projects... such as the Carmen Orozco House." The word contrast tells us the Carmen Orozco House represents the OLD approach that the new, plainer style replaced.
  • Conclusion: The Carmen Orozco House reflects an ornamental, traditional approach that Barragán moved away from once he embraced modernism. That is exactly choice D.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Out of Scope / Misrepresents): The text frames the Carmen Orozco House as a clear example of his EARLY phase, not a transitional point between phases. The transition occurred during and after his travels, with the modernist apartment building, not this house.
  • B (Wrong Subject): The exposure to international trends in the 1930s produced the apartment building at 14 Parque Melchor Ocampo, not the Carmen Orozco House. This option swaps the two buildings.
  • C (Extreme Language / Contradiction): "Throughout his career" contradicts the passage, which uses contrast to show this traditional style characterized only his earlier work and was later abandoned.
  • D (Correct): The house shows traditional, ornamental aesthetics; the text states his later unadorned modernist work contrasts with it — so this is an approach to ornamentation and shape he later stopped using.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a passage uses a contrast signal ("contrast with," "unlike," "whereas"), the example on the OLD side of the contrast represents something the subject moved away from. Match the answer choice to which side of the contrast the named item sits on, and watch for traps that assign one building's traits to the other.
questions.question_text: Information in the text best supports which statement about the design of the Carmen Orozco House?

question_options.option_text: It reflects an approach to ornamentation and shape that Barragán later stopped using.
It represents a transitional moment between the early and late phases of Barragán's development.
It displays the effects of Barragán's exposure to international architectural trends in the 1930s.
It is characteristic of the Guadalajaran architecture that influenced Barragán throughout his career.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Mick Herron's 2023 novel The Secret Hours.

The narrator is describing members of a government committee.

Finally, and adding much-needed gravitas, was Sir Winston Day, whose features seemed moulded to adorn a bust, or possibly a stamp, and whose forehead was so evidently bulging with grey matter that it would have been impertinent to inquire too closely into the actual achievements his half century of public service had produced. His recently published memoirs possibly cast light on this enigma, but given that such details were not provided until after the thirty-page mark, they might as well have remained state secrets.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the skill of Central Ideas and Details, rated hard. The task is to capture how the narrator characterizes Sir Winston Day across the whole passage.

Core Concepts
To describe a character accurately, you must read the narrator's tone, not just the literal words. A few vocabulary anchors here:

  • Gravitas = a dignified, serious, weighty presence.
  • Features "moulded to adorn a bust, or possibly a stamp" = he looks like the kind of important person whose face gets carved in stone or printed on a stamp.
  • Impertinent = rude or out of line.
  • Enigma = a mystery, something puzzling.
The key technique is verbal irony: the narrator praises Day's appearance of importance while quietly signaling that no one can confirm he has actually done anything important.

Step-by-Step Breakdown
Sentence 1 (appearance): Day adds "much-needed gravitas" and has features fit for a bust or a stamp, with a forehead "so evidently bulging with grey matter" that questioning his real accomplishments would seem "impertinent." Notice the hedge: his importance is something you'd be rude to question, not something the text actually proves.
Sentence 2 (substance): His "actual achievements" are an "enigma." His memoirs might explain them, but the details come only after the thirty-page mark, so they "might as well have remained state secrets" because no one reads that far.
Combine: Distinguished look + unverifiable substance = the narrator is gently mocking a man who seems important but whose accomplishments no one can actually point to.

Why Each Answer
A (Correct): "Appearance of a distinguished figure, but uncertain whether he has accomplished anything to earn distinction" matches the appearance/substance contrast exactly.
B (Factually Inaccurate): Says he kept a "modest profile" and "served the public capably." Both fail: he projects loud gravitas (not modesty), and the text never confirms capable service, it treats his achievements as a mystery.
C (Out of Scope / Unsupported): Claims his memoirs reveal "dishonorable" actions. The text never says his deeds were dishonorable, only that they are unknown because the memoirs go unread.
D (Distorts the Detail): Says he'd be celebrated if his achievements "did not have to be kept secret." Nothing requires secrecy; the "state secrets" line is a joke about details being buried too deep in an unread book, not an actual need for concealment.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a narrator lavishes praise yet keeps hedging ("it would have been impertinent to inquire," "might as well have remained state secrets"), that hedging is the real message. Trust the ironic undertone: praise the package, doubt the contents.
questions.question_text: Based on the text, which choice best describes Sir Winston Day?

question_options.option_text: He has the appearance of a distinguished figure, but it is uncertain whether he has accomplished anything to earn distinction.
He would be a celebrated public figure if his achievements did not have to be kept secret.
He has maintained a modest profile even though he has served the public capably for many years.
He looks like a person worthy of respect, but his memoirs reveal that some of his actions were dishonorable.

questions.passage: Edinburgh, Scotland, has installed engineered structures along 89% of its shoreline to protect infrastructure from wave erosion and other hazards, a practice known as shoreline hardening. To evaluate the responses of waterbirds to two types of hardening structures—riprap and bulkheads—Diann Prosser et al. surveyed waterbird communities consisting of the osprey, the common tern, and 62 other species at different sites in the Chesapeake Bay on the US East Coast. Utilizing the Index of Waterbird Community Integrity (IWCI), on which a high score corresponds to high community integrity, the researchers found that bulkheads are more strongly negatively correlated with waterbird community integrity than is riprap.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the Command of Evidence skill (medium difficulty). You must pick the hypothetical finding that best illustrates the researchers' stated conclusion.

Core Concepts
A few terms to lock in before reasoning:

  • Shoreline hardening: installing engineered structures (here, riprap and bulkheads) along a shoreline to protect against waves and erosion.
  • IWCI (Index of Waterbird Community Integrity): a score where a higher number means higher community integrity (healthier bird community), and a lower number means lower integrity.
  • Negative correlation: as one thing goes up, the other goes down. "Bulkheads are more strongly negatively correlated with integrity than riprap" means more bulkheads drags integrity down harder than the same amount of riprap does.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The researchers' conclusion: bulkheads hurt waterbird community integrity more than riprap does.
  • To illustrate this, a finding must hold one structure type against the other and show the bulkhead-heavy place coming out worse.
  • So the ideal example is: a site dominated by bulkheads scores LOWER on IWCI than a site dominated by riprap.
  • Option B states exactly this: Old Road (high % bulkheads) had lower IWCI scores than Miles (high % riprap). Bulkhead site = lower integrity, riprap site = higher integrity. That is the conclusion in concrete form.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Incorrect — Fails to Isolate the Variable): Both Curtis and Onancock are described by the combined amount of bulkheads and riprap, so it compares "lots of both" to "little of both." It never separates the effect of bulkheads from riprap, so it cannot show bulkheads are worse.
  • B (Correct): It directly contrasts a bulkhead-heavy site against a riprap-heavy site and shows the bulkhead site has lower integrity — a clean illustration of the conclusion.
  • C (Incorrect — Confused Comparison): Curtis is "equal percentages" of both and Miles has "different percentages," with the bulkhead-mixed site scoring higher. This neither isolates bulkheads nor matches the predicted direction (bulkheads should lower the score).
  • D (Incorrect — No Contrast / Null Result): Both Stony and Old Road have more bulkheads than riprap, so they're the same type of site, and a "statistically insignificant" difference shows no effect at all — the opposite of illustrating a difference between the two structures.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "illustrate/support the finding" Command of Evidence items, translate the conclusion into an if-then prediction first (here: more bulkheads → lower IWCI than more riprap), then keep only the choice that changes ONE variable (bulkhead vs riprap) and matches the predicted direction. Toss any option that lumps both structures together or reports no difference.
questions.question_text: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?

question_options.option_text: Waterbird communities at Old Road, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads, had lower average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Miles, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of riprap.

Waterbird communities at Curtis, a site with equal percentages of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap, had higher average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Miles, a site with different percentages of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap.

The difference in average IWCI scores for waterbird communities at Stony and Old Road, two sites with a higher percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads than of riprap, was statistically insignificant.

Waterbird communities at Curtis, a site with a high percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap, had lower average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Onancock, a site with a low percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap.

questions.passage: For its 2022 exhibition Guarding the Art, the Baltimore Museum of Art cast the security personnel typically responsible for safeguarding the institution's collections as the curators, whose individual selections from the museum's holdings culminated in a show amplifying a distinct perspective not typically given a formal platform.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C. This is an Information and Ideas question testing Command of Evidence (Text-Based). Difficulty: hard. Your job is to pick the quote that, if true, would most directly back up a specific claim already stated in the passage.

Core Concepts
A Command of Evidence (text) question gives you a claim and asks which quotation would best support it. To do this well:

  • Pin down the claim word-for-word and break it into its required pieces. The supporting quote must hit every piece, not just one.
  • "Support" means the quote provides a concrete example or detail that makes the claim true. A quote can be on-topic yet still fail if it misses part of the claim.
  • Watch for distractors that match the general subject (the exhibition, the guards) but address a different idea than the exact claim.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Locate the claim. The underlined portion says the personnel's selections "culminated in a show amplifying a distinct perspective not typically given a formal platform."
  • Split the claim into parts. (1) a distinct / individual perspective, and (2) one that is not typically given a formal platform (i.e., usually unheard or expressed only informally), now (3) amplified by being placed in the exhibition.
  • Test the quotes against both parts. The winning quote must show an individual viewpoint that previously had no formal outlet and is now showcased.
  • Match. Option C describes a guard's "personal interpretation" (part 1: a distinct perspective) that they had "previously shared only in small impromptu conversations" (part 2: no formal platform) and is now "accompanied by a statement" in the show (part 3: amplified formally). All three pieces are satisfied.

Why Each Answer

  • A: Correct trap type: Out of Scope. It praises the show's range of "genres, mediums, cultures, and eras" and the guards' "affinity" for the art, but never describes a personal viewpoint that previously lacked a formal platform.
  • B: Wrong Focus / Half-Match. It addresses publicizing "lesser-known artifacts" (the objects), not amplifying a distinct perspective of the personnel that had no formal outlet.
  • C: Correct. It supplies both required pieces: a distinct personal interpretation and the fact that it was formerly confined to "small impromptu conversations," now formally presented.
  • D: Out of Scope. It emphasizes collaboration with professional curators and conservators, which speaks to expertise-sharing, not to elevating a previously unplatformed individual perspective.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "which quote supports the claim" items, underline the claim and chop it into its 2-3 conditions, then eliminate any quote that misses even one condition. Here the deciding phrase was "not typically given a formal platform" - only C explicitly contrasts an informal past ("impromptu conversations") with the formal exhibition.
questions.question_text: Which quote from one of the personnel who curated the exhibition would best support the underlined claim?

question_options.option_text: "Throughout the exhibition's development, my colleagues and I partnered closely with other museum staff whose areas of expertise lie in curation and conservation, and whose insights enriched our understandings of the pieces we selected for the exhibition."

"My selections for the show were motivated by an interest in bringing publicity to lesser-known artifacts in the museum's collection, many of which tend to be overlooked or even dismissed as uninteresting by most visitors to the museum."

"The most enjoyable part of curating this show has been seeing the outcome of our efforts: a unique show that spans genres, mediums, cultures, and eras. We hope visitors will sense our genuine affinity for the pieces we are charged with protecting."

"The piece I chose is accompanied by a statement of the personal interpretation I've developed over countless hours overseeing the work and interacting with its visitors—an interpretation that I've previously shared only in small impromptu conversations with those visitors who are interested in discussing their reflections on the piece with me."

questions.passage: A student is writing an essay on the subject of cultured meat, which is grown in a laboratory and is intended to help reduce the number of livestock harvested for food. The student wants to make the case that cultured meat production may be useful in responding to an expected widespread change in the public's behavior.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C. This is an Information and Ideas question testing Command of Evidence (supporting a claim with a quotation). Difficulty: medium. Your job is to pick the quotation that best backs up the student's specific argument.

Core Concepts
A Command of Evidence claim-support question gives you a stated claim and asks which piece of text would most directly prove it. The rules:

  • Pin down the EXACT claim. Here the claim has two parts: (1) cultured (lab-grown) meat may be useful, and (2) it responds to an expected widespread change in the public's behavior.
  • The winning quotation must match the claim's key idea, not just the general topic. A quote can be about meat and still be wrong if it does not address the specific point.
  • The phrase change in the public's behavior means people, on a large scale, doing something differently — in this context, eating more meat.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Restate the claim: cultured meat could help deal with a coming, large-scale shift in how the public behaves.
  • Step 2 — Translate the needed evidence: we need a quote that names a widespread behavioral change (most logically, a rise in meat consumption or demand) that cultured meat could then help satisfy.
  • Step 3 — Test each quote against that requirement, keeping only the one that describes a behavioral shift.
  • Step 4 — Option C says a growing population is including significantly more meat in its diet, increasing demand for meat in the 21st century. That is precisely a widespread change in public behavior, and rising demand is exactly what cultured meat could help meet.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Out of Scope): Talks about consumers' beliefs regarding packaging and the environment. It never mentions a change in meat-eating behavior, so it cannot support the claim.
  • B (Wrong Focus): Describes how meat flavor varies by species, farming conditions, breed, and gender. This is about meat quality, not about a behavioral change cultured meat would address.
  • C (Correct): States that a growing population is eating significantly more meat, driving up demand — an expected, widespread behavioral change that cultured meat production could help respond to. Matches the claim directly.
  • D (Right Topic, Wrong Point): Mentions environmental advantages of lab-grown meat (less water). It is on the cultured-meat topic but describes a benefit, not a change in public behavior, so it misses what the claim actually argues.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For claim-support questions, underline the most specific phrase in the claim — here, change in the public's behavior. Then reject any choice that is merely on-topic but does not hit that exact phrase. Three of the four meat-related quotes are traps precisely because they are about meat in general; only one describes a behavioral shift.
questions.question_text: Which quotation from a publication by a researcher would most effectively support the student's claim?

question_options.option_text: "The flavor of meat from livestock differs across species (from pig to chicken to cow), and is also influenced by farming conditions and the breeds and genders of animals."
"Researchers who advocate for the development of lab-grown meat claim that it's better for the environment than conventional meat because it requires less water consumption."
"Consumers tend to believe that using less packaging when selling meat products in stores would have a significant effect on the environment."
"A growing population that is including significantly more meat in its diet will contribute to an increasing demand for meat products in the 21st century."

questions.passage: Born in Chile in 1917, artist and ethnomusicologist Violeta Parra was a pioneer in the nueva canción chilena (Chilean New Song) movement that emerged in the late 1950s and then spread throughout Latin America, Portugal, and Spain as nueva canción. Parra traveled all over Chile compiling extensive records of authentic folk music as well as recipes, proverbs, and other facets of cultural history. These records formed the foundation for the early movement's revival of traditional Chilean folk forms in new songs that represented modern realities of the working class and strongly advocated for social change. As the movement spread beyond Chile, the breadth of musical traditions incorporated into its foundation also expanded.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is an Information and Ideas question testing Command of Evidence at a medium difficulty. Your job is to find the single detail that, if true, would best support (illustrate) a specific claim made in the passage.

Core Concepts
An "illustrate the claim" question gives you a claim and asks which new fact would serve as the strongest, most direct example of it. The winning choice must match the claim word-for-word in meaning, not just touch the same topic. Key vocabulary here:

  • nueva canción: a folk-rooted song movement that began in Chile and spread across Latin America and Europe.
  • "musical traditions incorporated into its foundation": the actual styles, genres, and instruments that the music is built from, not its lyrics or its geography.
  • "breadth expanded": the variety of those traditions grew to include sources from outside Chile.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The underlined claim states: as the movement spread beyond Chile, the breadth of musical traditions incorporated into its foundation also expanded.
  • Break the claim into two requirements the correct detail must satisfy: (1) it must point to a musical tradition (a genre, style, or instrument), and (2) that tradition must come from outside Chile, showing the foundation widening.
  • Test each choice against both requirements and keep only the one that meets both.

Why Each Answer

  • B (Correct): It says many songs show the stylistic influence of corrido, a narrative song genre from Mexico. This is a musical tradition (requirement 1) sourced from a country other than Chile (requirement 2), so it directly demonstrates the foundation expanding as the movement spread. It meets both parts of the claim.
  • A (Out of Scope): It describes lyrical/thematic content (political commentary about colonization), not a musical tradition added to the foundation. It addresses what the songs are about, not what they are built from, so it fails requirement 1.
  • C (Wrong Direction): The quena flute is a musical tradition, but the choice notes it is used across Andean countries "including Chile." Since it is already tied to Chile, it does not show the breadth expanding beyond Chilean origins, failing requirement 2.
  • D (Confuses geography with musical sources): It reports where artists were located (Argentina, then elsewhere), which shows the movement spreading geographically but says nothing about new musical traditions entering its foundation. It fails requirement 1.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "illustrate the claim" questions, underline the exact noun the claim is about, here it is "musical traditions." Then eliminate any choice that swaps in a different noun (lyrics, themes, geography, dates). The mental trigger: the right answer echoes the claim's keyword and adds a concrete out-of-scope example, B adds a non-Chilean genre.
questions.question_text: Which detail about songs associated with nueva canción, if true, would best illustrate the underlined claim?

question_options.option_text: Many were produced by Argentinian artists in the late 1950s, with others by artists in additional Latin American countries first emerging soon after.
Many demonstrate the stylistic influence of corrido, a genre of narrative songs from Mexico that had come to be characterized by political themes in the early 1800s.
Many feature political commentary addressing contemporary issues that stemmed from shared experiences of European colonization in Latin American countries.
Many were written with parts meant to be played on the quena, a traditional flute used across Andean countries, including Chile.

questions.passage: The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires US federal agencies to assess environmental effects of potential actions, such as building highways. While many NEPA reviews require public comment, categorical exclusions (CEs) allow quick reviews with no public comment for actions that will minimally affect the environment. In 2020 the rule governing CEs was revised: before, CEs could be granted for actions that "do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment," but the revised rule allowed CEs if actions "normally do not have a significant effect on the human environment." Environmentalists found this revision to be potentially detrimental because __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D. This is a Reading and Writing question in the Information and Ideas domain, testing the Inferences skill. Difficulty: hard. The task is to logically complete the final sentence, which explains why environmentalists viewed the 2020 rule change as harmful.

Core Concepts
A few terms to define from scratch:

  • NEPA review: a federal check on the environmental effects of a proposed action (e.g., building a highway).
  • Categorical exclusion (CE): a fast-track review with no public comment, granted when an action is expected to have minimal environmental impact.
  • Individually vs. cumulatively: "Individually" means the effect of one action by itself. "Cumulatively" means the combined effect of many actions added together. A single small project may be harmless alone but harmful when many such projects pile up.
  • Logical completion: the blank must state a consequence of the wording change that genuinely justifies the word "detrimental."

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets context: NEPA requires environmental assessment of federal actions.
  • Sentence 2 defines CEs as quick, no-comment reviews for minimal-impact actions.
  • Sentence 3 contrasts the old and new wording. Old rule: CEs for actions that "do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect." Revised rule: CEs for actions that "normally do not have a significant effect."
  • The pivotal change is what disappeared: the old standard explicitly required that an action be harmless both on its own AND in combination with others. The new standard drops the "cumulatively" condition entirely.
  • Therefore, an action that is minor by itself but significant when stacked with many similar actions could now slip through as a CE, escaping full review and public comment.
  • That loophole is exactly what would make environmentalists call the revision "potentially detrimental," so the blank should describe this cumulative-impact gap.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Out of Scope): The passage never mentions a growing need to build or repair highways or any incentive to grant CEs for newly "valid" reasons. This invents motivation the text does not supply.
  • B (Factually Inaccurate / Self-contradicting): More exclusions would mean fewer full reviews, not more, and CEs speed up the process. Claiming the change causes more reviews and a slower process contradicts how CEs work.
  • C (Reverses the Logic): The pre-2020 rule did not grant expedited reviews to actions with significant effects; it excluded them. This option flips the cause and effect of the rule change.
  • D (Correct): It precisely captures the lost "cumulatively" safeguard: actions with "a minimal environmental effect when considered on their own but a significant effect when considered together" could now receive expedited CE reviews. This is a concrete, well-supported reason the revision is detrimental.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
On "complete the text" inference items, anchor on the exact contrast the passage highlights. Here, compare the two quoted phrases word-for-word: the only thing removed is "cumulatively." The right answer almost always names that specific deleted or changed element, so let the wording difference point you straight to choice D.
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: the 2020 revision of the rule governing CEs would allow expedited reviews of actions that had a minimal environmental effect when considered on their own but a significant effect when considered together.
the 2020 relaxation of the rule regarding CEs would permit more exclusions, resulting in more reviews of actions by federal agencies and a paradoxically slower review process.
the increasing need to build new highways and rehabilitate older highways in the US incentivizes agencies to grant CEs after 2020 for reasons that would not have been considered valid prior to 2020.

the rule that governed CEs before 2020 allowed expedited reviews of actions that might have significant effects on the environment if those effects were believed to be rare, while the 2020 revision of the rule subjected such actions to slower reviews.

questions.passage: Microbial fuel cells (MFCs) capitalize on the ability of some species of bacteria to metabolize metal, liberating electrons. The bacteria form a dense biofilm on the surface of an electron-collecting anode, but moving the electrons from the bacterial cytoplasm to an external electrode requires that the electrons pass through a series of inefficient oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. Accordingly, MFC power output rarely exceeds a density of \(0.30\) milliwatts per square centimeter (\(mW/cm^{2}\)). In an experiment, researchers added silver nanoparticles to carbon paper covering the anode in an MFC. The resulting power density was \(0.66 \text{ mW/cm}^2\). Since metals such as silver exhibit high electrical conductivity, the researchers hypothesized that __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the Inferences skill, rated hard. Your job is to complete the researchers' hypothesis with the conclusion that follows most logically from the evidence in the passage.

Core Concepts

  • Hypothesis completion: The blank follows the word "hypothesized that," so the right choice must be a claim the researchers could reasonably propose to explain their result. It must be supported by the passage's stated cause-and-effect logic, not introduce a new idea.
  • The bottleneck described: In a microbial fuel cell (MFC), bacteria release electrons, but those electrons must travel through "a series of inefficient oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions" to reach the electrode. "Inefficient" means power is lost along this path, which is why output rarely exceeds \(0.30 \text{ mW/cm}^2\).
  • The change made: Researchers added silver nanoparticles, and the passage stresses one property of silver: "high electrical conductivity." Conductivity means electrons move easily and directly through a material.
  • The result: Power density rose to \(0.66 \text{ mW/cm}^2\), more than double the typical maximum.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify the problem: the inefficient redox chain is what limits power.
  • Identify the fix: a highly conductive material (silver) was added and performance jumped.
  • Connect them: if a conductor improved output, the natural explanation is that the conductor gave the electrons a better, more direct route, sidestepping the inefficient redox steps.
  • Therefore the hypothesis should say silver lets electrons avoid the inefficient redox reactions and move straight to the electrode. That is choice D.

Why Each Answer

  • D (Correct): States that silver nanoparticles "may allow electrons to bypass the series of redox reactions and transfer directly to the electrode." This directly links the stated cause (silver's high conductivity) to the observed effect (higher power), exactly the reasoning the passage sets up.
  • A (Out of Scope): Claims silver boosts the bacteria's metabolism to free more electrons. The passage attributes silver's relevance to electrical conductivity, never to any biological effect on the bacteria.
  • B (Contradicts the Setup): Credits the improvement to biofilm density acting "independent of the presence of the silver nanoparticles." Silver was the one variable researchers changed, so a hypothesis dismissing silver cannot explain why they got the result.
  • C (Misrepresents the Evidence): Calls silver a catalyst of the redox reactions. The passage describes silver as a conductor, not a catalyst, and the phrasing is muddled. Silver's role is to carry electrons, not to speed up the inefficient reactions.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "complete the hypothesis" questions, underline the single property the author emphasizes (here, "high electrical conductivity") and the single problem they raise ("inefficient redox reactions"). The answer almost always ties that property directly to solving that problem. Reject any choice that introduces a different mechanism (metabolism, catalysis) or ignores the variable that was actually tested.
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: silver nanoparticles may increase the metabolic processes of the bacteria, thereby increasing the number of free electrons available to transfer to the electrode.
as the density of the biofilm increases, the series of redox reactions may accelerate independent of the presence of the silver nanoparticles.
silver nanoparticles may allow electrons to bypass the series of redox reactions and transfer directly to the electrode.
electrons may be conducted directly to the electrode before the silver nanoparticles catalyze the redox reactions.

questions.passage: Included in Serial Intent, a 2017 group exhibition at the Akron Art Museum in Ohio, was the work of artist Lorna Simpson, who is best known for her multimedia artworks that juxtapose images of African American women with text fragments. Her work challenges conventional notions of race, gender, history, and __________ she is credited with expanding the horizons of conceptual photographic art.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D ("memory, and"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill, at medium difficulty. The task is to choose the punctuation/conjunction that correctly connects the two halves of the sentence.

Core Concepts

  • Independent clause: a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence (e.g., "she is credited with expanding the horizons of conceptual photographic art").
  • Joining two independent clauses: two complete sentences cannot simply be pushed together. One valid method is a comma + a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — "FANBOYS").
  • Comma splice: the error of joining two independent clauses with only a comma and no conjunction.
  • Run-on (fused sentence): the error of joining two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction at all.
  • Serial list: the items "race, gender, history, and memory" form a list; the word "and" with the blank is what completes that list.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • First clause: "Her work challenges conventional notions of race, gender, history, and memory" — this has a subject ("Her work") and a verb ("challenges"), so it is independent. The blank fills the final list item "memory."
  • Second clause: "she is credited with expanding the horizons of conceptual photographic art" — this has a subject ("she") and a verb ("is credited"), so it is also independent.
  • Because two independent clauses meet at the blank, we need a way to join them. The reliable fix is a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction: "memory, and she is credited..."
  • Note the two "and" roles are separate: the "and" before the blank closes the list, and the added ", and" supplies the conjunction that links the clauses.

Why Each Answer

  • D "memory, and" — Correct. Supplies both the comma and the coordinating conjunction, properly joining the two independent clauses.
  • A "memory," — Incorrect (Comma Splice). A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
  • B "memory and" — Incorrect (Missing Comma). A coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses still requires a comma before it; without the comma the boundary is not punctuated correctly.
  • C "memory" — Incorrect (Run-on). Provides neither punctuation nor a conjunction, fusing the two clauses.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a blank sits between two word groups that could each stand alone as sentences, test for the comma + FANBOYS pattern. Mentally split the sentence at the blank: if both sides are complete thoughts, the safest connector is ",and / ,but / ,so" — a bare comma is a splice and no mark at all is a run-on.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: Enacted in 2006, Nepal's constitution, according to legal __________ contains all of the six constitutional features that enhance judicial independence. Explicit provisions for judicial independence, Melton and Ginsburg's research explains, are more likely to be found in constitutions enacted after 1985.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill (punctuating a nonessential interrupting phrase). Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • Subject and verb: Every sentence has a main subject (who/what the sentence is about) and a main verb (the action or state). Here the subject is "Nepal's constitution" and the verb is "contains."
  • Nonessential interrupter: An interrupting phrase that adds extra information between the subject and verb, but is not the verb itself, must be set off by a matching pair of commas - one before it and one after it. If only one comma appears, the pair is incomplete and the punctuation is wrong.
  • Essential appositive: When a noun is immediately followed by specific names that identify exactly who is meant ("researchers James Melton and Tom Ginsburg"), the names are essential and take no comma before them.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The sentence frame is: "Nepal's constitution, according to legal __________ contains all of the six constitutional features..."
  • The phrase "according to legal researchers James Melton and Tom Ginsburg" interrupts the subject ("Nepal's constitution") and the verb ("contains").
  • A comma already appears before this phrase (right after "constitution"). To complete the pair, a comma is required after the phrase, just before "contains."
  • So the blank must end with a comma: "...researchers James Melton and Tom Ginsburg,"
  • Within the phrase, "James Melton and Tom Ginsburg" specifies exactly which researchers, so it is essential and gets no comma after "researchers."

Why Each Answer

  • A. Incorrect - Missing Closing Comma. It omits the comma after "Ginsburg," leaving the interrupter only half-bracketed and incorrectly joining the phrase to the verb.
  • B. Correct. It supplies the closing comma after "Ginsburg" to complete the comma pair, and correctly treats the names as an essential appositive (no comma after "researchers").
  • C. Incorrect - Wrong Comma Placement. It inserts an unneeded comma after "researchers" (the names are essential) and still omits the required closing comma before "contains."
  • D. Incorrect - Extra Comma. It includes the closing comma but also wrongly separates "researchers" from the essential names with a comma.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a phrase squeezes between the subject and its verb, check both ends for commas: an opening comma demands a matching closing comma. Also, names that pin down exactly which noun is meant are essential - never wall them off with a comma.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

question_options.option_text: researchers, James Melton and Tom Ginsburg,
researchers, James Melton and Tom Ginsburg
researchers James Melton and Tom Ginsburg
researchers James Melton and Tom Ginsburg,

questions.passage: Although 60558 Echeclus and 2014 YX49 are both classified as centaur objects—outer solar system bodies in unstable orbits—they exhibit striking differences in __________ object 60558 Echeclus is considered an active centaur, showing sporadic comet-like activity (such as clouds of dust and gas on its surface), 2014 YX49, showing no such activity, is considered dormant.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B (behavior: while the). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill at medium difficulty. The job is to choose the punctuation (and added word) that joins the clauses around the blank without creating a run-on or a comma splice.

Core Concepts
You need three boundary tools:

  • Independent clause: a word group that can stand alone as a complete sentence (it has its own subject and verb), e.g. "they exhibit striking differences in behavior."
  • Comma splice / run-on: the error of joining two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splice) or with no punctuation at all (run-on). Both are incorrect.
  • Colon: a colon may follow a complete independent clause to introduce an explanation, elaboration, or example of what just preceded it.
  • Subordinating conjunction "while": placing "while" in front of a clause turns it into a dependent clause, so it can no longer be comma-spliced to a second independent clause; instead "while [dependent], [independent]" is correct.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — identify the first clause. "Although ... they exhibit striking differences in behavior" is a complete independent clause. Whatever follows must be attached to it correctly.
  • Step 2 — see what follows. The rest of the text describes the two centaurs: "the object 60558 Echeclus is considered an active centaur ... 2014 YX49 ... is considered dormant." This material elaborates on the "differences in behavior," so a colon is the ideal bridge after the first independent clause.
  • Step 3 — spot the second boundary problem. The elaboration itself contains two independent clauses: "the object 60558 Echeclus is considered an active centaur" and "2014 YX49 ... is considered dormant." In the original text these are separated only by a comma, which would be a comma splice.
  • Step 4 — fix both at once. Adding "while" in front of "the object 60558 Echeclus ..." makes that clause dependent. Now the structure reads "behavior: while [dependent clause], [independent clause]" — the colon introduces the elaboration and "while" removes the comma splice between the two objects. Option B does exactly this.

Why Each Answer

  • B (correct): "behavior: while the" — the colon properly follows the first independent clause to introduce the elaboration, and "while" subordinates the Echeclus clause so the later comma correctly joins a dependent clause to the independent "2014 YX49 ... is considered dormant."
  • A. "behavior. The": Comma-splice trap. The period correctly ends the first sentence, but with no "while" the second sentence still joins two independent clauses ("the object ... active centaur" and "2014 YX49 ... dormant") with only a comma.
  • C. "behavior, while the": Boundary trap. A comma cannot bridge the complete independent clause "they exhibit striking differences in behavior" to the lengthy elaboration the way a colon can; the comma leaves the relationship weakly punctuated and the sentence improperly fused.
  • D. "behavior; the": Comma-splice trap. The semicolon correctly separates "behavior" from "the object ...," but, like A, it adds no "while," so the two independent clauses describing the objects remain joined by only a comma.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a blank sits between two big chunks of text, check both sides: a colon or semicolon may fix the first boundary, but the part after the blank can hide a second comma splice. The right choice is the one that repairs every join at once — here, the colon introduces the explanation and "while" defuses the comma splice between the two centaurs.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: In a US national election, one might expect major-party campaigns to focus on the most populous states. However, if polls and past voting data suggest that the outcome in a given state is a foregone conclusion, a campaign will not invest its resources there. Ultimately, a state's voting record and polling data, not its population size, __________ its importance to campaigns.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D ("determine"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the skill of Form, Structure, and Sense. Difficulty: easy. The task is to choose the verb form that correctly completes the sentence by agreeing with its subject.

Core Concepts

  • Subject-verb agreement: A verb must match its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb ("the data is"); a plural subject takes a plural verb ("the records are").
  • Compound subject: When two or more nouns are joined by the word "and," they form a plural subject, even if each noun by itself is singular. Example: "The cat and the dog run" (not "runs").
  • Interrupting phrase: Words set off by commas (here, ", not its population size,") add information but are NOT part of the subject. You ignore them when deciding whether the verb is singular or plural.
  • Present-tense verb forms: In the present tense, a plural subject uses the base form ("they determine"), while a singular subject adds -s ("it determines"). A word ending in -ing (a participle) cannot act as the main verb on its own.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 - Find the subject: The blank is the main verb of the final sentence. Strip away the interrupting phrase ", not its population size," and the subject reads: "a state's voting record and polling data."
  • Step 2 - Count the subject: Two nouns, "voting record" and "polling data," are joined by "and." A compound subject joined by "and" is plural.
  • Step 3 - Match the verb: A plural subject in the present tense needs the base-form verb. The base form of the verb is "determine."
  • Step 4 - Plug it in: "...a state's voting record and polling data, not its population size, determine its importance to campaigns." The sentence is now complete and grammatical.

Why Each Answer

  • D ("determine") - Correct: It is the plural, present-tense base form that agrees with the plural compound subject and serves as a complete main verb.
  • A ("has determined") - Incorrect (Agreement error): "has" is the singular helping verb. A plural subject requires "have," so "has determined" does not agree.
  • B ("determines") - Incorrect (Agreement error): The -s ending marks a singular subject ("it determines"). It clashes with the plural compound subject.
  • C ("determining") - Incorrect (Sentence fragment): An -ing participle cannot be the main verb without a helping verb such as "is" or "are." Used alone, it leaves the sentence with no working verb.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a subject is interrupted by a comma phrase, mentally cross it out and read the subject straight into the verb: "voting record and polling data __________ its importance." Then check for the word "and" joining the nouns - if it is there, the subject is plural and needs the plural verb (the base form with no -s). This quick trim-and-join trick defuses most subject-verb agreement traps.

questions.passage: That the repeated thermonuclear outbursts of U Scorpii, a recurrent nova system consisting of a white dwarf star and a companion star, have occurred on timescales as brief as eight years—shorter intervals between outbursts than have been observed in some other novae of its class—__________ to the white dwarf's extremely large mass and rapid accretion of hydrogen from its companion star.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A ("is due"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense (specifically subject-verb completeness). Difficulty: hard.

Core Concepts
A complete sentence (an independent clause) must contain a finite main verb — a verb that shows tense and agrees with its subject (for example, "is," "was," "have"). Forms that are NOT finite verbs cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence:

  • Adjectives (like "due") describe nouns but carry no tense.
  • Present participles (the "-ing" form, like "being") and past/perfect participles (like "having been") are non-finite; on their own they create a fragment, not a complete sentence.

A long subject can hide this requirement. Here the entire subject is a noun clause: "That the repeated thermonuclear outbursts of U Scorpii… have occurred on timescales as brief as eight years." That whole clause is the thing being described, so the sentence still needs one finite verb to make a statement about it.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Find the subject: Everything from "That" up to the dash is a single noun clause acting as the subject. (The internal verb "have occurred" belongs to the smaller clause inside the subject — it is not the main verb of the whole sentence.)
  • Find what follows: After the dashed aside ("—shorter intervals… of its class—"), the sentence resumes with the blank, then "to the white dwarf's extremely large mass and rapid accretion…"
  • Identify the gap: The sentence has a subject but no finite main verb yet. We need a word group that supplies one and fits the idiom "__________ to" meaning caused by.
  • Test the blank: "is due to" gives a finite verb ("is") plus the predicate adjective "due," producing the complete idea "[The subject] is due to the white dwarf's… mass." Sentence complete.

Why Each Answer

  • A. "is due" — Correct. "is" is a finite verb agreeing with the singular noun clause subject; "due to" idiomatically attributes a cause. The clause is now grammatically complete.
  • B. "due" — Fragment (missing verb). "due" is only an adjective; with no finite verb, the whole construction has a subject but no predicate verb, leaving a sentence fragment.
  • C. "being due" — Fragment (non-finite participle). "being" is a present participle, not a finite verb, so it cannot serve as the main verb; the result is still a fragment.
  • D. "having been due" — Fragment (non-finite participle phrase). "having been" is a perfect participle phrase, also non-finite, so it likewise fails to complete the sentence.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a Standard English question gives you a very long subject and one short blank, mentally strip away the modifiers and ask: "Does this sentence have one real, tense-carrying verb?" If the only candidates are "-ing" or "-ed/-en" participles or a bare adjective, they are traps — choose the option that adds a true finite verb (here, "is").

questions.passage: In his 2011 book, historian Sebouh David Aslanian quantifies the reading patterns of early modern Armenian merchants from New Julfa. Aslanian's macroanalysis __________ nearly 1,000 book titles published between 1512 and 1800 shows not only the steady popularity of religious texts but also a broadening interest in secular books, especially those on history and geography.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B ("examining"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense at a medium difficulty level. The task is to choose the verb form that fits the grammatical structure of the sentence.

Core Concepts

  • Subject: the noun that performs the main action of a sentence.
  • Finite (main) verb: a verb that shows tense and carries the action of a clause (e.g., "shows," "examines," "had examined," "examined"). An independent clause needs exactly one finite verb for its subject.
  • Participle (non-finite verb): an "-ing" form (present participle) or "-ed" form used not as the main verb but to begin a modifying phrase that describes a noun. A participial phrase does NOT count as the clause's main verb.
  • Rule of one main verb: a single subject in one clause may have only one finite verb unless two verbs are joined by a conjunction such as "and."

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify the subject: "Aslanian's macroanalysis."
  • Scan the sentence for the verb that belongs to that subject. After the blank comes the phrase "nearly 1,000 book titles published between 1512 and 1800," and then the verb "shows."
  • "shows" is the finite main verb for "macroanalysis" (the macroanalysis shows...). That role is already filled.
  • Therefore the blank cannot hold a second finite verb; doing so would give one subject two competing main verbs with no conjunction.
  • The blank needs a participle that starts a modifying phrase: "Aslanian's macroanalysis examining nearly 1,000 book titles ... shows..." Here "examining nearly 1,000 book titles" describes the macroanalysis, and "shows" remains the lone main verb.

Why Each Answer

  • B ("examining") — Correct: a present participle. It opens a participial phrase modifying "macroanalysis" and leaves "shows" as the single main verb, producing a grammatically complete sentence.
  • A ("had examined") — Incorrect (Extra finite verb): a past-perfect finite verb. It creates a second main verb for "macroanalysis," colliding with "shows."
  • C ("examines") — Incorrect (Extra finite verb): a present-tense finite verb. Same flaw: the subject would have two main verbs without a conjunction.
  • D ("examined") — Incorrect (Extra finite verb): a simple-past finite verb. It also functions as a competing main verb, leaving the sentence ungrammatical.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a sentence already has a main verb further along (here, "shows"), the blank usually needs an "-ing" participle to form a describing phrase rather than another tensed verb. Quick trigger: find the real main verb first, then if it already exists, reject every finite option and choose the participle.
