  • Relationship: The underlined sentence rejects the "do as you like" ideal from sentence 1 and replaces it with the author's own philosophy: culture pursues an objective standard of beauty and grace. So its job is to counter the prior viewpoint by stating the author's contrasting view.

Why Each Answer

  • D (correct): The sentence begins with "But" and sets the author's philosophy of culture against the previously reported ideal of unrestricted personal preference. This precisely captures both the contrast and the content.
  • A (Out of Scope): The underlined sentence says nothing about whether critiques of the English are fair or unfair; it defines what culture aims to do. The "unfair critiques" idea borrows loosely from the passage's mention of "foreign strictures" but is not the sentence's function.
  • B (Half-Right / Misattributed Viewpoint): The underlined sentence expresses the view the author endorses, not one the author disagrees with. The opinion the author opposes is in the first sentence, so this reverses the roles.
  • C (Factually Inaccurate): The sentence introduces a contrasting principle, not a supporting example. There is no specific instance or illustration offered here.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a sentence opens with a contrast word like "But," expect its function to involve pushing against the idea right before it. Then ask one quick question: whose opinion is this? Matching the right viewpoint to the right speaker eliminates traps like B that simply flip the attribution.
questions.question_text: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

question_options.option_text: It introduces an example that supports the author's main assertion.
It counters the viewpoint presented in the previous sentence by expressing the author's contrasting philosophy of culture.
It asserts that the English are often subject to unfair critiques of their sense of taste.
It presents an opinion with which the author disagrees.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Brown University and the investment bank Barclays are two of the many institutions offering training programs in entrepreneurship. But what results do such programs produce? In a study of business school graduates in Norway, researchers Lars Kolvereid and Øystein Moen addressed this question and convincingly demonstrated that participants showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs as a result of receiving entrepreneurial training.

Text 2

While studies of entrepreneurial training typically report positive results, a close look at these studies reveals widespread methodological shortcomings. For instance, a 1997 study by Lars Kolvereid and Øystein Moen found benefits of entrepreneurial education for graduates of Norwegian business schools, but the study only collected data on subjects after the training, not before, making it unclear whether the training actually had an effect.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is a Craft and Structure question testing the skill of Cross-Text Connections, and its difficulty is rated hard. The task is to find the one question that the two authors would answer differently based on what each text actually claims.

Core Concepts
A Cross-Text Connections question asks you to compare two short passages and identify how they relate. "Most likely disagree about the answer to which question" means you need a yes/no (or similar) question where:

  • One author would clearly answer one way, and
  • The other author would clearly answer the opposite way.
A few useful terms: a causal claim says one thing actually caused another. Attributable to means "caused by" or "explained by." A methodological shortcoming is a flaw in how a study was designed that weakens its conclusions. The key trap to avoid is picking a statement that both authors agree on, or one that neither author addresses.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Text 1's central claim: the Kolvereid and Moen study "convincingly demonstrated that participants showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs as a result of receiving entrepreneurial training." Text 1 treats the study as solid proof of a cause-and-effect link.
  • Text 2's central claim: such studies have "widespread methodological shortcomings." Specifically, this same study "only collected data on subjects after the training, not before, making it unclear whether the training actually had an effect." Text 2 accepts that benefits were found but doubts that the study proves the training caused them.
  • The point of conflict: Did the study provide persuasive evidence that its results are due to the training? Text 1 says yes (it was convincing); Text 2 says no (the design flaw makes the causal link unclear). That is a direct disagreement, which matches option B.

Why Each Answer

  • A — Out of Scope. Neither text discusses the financial cost of running the programs or whether benefits offset that cost, so the authors have no stated positions to disagree about.
  • B — Correct. Text 1 would answer "yes, the evidence is persuasive," while Text 2 would answer "no, the before/after design flaw makes it unconvincing." Opposite answers, so this is the disagreement.
  • C — Agreement, not disagreement. Text 2 explicitly says the study "found benefits," and Text 1 reports the same positive finding. Both authors would answer "yes," so they do not disagree here.
  • D — Out of Scope. Neither text compares different types of training programs against different outcomes; both discuss one study, so there is no basis for disagreement.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "disagree about which question" items, restate each answer choice as a yes/no question and predict how each author would respond. The right answer is the only one where you can write a confident "yes" for one author and a confident "no" for the other. Watch for choices both authors share (like C here) — shared facts are agreement traps, not disagreements.
questions.question_text: Based on the texts, the author of Text 1 and the author of Text 2 would most likely disagree about the answer to which question?

question_options.option_text: Did Kolvereid and Moen report that participants who received the entrepreneurial training showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs?
Is the cost of conducting entrepreneurial training programs typically offset by the programs' benefits?
Did Kolvereid and Moen's study provide persuasive evidence that its results are attributable to the entrepreneurial training participants received?
Are there convincing experimental results showing that different types of entrepreneurial training programs are associated with different outcomes?

questions.passage: One challenge faced by researchers studying global urbanization is that different countries have different definitions of what constitutes an urban settlement. Many countries define urban settlements based on the number of people living in them. However, countries do not all use the same number; for example, Greenland uses a minimum population of 200, while Benin uses 10,000. Other countries use a combination of population and other factors, like how close buildings are to each other. This variation makes it difficult for researchers to compare aspects of urbanization in different countries.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the skill of Central Ideas and Details. Difficulty: medium. Your job is to find the choice that captures the single most important point the whole passage is built around.

Core Concepts

  • Main idea: the overarching point a passage makes. It is the claim that every sentence supports, not just one small detail.
  • Detail vs. main idea: a detail is a specific fact or example (like one country's exact population number). A detail supports the main idea but is too narrow to BE the main idea.
  • Strategy: read for the author's central claim, then predict the answer in your own words before checking the options. The right choice will be a paraphrase of that prediction.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 states the challenge directly: countries have different definitions of what counts as an urban settlement.
  • Sentences 2-3 give supporting examples: many countries use a population threshold, but the threshold differs (Greenland uses 200, Benin uses 10,000). These are details that illustrate the variation.
  • Sentence 4 adds that some countries combine population with other factors, like how close buildings are. More evidence of variation.
  • The final sentence delivers the payoff: "This variation makes it difficult for researchers to compare aspects of urbanization in different countries." That sentence is the main idea, and the examples exist only to support it.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): "It is difficult for researchers to compare aspects of urbanization globally because of the various ways different countries define urban settlements." This is a clean paraphrase of the passage's central claim, tying the difficulty (comparing urbanization) to its cause (differing definitions).
  • B (Factually Inaccurate / Detail Misuse): The passage never says researchers treat any area of at least 10,000 people as urban. The number 10,000 is only Benin's threshold, not a universal standard. It twists a supporting detail into a false claim.
  • C (Out of Scope): Greenland is mentioned only as an example of a low population threshold (200). The passage says nothing about researchers focusing on non-population factors in Greenland; this invents a claim the text does not make.
  • D (Contradicts the Text): The passage's whole point is that comparison is difficult. D claims urbanization is "easily compared" when total populations are similar, which reverses the author's argument and introduces a factor (total population size) the passage never raises.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For main idea questions, find the sentence that states a problem, conclusion, or "so what" (often signaled by words like "This" or "As a result") and predict the answer from it. Then eliminate any choice built on a single example (like a specific number or country) since a lone detail is almost never the main idea.
questions.question_text: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

question_options.option_text: Urbanization is easily compared between countries when they have similar total populations.
Researchers focus on factors other than population when conducting studies on urbanization in Greenland.
Even though countries use different methods to define urban settlements, researchers consider any area having a population of at least 10,000 to be urban.
It is difficult for researchers to compare aspects of urbanization globally because of the various ways different countries define urban settlements.

questions.passage: Scientists study the abundance and the activity ratios (AR)-the relative radioactive decay rates of two isotopes-of uranium (U) isotopes in bodies of water to track sediment transport and deposition and to monitor groundwater quality. However, isotope abundance and AR are not always uniform across a single body of water, which may affect the reliability of results if sampling is not sufficiently representative. Chen Zhao et al. analyzed concentrations of the isotope U-238 and the U-234/U-238 AR at multiple depths and locations in two lakes in China, finding no significant variation in values within the same lake.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
Correct answer: C. Domain: Information and Ideas; Skill: Command of Evidence (Textual). Difficulty: Hard. The task is to find the statement about Zhao et al.'s findings that the text most directly supports.

Core Concepts

  • Command of Evidence (inference): The right answer must follow logically from what the passage actually states, with no extra claims smuggled in. Avoid choices that go beyond the data.
  • Key vocabulary: Isotopes are forms of an element. Activity ratio (AR) compares the radioactive decay rates of two isotopes (here \(\text{U-234}/\text{U-238}\)). Representative sampling means a small sample reflects the whole; if a quantity is uniform throughout, then a sample from any spot represents the entire body.
  • The pivotal fact: Within a single lake, values showed no significant variation across multiple depths and locations.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1: Scientists measure U abundance and AR in water to track sediment and monitor groundwater quality (sets up why these measurements matter).
  • Sentence 2: These values are not always uniform within one body of water, which can undermine reliability if sampling is not representative (raises the concern).
  • Sentence 3: Zhao et al. measured U-238 and the U-234/U-238 AR at many depths and locations in two Chinese lakes and found no significant variation within the same lake (the finding that resolves the concern for these lakes).
  • Logical implication: If values do not vary within a lake, then a sample from any single depth or location reflects the whole lake, so localized sampling should be reliable there. That matches Option C.

Why Each Answer

  • C (Correct): Uniform values within each lake mean any one location or depth is representative, so researchers can rely on localized sampling in these lakes. This is the direct consequence of the finding.
  • A (Incorrect) - Reverses the implication: The findings show distribution was already even within these lakes, which supports relying on localized sampling, not a general rule that scientists must always evaluate how evenly values are distributed.
  • B (Incorrect) - Misreads scope: The text reports consistency within each lake, not consistency across lakes. The passage never claims values matched from one lake to another, so this is unsupported.
  • D (Incorrect) - Out of scope / overreach: The passage addresses the uniformity of values, not whether the number of samples was sufficient to draw reliable conclusions about sediment transport. Sample-count adequacy is never established.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For inference questions, anchor on the single concrete finding ("no significant variation within the same lake") and ask what must be true if that is the case. Watch for traps that swap within for across (B) or that reverse the takeaway (A). Pick the choice that the evidence forces, not one that merely sounds reasonable.
questions.question_text: Information in the text best supports which statement about Zhao et al.'s findings?

question_options.option_text: They indicate that researchers performing isotopic analysis in the lakes Zhao et al. studied can likely rely on localized sampling within each lake, since values from any one location or depth are representative of the entire lake.
They challenge the assumption that U abundance and AR sometimes vary from lake to lake, since the U-238 concentration and U-234/U-238 AR were consistent across the sampled lakes.

They illustrate why scientists investigating sediment transport and deposition and groundwater quality ought to evaluate how evenly U abundance and AR are distributed in the bodies of water they are examining.

They demonstrate that the number of samples Zhao et al. collected from the two lakes is sufficient to yield equally reliable information about sediment transport and deposition and groundwater quality in those two lakes.

questions.passage: Scientists collected information about brown bears in Katmai National Park in Alaska. This information included each bear's sex, age, and approximate weight. Among the bears whose information is shown in the table, the youngest one was the bear with identification number __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is D (bear 122). This is an Information and Ideas item testing Command of Evidence, at an easy difficulty. The task is to use the table data to identify the youngest bear.

Core Concepts Command of Evidence (quantitative) questions ask you to read a value from a table and use it to complete a claim. Here the claim is about which bear is youngest, meaning the bear with the smallest value in the “Age (years)” column. A specific number (such as 3) is always smaller than a category described only as “older than 3,” so the exact age beats any “older than” entry.

Step-by-Step Breakdown Step 1: Locate the “Age (years)” column in the table. Step 2: Read each entry — bear 123 is “older than 3,” bear 157 is “older than 3,” bear 117 is “older than 3,” and bear 122 is exactly “3.” Step 3: Compare the ages. An age of exactly 3 is less than any age that is “older than 3,” so bear 122 has the lowest age. Step 4: Match that bear’s identification number to the choices — bear 122 corresponds to choice D.

Why Each Answer D (122) is correct because its age of 3 is the only value that is not “older than 3,” making it the youngest. A (123) is wrong — this bear is listed as “older than 3,” so it is older than bear 122 (Factual error from the table). B (157) is wrong for the same reason, “older than 3” (Factual error). C (117) is also “older than 3” and additionally is the heaviest bear at 400 lbs, which may tempt a reader who confuses weight with age (Wrong column / Factual error).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway When a table mixes exact numbers with “older than” or “more than” phrases, the single exact number is your anchor: it is the only value you can pin down, and for a “youngest/smallest” question it almost always wins. Read the column the question names, not the most eye-catching number.
questions.question_text: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

questions.passage: In the 1980s and 1990s, many countries began allowing foreign investors to purchase shares of companies based in those countries.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot The correct answer is D (1986). This is an Information and Ideas item testing Command of Evidence (quantitative): the task is to read a single data point off a table. Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts A data-interpretation question asks you to locate a specific value in a table or graph that directly answers the prompt. The strategy is simple: identify the exact row and column the question names, then read off the value. The surrounding passage only supplies context (here, the "change" is allowing foreign investors to buy shares); it does not change which cell you must read.

Step-by-Step Breakdown Step 1: The passage explains that in the 1980s and 1990s many countries began allowing foreign investors to purchase shares of domestic companies. Step 2: The question asks specifically for the year India made this change. Step 3: Scan the table's "Country" column for the "India" row. Step 4: Read the value in the "Year" column for that row, which is 1986. Step 5: Match 1986 to the answer choices, which is option D.

Why Each Answer D (1986) is correct because the India row of the table lists 1986. A (1981) is a Factual error: 1981 does not appear anywhere in the table. B (1998) is a Factual error: 1998 does not appear in the table. C (1983) is a Wrong-row trap: 1983 is in the table, but it is the year for Brazil, not India.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway For table-lookup questions, anchor on the exact label the prompt names (here, "India") before looking at the answer choices. Reading the row first prevents you from being lured by real numbers from the wrong row, like Brazil's 1983.
questions.question_text: According to the table, in what year did India make the change mentioned in the text?

questions.passage: Psychologists Gregory Bryant, Dorsa Amir, and colleagues investigated cross-cultural perceptions of spontaneous (real) laughter and volitional (fake or forced) laughter. Study participants from 21 societies, including those in Japan and Turkey, listened to randomized recordings of 18 spontaneous laughs taken from natural conversations between pairs of women and 18 volitional laughs produced separately by 18 different women in response to an instruction to laugh. Analysis of the participants' evaluations of the laughs prompted the team to conclude that the ability to distinguish between spontaneous and volitional laughter appears to be universal across cultures.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is an Information and Ideas question testing Command of Evidence, rated hard. The task is to find a hypothetical finding from another study that, if true, would most directly strengthen the research team's conclusion.

Core Concepts
To answer a strengthen question you need three things clear in your mind:

  • The conclusion: the exact claim the team is making. Here it is that the ability to tell spontaneous (real) laughter apart from volitional (fake/forced) laughter appears to be universal across cultures.
  • Strengthen vs. weaken: a strengthening fact gives an additional reason to believe the conclusion is true. A weakening fact gives a reason to doubt it. An irrelevant fact does neither.
  • Universal claim: "universal across cultures" means the same thing holds no matter which society a person is from. So the best support is evidence of something consistent that does not change from culture to culture.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The team played listeners from 21 societies a mix of real and fake laughs, and listeners could reliably tell them apart everywhere. The team concluded the skill is universal.
  • Ask: what would explain why people everywhere can do this? If there is a built-in, society-independent acoustic signal that marks real laughter, then any listener anywhere has the same cue to rely on. That is exactly what a universal ability needs.
  • So the ideal strengthener describes a measurable acoustic feature that reliably separates spontaneous from volitional laughter regardless of the speakers' society.
  • Choice B matches this exactly: spontaneous laughter has a recognizably higher pitch than volitional laughter, regardless of what society the speakers are from.

Why Each Answer

  • B (Correct): A consistent, society-independent pitch difference is a concrete reason listeners from any culture could distinguish the two laugh types. It supplies the universal cue that makes a universal ability plausible, directly strengthening the conclusion.
  • A (Out of Scope): Whether listeners can judge how well two people know each other is about relationship closeness, not about telling real from fake laughter. It does not bear on the team's conclusion.
  • C (Weakens / Reverses): A correlation between a society's community size and how listeners judge laughter implies the judgments vary by culture. That points toward cultural difference, the opposite of universality, so it undermines rather than supports the claim.
  • D (Weakens / Opposite): Saying the acoustic features of spontaneous laughter vary both within and across societies means the cue is inconsistent from culture to culture. An inconsistent cue makes a universal ability harder to explain, so this works against the conclusion.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "strengthen a universal claim" questions, hunt for the answer that says "the same thing happens regardless of group/culture." Phrases like regardless of society (B) reinforce universality, while phrases like varies across societies or correlates with a cultural trait (C, D) signal a weakener in disguise.
questions.question_text: Which potential finding from another study, if true, would most directly strengthen the team's conclusion?

question_options.option_text: Acoustic features of spontaneous laughter, such as pitch and intensity, have measurable variations both within and across societies.
Spontaneous laughter typically has a recognizably higher pitch than volitional laughter, regardless of what society the speakers in a conversation are from.
Listeners from both Japan and Turkey tend to be able to determine how well two people know each other based on recordings of their conversation.
There is some evidence of correlation between the average size of communities in a society and judgments of spontaneous and volitional laughter by listeners in that society.

questions.passage: Certain species, such as Hay's Spring amphipods (Stygobromus hayi), lack functional eyes or ocular organs altogether and rely on other mechanisms for navigation. Licheng Yuan and colleagues investigated such mechanisms in the Chinese red-headed centipede (Scolopendra subspinipes mutilans), which has no organs with photoreceptors (light-detecting cells) but can sense and avoid sunlight. The researchers placed individual specimens in a clear container (container 1) connected to a container covered in black tape (container 2) and then exposed the containers to simulated sunlight. They observed a rapid increase in the temperature of the centipedes' antennae with the onset of exposure, followed by the centipedes' escape to container 2. Based on their observations, the researchers concluded that thermal receptors in the antennae are likely responsible for light detection in the centipedes.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D. This is an Information and Ideas question testing Command of Evidence at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to find the additional experimental result that would most strongly back up the researchers' conclusion.

Core Concepts
A few ideas make this question solvable from scratch:

  • Conclusion: the single claim the researchers are arguing for. Here it is that thermal receptors in the antennae are likely responsible for light detection in the centipedes.
  • Supporting evidence: a new fact that makes the conclusion more likely to be true. Good support targets the specific cause-and-effect link the conclusion proposes.
  • The proposed mechanism here is a chain: sunlight heats the antennae, the heat is sensed, and the centipede escapes. Strong support either confirms a step in this chain or shows the behavior breaks when you block a step.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The centipedes have no photoreceptors, yet they still avoid sunlight, so something other than light-detecting cells must be doing the sensing.
  • In the experiment, exposure to simulated sunlight caused the antennae to heat up rapidly, and then the centipedes fled to the dark container.
  • The researchers infer that the antennae's heat sensing is what triggers the escape, i.e., the antennae act as the light detector by detecting heat.
  • To support this, you want a follow-up showing that if the antennae are prevented from heating, the escape behavior fails. That isolates the antennae's heating as the necessary cause.
  • Option D does exactly this: covering the antennae with a reflective material blocks them from heating up, and the centipedes then stay in the lit container longer (they fail to escape). Removing the proposed cause removes the effect, which is powerful support.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Incorrect) - Out of Scope / Undermines: Showing that other body segments also heat up does nothing to confirm the antennae are the sensor; if anything it suggests the antennae are not special, weakening the specific conclusion.
  • B (Incorrect) - Contradicts the conclusion: If the centipedes still escape even when the temperature is artificially reduced, then heat is not needed for the behavior, which argues against thermal receptors being responsible.
  • C (Incorrect) - Irrelevant Comparison: Comparing how well this species detects light to other species says nothing about the biological mechanism (thermal receptors) behind the detection.
  • D (Correct): Blocking the antennae from heating stops the escape behavior, directly confirming that antenna heating is the trigger for light detection.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "which finding best supports the conclusion" questions, restate the conclusion as a cause-and-effect claim, then look for the choice that tests that exact link. The strongest support often comes from a result where removing the proposed cause makes the effect disappear.
questions.question_text: Which additional finding from Yuan and colleagues' study, if true, would best support the researchers' conclusion?

question_options.option_text: When body segments other than the centipedes' antennae were monitored, the temperature of these body segments were found to increase in the presence of sunlight.
When their antennae were covered with a reflective material, the centipedes remained exposed in container 1 for longer durations.
Chinese red-headed centipedes are more proficient at detecting light than other centipede species are.
The centipedes showed the same tendency to move to container 2 when simulated sunlight was accompanied by artificially reduced temperatures.

questions.passage: Introducing a new species into a delicate ecosystem can often be harmful. The common waxbill and other fruit-eating birds have established themselves on the Hawaiian island of Oahu after being brought there in the last 150 years. Many plant species on the island rely on the activity of fruit-eating birds to maintain and increase their populations. In recent studies, common waxbills have been found to spread seeds of native forest plants that are at risk of extinction, such as the olomea shrub and the alahee tree, suggesting that __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D. This is a Reading & Writing question in the Information and Ideas domain, testing the Inferences skill at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to choose the conclusion that follows most logically from the evidence in the passage.

Core Concepts
An inference question asks you to draw the conclusion the text is building toward without going beyond what the evidence supports. Key ideas to track here:

  • Native vs. non-native species: A native species naturally occurs in a place; a non-native (introduced) species was brought there by humans. The waxbill is non-native to Oahu.
  • Setup-and-twist structure: The passage opens with a general expectation (introducing species "can often be harmful") and then presents evidence that goes against that expectation. The blank should capture the surprising conclusion that the evidence supports.
  • Stay within the evidence: The right answer must be fully supported by the sentences given, with no added claims.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 establishes the general principle: introducing a new species "can often be harmful." This sets an expectation of damage.
  • Sentence 2 tells us the common waxbill is a non-native, fruit-eating bird that established itself on Oahu over the last 150 years.
  • Sentence 3 explains that many island plants depend on fruit-eating birds to maintain and grow their populations.
  • Sentence 4 gives the crucial evidence: waxbills spread the seeds of native plants that are at risk of extinction (the olomea shrub and alahee tree). This is a clearly positive effect.
  • The logical conclusion: even though introducing species is often harmful, this particular non-native bird is actually helping the ecosystem. The blank should state that some non-native birds provide a benefit rather than cause harm. That is exactly option D.

Why Each Answer

  • D (Correct): It directly resolves the contrast set up in the passage: instead of harming the ecosystem (the expected outcome), some non-native birds provide an important benefit. This is fully supported by the seed-spreading evidence.
  • A (Out of Scope): The text discusses native forest plants and never addresses whether the birds eat fruits from non-native plants, so this claim about their eating preferences has no support.
  • B (Half-Right / Unsupported): The passage shows only positive effects from the waxbills. It never provides evidence of negative effects on Oahu's native plants, so "both positive and negative" overreaches.
  • C (Unsupported Detail): Nothing in the text says the birds first damaged the plants and only later became useful. The "initially damaged" claim is invented, making this a distorted version of the evidence.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a passage opens with a general warning and then piles on contrary evidence, the blank almost always states the reversal ("contrary to expectation, X is beneficial"). Eliminate any choice that adds harm or negative effects the text never mentions, and you are usually left with the single fully-supported conclusion.
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: rather than harming Oahu's ecosystem, some non-native birds provide an important benefit on Oahu.
non-native birds have had both positive and negative effects on Oahu's native plants.
although non-native birds initially damaged the plants in Oahu's ecosystem, they are now proving useful to them.
non-native birds, such as the common waxbill, are unlikely to eat fruits from non-native forest plants on Oahu.

questions.passage: Many Indigenous songs serve as repositories of ecological knowledge—e.g., Yi songs about the natural environment and O'odham songs about desert plants. In a study by ethnobiologist Dana Lepofsky et al., a song keeper for the Kwakwaka'wakw people provided access to ancient songs referring to the people's creation of terraced intertidal gardens to foster clams for consumption. Cross-references of that information with both archaeological and paleoecological records have revealed significant increases in clam size and productivity concurrent with the most prevalent use of these clam gardens. This finding suggests that researchers should consider __________
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B. This is an Information and Ideas question testing the Inferences skill, rated hard. The task is to choose the phrase that most logically completes the final sentence, drawing a conclusion that the passage's evidence supports.

Core Concepts
A completion-inference question asks you to finish a sentence with the idea that follows most logically from the information given. Key strategy:

  • Find the main point the passage is building toward.
  • The blank usually states a conclusion or implication that the prior sentences justify.
  • The right answer stays inside the scope of the evidence and does not contradict it.

Useful vocabulary here: a "repository" is a store or container of something (here, of ecological knowledge). "Paleoecological" records are records of past ecosystems. "Concurrent" means happening at the same time.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up the general claim: many Indigenous songs hold real ecological knowledge, with two example cultures named.
  • Sentence 2 gives a specific case: Kwakwaka'wakw songs describe building terraced intertidal gardens to grow clams.
  • Sentence 3 supplies independent confirmation: archaeological and paleoecological records show clam size and productivity rose at the same time the gardens were most used. So the song's information lined up with measurable, practical results.
  • Final sentence: "This finding suggests that researchers should consider __________." Because one culture's song proved to contain useful, verifiable ecological practice, the logical takeaway generalizes back to the opening claim: other Indigenous peoples' songs might also carry ecological information with practical value.

That reasoning points directly to choice B.

Why Each Answer

  • B (correct): It extends the proven specific case to the general possibility that other Indigenous songs likewise transmit practically useful ecological knowledge — exactly the inference the evidence supports.
  • A (Factually Inaccurate / contradicts text): The passage credits the clam improvements to the gardens the Kwakwaka'wakw people built, so claiming the benefits come from unrelated ecological factors directly opposes the stated finding.
  • C (Out of Scope): The archaeological and paleoecological records are presented as trustworthy tools that confirmed the song's information; the passage never raises doubts about their reliability.
  • D (Out of Scope): Whether the people invented or borrowed the cultivation method is never discussed; the focus is that the songs recorded an effective, verifiable practice.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
On "completes the text" questions, the last blank almost always restates or generalizes the passage's main point. Re-read the first sentence: the correct ending usually loops back to that opening claim. Eliminate any choice that contradicts the evidence (A) or introduces a topic the passage never raised (C, D).
questions.question_text: Which choice most logically completes the text?

question_options.option_text: whether the Kwakwaka'wakw people originated the method of cultivation detailed in the songs or adapted methods observed among other groups of Indigenous peoples.
the strong implication that the beneficial effects are primarily attributable to ecological factors unrelated to the activities of the Kwakwaka'wakw people.
the possibility that other songs of other Indigenous peoples transmit ecological information that has useful practical applications.
the reliability of archaeological and paleoecological evidence that often underpins conclusions drawn from Indigenous songs.

questions.passage: The smoke point of corn oil __________ around 450 degrees Fahrenheit. When corn oil is heated past this temperature, it will begin to combust and emit smoke.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C ("is"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the Boundaries skill, at an easy difficulty. The task is to choose the punctuation that correctly joins the verb to the rest of the sentence.

Core Concepts

  • Subject: the noun or noun phrase that the sentence is about. Here it is the full phrase "The smoke point of corn oil."
  • Linking (or "to be") verb: a verb such as "is" that connects the subject to information describing it. It does not show action; it links.
  • Complement: the word or phrase after a linking verb that completes the meaning. Here it is "around 450 degrees Fahrenheit."
  • Key punctuation rule: never separate a verb from the information it directly needs (its complement) with a dash, semicolon, or comma. The verb and its complement must stay connected with no punctuation between them.
  • Semicolon rule: a semicolon must join two complete, independent clauses (each able to stand alone as a sentence).

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify the subject: "The smoke point of corn oil."
  • The blank needs to supply the main verb. The intended verb is "is."
  • After "is" comes the complement "around 450 degrees Fahrenheit," which finishes the thought (it tells us what the smoke point is).
  • Because "is" links directly to "around 450 degrees Fahrenheit," no punctuation may interrupt that connection.
  • Therefore the blank should be simply "is" with nothing after it: "The smoke point of corn oil is around 450 degrees Fahrenheit."

Why Each Answer

  • A. "is-": Incorrect. Punctuation between verb and complement. A dash improperly breaks the link between "is" and its complement.
  • B. "is;": Incorrect. Misused semicolon. A semicolon must connect two independent clauses, but "around 450 degrees Fahrenheit" cannot stand alone as a sentence.
  • C. "is": Correct. The verb connects smoothly to its complement with no interrupting punctuation, producing a clean, grammatical sentence.
  • D. "is,": Incorrect. Punctuation between verb and complement. A comma here wrongly separates "is" from the phrase it must attach to.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When every answer choice is the same word followed by different punctuation marks, ask whether anything should interrupt the flow at that spot. A verb almost never gets cut off from the words that complete it, so the no-punctuation option is usually right. Mental trigger: "Don't fence a verb off from what it links to."

questions.passage: Because many of the first cattle ranchers in the US learned the trade from Spanish-speaking Mexican vaqueros (cowboys), many ranching terms in the English language come from Spanish. One example is the word "lasso." It comes from the Spanish word lazo. Another example is "rodeo." __________ comes from the Spanish word rodear.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A ("It"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the skill of Form, Structure, and Sense (pronoun choice). Difficulty: easy.

Core Concepts

  • A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun so we do not repeat the noun. Example: instead of "The word comes from Spanish," we can say "It comes from Spanish."
  • A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces (its antecedent) in two ways: number (singular vs. plural) and person/animacy (whether it refers to a person or a thing).
  • Key personal pronouns: It = one singular thing (not a person). He = one male person. She = one female person. Someone = an unspecified single person.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up the pattern: many English ranching terms come from Spanish.
  • The next sentences give examples. "One example is the word 'lasso.' It comes from the Spanish word lazo." Here "It" already refers to the singular thing "the word 'lasso.'"
  • The text then says: "Another example is 'rodeo.' __________ comes from the Spanish word rodear."
  • The blank is the subject of "comes from the Spanish word rodear." Ask: what comes from rodear? The word rodeo does.
  • "rodeo" is a single, non-human thing (a word), so the pronoun replacing it must be singular and non-human: It.

Why Each Answer

  • A. It — Correct. "It" is singular and refers to a thing, matching the antecedent "rodeo" (a word). It also mirrors the parallel earlier sentence about "lasso."
  • B. Someone — Incorrect (Wrong Antecedent / Animacy error). "Someone" refers to an unidentified person, but a word is not a person.
  • C. She — Incorrect (Animacy error). "She" refers to a single female person, not to a word.
  • D. He — Incorrect (Animacy error). "He" refers to a single male person, not to a word.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a pronoun should refer back to a thing (an object, a word, an idea) rather than a person, your default is it. A quick mental trigger: if you cannot picture a human doing the action, reject he, she, and someone, and reach for "it."
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: Located in what is now Egypt, the Pyramid of Userkaf is one of the oldest known structures in the world, __________ researchers a glimpse into ages long gone.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D) providing. This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense (verb forms and sentence boundaries). Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • An independent clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence (e.g., "the Pyramid of Userkaf is one of the oldest known structures in the world").
  • A comma splice is the error of joining two independent clauses with only a comma. It is incorrect.
  • A present participle is the -ing form of a verb (e.g., "providing"). When it begins a phrase placed after a complete clause and set off by a comma, it forms a participial phrase that modifies the preceding clause and does NOT create a second independent clause.
  • An infinitive is the "to + verb" form (e.g., "to provide"); it usually signals purpose.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Read the part before the blank: "Located in what is now Egypt, the Pyramid of Userkaf is one of the oldest known structures in the world,". The portion "the Pyramid of Userkaf is one of the oldest known structures in the world" is already a complete independent clause (subject = Pyramid, verb = is).
  • The comma after "world" cannot be followed by a second full independent clause, or it becomes a comma splice.
  • What follows the blank — "researchers a glimpse into ages long gone" — needs a word that links smoothly to the complete clause and adds extra information about it.
  • A present participle ("providing") attaches the new information as a modifying phrase: the pyramid IS one of the oldest structures, providing researchers a glimpse. This is grammatically correct and concise.

Why Each Answer

  • D) providing — Correct. The present participle opens a participial phrase that modifies the entire preceding independent clause, with no new subject and no comma splice.
  • A) to provide — Incorrect (Wrong verb form / implies purpose). The infinitive signals purpose, suggesting the pyramid exists in order to provide a glimpse, which distorts the meaning; the sentence is describing a result/characteristic, not a goal.
  • B) provides — Incorrect (Comma splice). "provides" is a finite verb that needs a subject, creating a second independent clause ("it provides researchers a glimpse") joined to the first by only a comma.
  • C) provide — Incorrect (Subject-verb agreement / comma splice). The bare plural verb "provide" has no plural subject to agree with and still tries to start a new clause after the comma, producing an ungrammatical join.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a comma separates a complete sentence from added detail, an -ing participle is almost always the safe, correct choice, while a finite verb ("provides," "provide") creates a comma splice. Mental trigger: complete clause + comma + extra info usually wants the -ing form.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: In the Suzuki method, folk songs like "Mary Had a Little Lamb" are taught to beginning music students as young as three, while students of traditional methods often only __________ such songs at the age of five.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A ("begin learning"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense (verb forms). Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • Finite (main) verb: Every complete clause needs a finite verb — a verb that is conjugated for tense and subject (e.g., "walk," "walks," "walked"). It can stand on its own as the action of the sentence.
  • Non-finite verb forms: Participles ("-ing" forms like "beginning," or "having begun") and infinitives ("to begin") are NOT main verbs. They cannot, by themselves, supply the verb a clause requires; they need a helping (auxiliary) verb such as "are" or "have."
  • Subject-verb agreement: The plural subject "students" needs a plural present-tense verb form.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • The sentence has two parts joined by "while." The first part is complete: "folk songs ... are taught ... as young as three."
  • The second part is its own clause: "students of traditional methods often only __________ such songs at the age of five." Its subject is "students."
  • This clause has no other verb, so the blank must supply the finite main verb.
  • The surrounding context is present tense ("are taught"), so we need a present-tense verb agreeing with the plural "students."
  • Test A: "students often only begin learning such songs" — "begin" is a finite plural present verb. The clause is complete. Correct.

Why Each Answer

  • A — "begin learning" (Correct): "begin" is a finite present-tense verb agreeing with "students," giving the clause the main verb it needs.
  • B — "beginning to learn" (Wrong, Non-finite verb form): "beginning" is a present participle; without a helping verb like "are," it cannot serve as the main verb, leaving the clause a fragment.
  • C — "having begun to learn" (Wrong, Non-finite verb form): "having begun" is a perfect participle phrase, not a finite verb; the clause still lacks a main verb.
  • D — "to begin learning" (Wrong, Non-finite verb form): "to begin" is an infinitive, which never functions as a clause's main verb on its own.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a blank is the only candidate for a clause's verb, eliminate every "-ing" form, "having + -ed" form, and "to + verb" form on sight — these are non-finite and cannot stand alone. The choice that reads as a plain conjugated verb (here, "begin") is almost always the answer.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: Marché Monge has operated for more than a century, making __________ both a popular shopping destination and an important piece of Paris's history.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B ("it"). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing the skill of Form, Structure, and Sense, at an easy difficulty level. The task is to choose the pronoun that correctly fills the blank.

Core Concepts
A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun (the antecedent). The key rule here is pronoun-antecedent agreement:

  • A pronoun must match its antecedent in number (singular pronoun for a singular noun, plural pronoun for a plural noun).
  • Singular pronouns include it, this, that, one; plural pronouns include they, these, those.

The antecedent here is "Marché Monge," the name of a single market. Even though it ends in an "s" sound, it names one specific place, so it is grammatically singular.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify what the blank refers to: the subject "Marché Monge" (one specific market).
  • Because Marché Monge is a single named entity, the pronoun must be singular.
  • Substitute the pronoun into the sentence: "...making it both a popular shopping destination and an important piece of Paris's history." This reads clearly and agrees in number.
  • The pronoun "it" correctly points back to the one market being described.

Why Each Answer

  • A ("those") — Incorrect. "Those" is a plural pronoun, but the antecedent Marché Monge is singular (Wrong Number / agreement error).
  • B ("it") — Correct. "It" is the singular pronoun that agrees with the singular antecedent Marché Monge.
  • C ("these") — Incorrect. "These" is plural, so it fails pronoun-antecedent agreement with the singular subject (Wrong Number / agreement error).
  • D ("one") — Incorrect. "One" refers vaguely to an unspecified member of a group rather than to a specific named place, so it does not logically refer back to Marché Monge (Wrong Pronoun / unclear reference).

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a blank needs a pronoun, locate the exact noun it replaces and check the number first. A single named thing (even one ending in "s") takes the singular pronoun "it." Mentally re-read the sentence with each choice plugged in; the one that sounds grammatical and points to the right noun is correct.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: When a soil is classified using the International Union of Soil Sciences' system, its similarity to each of the 32 soil reference groups—defined by several criteria—__________ evaluated, one group at a time, until a match is found. The comparisons are made in a specific order; thus, the criteria for kastanozems (soils with highly organic topsoil) are only applied if the soil doesn't match the criteria for planosols.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is D (“is”). This is a Standard English Conventions question testing Form, Structure, and Sense — specifically subject-verb agreement and verb tense. Difficulty: medium.

Core Concepts

  • Subject-verb agreement: A verb must match its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb (“is”), and a plural subject takes a plural verb (“are”).
  • Finding the real subject: The subject is the noun the sentence is actually about. Words inside prepositional phrases (phrases starting with words like “to,” “of,” “for”) are NOT the subject — they just describe it. You can mentally cross them out.
  • Verb tense: The tense must match the time frame established by the surrounding sentences. Here the passage describes a general, ongoing process, so it uses the present tense.
  • Passive voice: “is evaluated” is a passive construction (something is acted upon). The helping verb (“is”) still must agree with the subject in number and tense.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Locate the subject of the blank's clause: “its similarity to each of the 32 soil reference groups ... __________ evaluated.”
  • Strip out the modifiers: “to each of the 32 soil reference groups” and “defined by several criteria” are both describing phrases, not the subject. Remove them and you are left with “its similarity __________ evaluated.”
  • The subject is similarity — singular. So the verb must be singular.
  • Check the tense: the surrounding verbs are present tense (“is classified,” “are made,” “are applied,” “doesn't match”). The blank must also be present tense.
  • A singular, present-tense verb that fits “similarity __________ evaluated” is “is”: “its similarity ... is evaluated.”

Why Each Answer

  • D “is” — Correct: Singular and present tense, matching the singular subject “similarity” and the present-tense context of the passage.
  • A “are” — Subject-Verb Disagreement: “are” is plural. It is likely chosen by mistaking the nearby plural “groups” or “criteria” for the subject, but the true subject “similarity” is singular.
  • B “was” — Wrong Tense: “was” is singular but past tense, which clashes with the present-tense process described throughout the passage.
  • C “have been” — Subject-Verb Disagreement: “have been” is plural (it would pair with a plural subject like “they have been”), so it does not agree with the singular “similarity.”

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a verb question has a long phrase between the subject and the blank, cover up everything between them and read just “subject ... verb.” Here “similarity ... is evaluated” instantly sounds right, while “similarity ... are evaluated” sounds wrong. Then confirm the tense matches the other verbs in the passage.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: In the early 1920s, researchers at the US Geological Survey determined the geographic center of Maine using a simple method. First, they attached a string to the middle point of a cardboard cutout of the state and suspended it in the air. __________ they adjusted the suspension point until the cutout hung perfectly flat. Ultimately, this point was determined to be the center.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is (A) Then,. This is a Transitions question in the Expression of Ideas domain. Difficulty: Easy.

Core Concepts
A transition is a word or phrase that signals the logical relationship between two sentences. To choose one, identify what the sentence before the blank says and what the sentence after the blank says, then pick the transition that names their relationship. Key transition families to know:

  • Sequence / time order (Then, Next, After that): the second event happens after the first in a series of steps.
  • Restatement (In other words, That is): the second sentence repeats the first idea in different words.
  • Contrast / replacement (Instead, However): the second sentence opposes or replaces the first.
  • Ordering a list (First of all, To begin): the sentence is the opening item of a list.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Sentence 1 sets up a method for finding the center of Maine.
  • Sentence 2 begins with the word First and describes step one: they attach a string and suspend the cutout.
  • The blank opens the next sentence, which describes a further action: they adjust the suspension point until the cutout hangs flat.
  • The final sentence begins with Ultimately, signaling the end of the process.
  • Because the text moves First → (blank) → Ultimately, the blank must mark the next step in a time sequence. A sequence transition fits.

Why Each Answer

  • (A) Then, — Correct. It signals the next action in a chronological series, matching the First/Ultimately framework.
  • (B) In other words, — Trap: Restatement. The adjusting step is a new action, not a rewording of attaching the string.
  • (C) Instead, — Trap: Contrast/Replacement. The two steps are not opposites; the second does not replace the first, so contrast is illogical.
  • (D) First of all, — Trap: Wrong list position. The previous sentence already used First, so labeling this step as the first point is contradictory.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a paragraph reads like a recipe and you see signal words like First and Ultimately, the blanks between them almost always call for a plain sequence transition such as Then or Next. Cover the choices, predict the relationship first, then match.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

questions.passage: When the first railroads were built in Australia in the 1800s, a variety of track sizes (gauges) were used across the continent, resulting in what historians call the "railway gauge muddle." The Mornington Railway line in Victoria used broad tracks. __________ the Rockhampton Steam Tramway line in Queensland used narrow tracks.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is B, "By contrast,". This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Transitions skill, at a medium difficulty level. Your job is to choose the transition word or phrase that best captures the logical relationship between the two sentences on either side of the blank.

Core Concepts
A transition is a word or phrase that signals how one idea relates to the idea before it. Different transitions signal different relationships:

  • Contrast (by contrast, however, on the other hand): signals that the second idea is different from or opposes the first.
  • Similarity (similarly, likewise): signals that the second idea is the same kind of thing as the first.
  • Example (for instance, for example): signals that the second idea is a specific case of a general point just made.
  • Summary (in sum, in conclusion): signals that the writer is wrapping up and restating the main point.

The trick is always to read the idea before the blank and the idea after it, then name the relationship between them.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Idea before the blank: The Mornington Railway line in Victoria used broad tracks.
  • Idea after the blank: The Rockhampton Steam Tramway line in Queensland used narrow tracks.
  • Relationship: Broad and narrow are opposites. Two different railway lines are being set against each other to highlight that they used opposite track sizes. This is a textbook contrast.
  • Conclusion: The blank needs a contrast transition, so "By contrast," fits perfectly.

Why Each Answer

  • A, "In sum," (Wrong - Summary trap): This signals a concluding restatement of a point. The sentence after the blank introduces a brand-new fact about a different railway line, not a wrap-up, so it does not fit.
  • B, "By contrast," (Correct): It directly signals that the two railway lines differ - one used broad tracks, the other narrow - which is exactly the relationship in the text.
  • C, "Similarly," (Wrong - Opposite relationship): This signals that two things are alike. But broad and narrow tracks are opposites, so a similarity transition contradicts the logic.
  • D, "For instance," (Wrong - Example trap): This introduces a specific example of a general claim. The second sentence is not an example of the first; it is a separate, contrasting case, so this does not fit.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For transition questions, cover the answer choices, read the sentences before and after the blank, and predict the relationship in your own words (here: "these two are opposites"). Then match your prediction to a choice. Spotting an opposite pair of words like broad vs. narrow is a strong signal that a contrast transition is needed.
questions.question_text: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Snow hydrologist Zoe Wellschlager helps maintain automated snow measurement stations throughout the western United States.
  • They are called SNOTEL sites.
  • There are around 90 sites throughout Wyoming.
  • There is one at Cottonwood Creek.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing Rhetorical Synthesis at an easy difficulty. You are given bullet-point research notes and must choose the sentence that best accomplishes a stated writing goal: emphasizing the number of SNOTEL sites in Wyoming.

Core Concepts
A Rhetorical Synthesis question gives you a set of notes and a specific goal. Your job is not to find the most detailed or most interesting sentence, but the one that does exactly what the goal asks. Two ideas matter here:

  • Emphasize means to make something the main, prominent point of the sentence. The thing being emphasized should be front and center, not buried.
  • The goal is about a number (how many sites). So the winning choice must clearly state a quantity of SNOTEL sites in Wyoming and make that quantity the focus.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1 — Identify the goal: emphasize the number of SNOTEL sites in Wyoming.
  • Step 2 — Find the supporting note: "There are around 90 sites throughout Wyoming." This is the only note that gives a count for Wyoming.
  • Step 3 — Set the test: the correct choice must (a) include that number and (b) make the number the central idea of the sentence.
  • Step 4 — Check each option against that test and keep only the one that states the quantity prominently.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Correct): "In Wyoming alone, there are around 90 SNOTEL sites located throughout the state." The phrase "In Wyoming alone" signals scale, and the sentence immediately delivers the figure "around 90 SNOTEL sites." The quantity is the main claim, so the goal of emphasizing the number is fully met.
  • B (Out of Scope for the goal): "One particular SNOTEL site is located at Cottonwood Creek in Wyoming." This zooms in on a single site. Highlighting one location works against the goal of emphasizing a large total number.
  • C (Wrong Focus): "SNOTEL sites collect snow measurement data throughout the state of Wyoming." This describes what the sites do (their function), not how many there are. The number 90 never appears, so the goal is not addressed.
  • D (Wrong Focus): "Snow hydrologist Zoe Wellschlager helps maintain SNOTEL sites, such as the one at Cottonwood Creek, Wyoming." This shifts attention to a person and a single example site. The total count is absent, so it fails the goal.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "emphasize the number/amount" goals, scan the choices for the one that actually states a quantity and puts it up front. Any choice that talks about a person, a function, or a single example is almost always a trap. Match the choice to the exact word in the goal ("number") and ignore choices that are merely true but off-target.
questions.question_text: The student wants to emphasize the number of SNOTEL sites in Wyoming. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

question_options.option_text: In Wyoming alone, there are around 90 SNOTEL sites located throughout the state.
One particular SNOTEL site is located at Cottonwood Creek in Wyoming.
Snow hydrologist Zoe Wellschlager helps maintain SNOTEL sites, such as the one at Cottonwood Creek, Wyoming.
SNOTEL sites collect snow measurement data throughout the state of Wyoming.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Wind is a renewable energy source.
  • A wind farm uses turbines to convert wind into electrical power.
  • A wind farm's maximum electrical output is called its nameplate capacity.
  • Hornsdale Wind Farm is located in Hornsdale, Australia.
  • Its nameplate capacity is 316 megawatts.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the skill of Rhetorical Synthesis, rated easy. Your job is to pick the sentence that best uses the notes to emphasize the location of Hornsdale Wind Farm.

Core Concepts
Rhetorical Synthesis questions give you a bulleted set of research notes plus a specific writing goal. The right answer is the one that accomplishes that exact goal, even if the other choices are factually true.

  • Match the goal, not the truth: Every choice may be a true statement drawn from the notes, but only one serves the stated purpose. Here the purpose is to emphasize where the wind farm is.
  • Emphasis through sentence structure: A detail is emphasized when it is placed in the grammatical subject (the front, focal position) of the sentence. To stress location, the location should be what the sentence is about.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Identify the goal keyword: location. The relevant note is "Hornsdale Wind Farm is located in Hornsdale, Australia."
  • Scan each choice and ask: Does this sentence foreground the place?
  • Choice C, "Hornsdale, Australia, is home to Hornsdale Wind Farm," places the location as the subject of the sentence, making the farm's location its central point.
  • The other three choices each discuss capacity, definitions, or how turbines work, none of which addresses location.

Why Each Answer

  • A (Out of Scope for the goal): "Hornsdale Wind Farm has a nameplate capacity of 316 megawatts" is true, but it emphasizes electrical output, not location.
  • B (Out of Scope for the goal): "Nameplate capacity is another name for a wind farm's maximum electrical output" only defines a technical term and never mentions a place.
  • C (Correct): It makes "Hornsdale, Australia" the subject, directly emphasizing the location of the wind farm exactly as the goal requires.
  • D (Out of Scope for the goal): "Turbines can be used to generate electricity from a renewable energy source: the wind" explains how wind power works in general and never references Hornsdale or its location.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For synthesis questions, circle the goal word in the stem (here, "location") before reading the choices. Then eliminate any choice that does not put that idea front and center, even if it is a true fact from the notes. The answer is the one whose subject matches the goal.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Wayang Windu geothermal power plant in Indonesia uses a flash steam system to generate electricity.
  • Flash steam technology requires geothermal reservoir temperatures above \(180^{\circ}C\).
  • The use of flash steam systems worldwide is limited because many geothermal reservoirs aren't hot enough.
  • The Raft River geothermal power plant in Idaho uses a binary cycle system.
  • Binary cycle technology can generate energy from lower-temperature (less than \(180^{\circ}C\)) geothermal reservoirs.
  • Binary cycle systems involve higher maintenance costs than flash steam systems.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is C. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the skill of Rhetorical Synthesis, rated hard. The task is to choose the sentence that best uses the notes to compare the disadvantages of the two geothermal systems.

Core Concepts
A Rhetorical Synthesis question gives you a goal and a set of bullet-point notes. Your only job is to pick the answer that fulfills the stated goal using accurate information from the notes. Key vocabulary:

  • Disadvantage means a drawback, weakness, or limitation of something.
  • Compare here means to address a feature of both things side by side. To compare the disadvantages of two systems, the answer must state a disadvantage of each system, not just one.

From the notes, the disadvantage of each system is:

  • Wayang Windu (flash steam): it requires geothermal reservoirs hotter than \(180^{\circ}C\), and many reservoirs worldwide are not that hot, so the technology is limited.
  • Raft River (binary cycle): it involves higher maintenance costs than flash steam.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • Step 1: Identify the goal precisely. We need ONE sentence that names a disadvantage of the Wayang Windu system AND a disadvantage of the Raft River system.
  • Step 2: From the notes, Wayang Windu's drawback is its high-temperature requirement (\(>180^{\circ}C\)). Raft River's drawback is higher maintenance cost.
  • Step 3: Test each choice for whether it names both drawbacks.
  • Step 4: Choice C says the Raft River system "overcomes the temperature limitations of the Wayang Windu plant's system" (this references Wayang Windu's disadvantage) "but is more costly to maintain" (this is Raft River's disadvantage). Both disadvantages appear, so C accomplishes the goal.

Why Each Answer

  • C (Correct): It pairs both drawbacks in one comparison: Wayang Windu's temperature limitation and Raft River's higher maintenance cost. This is exactly what "compare the disadvantages" requires.
  • A (Incomplete Comparison): It states only Raft River's disadvantage (cost) and gives no disadvantage for the Wayang Windu system, so it fails to compare the disadvantages of both.
  • B (Incomplete Comparison): It states only Wayang Windu's disadvantage (the need for less common high-temperature reservoirs) and says nothing about a disadvantage of the Raft River system.
  • D (Off-Goal / Neutral Contrast): It contrasts the operating temperatures of the two systems but presents them as neutral facts, not as disadvantages. Raft River's ability to run at lower temperatures is actually an advantage, and the sentence never mentions Raft River's maintenance-cost drawback.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
When a synthesis goal asks you to compare a specific feature (here, disadvantages) of two things, treat it as a checklist: the right answer must hit that feature for both items. Quickly eliminate any choice that only covers one item (A and B) or that describes a different feature like a neutral temperature contrast (D).

The system at the Wayang Windu plant requires temperatures above \(180^{\circ}C\) while the system at the Raft River plant can operate at lower temperatures.
Unlike the Raft River plant, the Wayang Windu plant uses a flash steam system, which requires a less common resource: geothermal reservoirs with temperatures above \(180^{\circ}C\).

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • ArcelorMittal Orbit is an artwork by Sir Anish Kapoor and Cecil Balmond.
  • It is a 375-foot steel tower with a spiraling staircase and working slide.
  • It is on display in a public park in London, England.
  • Čumil the Sewer Worker is a work of art by Viktor Hulík.
  • It is a bronze sculpture of a man emerging from under a manhole cover.
  • It is on display on a public street in Bratislava, Slovakia.
questions.explanation:
Question Snapshot
The correct answer is A. This is an Expression of Ideas question testing the Rhetorical Synthesis skill (difficulty: medium). The task: use the research notes to write a sentence that emphasizes a similarity between ArcelorMittal Orbit and Čumil the Sewer Worker.

Core Concepts
Rhetorical Synthesis questions give you a bulleted list of notes and a specific rhetorical goal. Your job is to pick the choice that (1) actually matches the stated goal and (2) is fully supported by the notes. For a goal that asks to emphasize a similarity, the right answer must name a trait that BOTH subjects share. Watch out for choices that instead point out a difference, that describe only ONE subject, or that misreport a fact from the notes.

Step-by-Step Breakdown

  • List what the notes say about each work. ArcelorMittal Orbit: artwork by Kapoor and Balmond; a 375-foot steel tower; on display in a public park in London.
  • Čumil the Sewer Worker: a work by Viktor Hulík; a bronze sculpture; on display on a public street in Bratislava.
  • Hunt for an overlap. The creators differ, the materials and forms differ, and the cities differ. The one shared trait is that each is on display in a public location (a public park and a public street).
  • The correct sentence must state that shared trait plainly. That is exactly choice A.

Why Each Answer

  • A (correct): "Both on display at public locations" captures the genuine overlap drawn from "public park" and "public street." It mentions both works and states a true similarity, satisfying the goal.
  • B — Wrong Goal (states a difference): It stresses that the Orbit, but NOT Čumil, is in London. That highlights a contrast, not a similarity, so it fails the goal.
  • C — Factually Inaccurate: It claims both works were created by Kapoor and Balmond. The notes credit Čumil to Viktor Hulík, so this misstates the facts.
  • D — Describes Only One Subject: It gives details about Čumil alone. With nothing said about the Orbit, no similarity is established, so the goal is not met.

Pro-Tip & Takeaway
For "emphasize a similarity" goals, scan the notes for the single feature that appears for BOTH subjects, then eliminate any choice that mentions only one subject, points out a difference, or changes a fact. The survivor is your answer.
